cards.question: A family stacks wood at the beach before lighting it. Can that fuel already be called buka?
cards.incorrectHint: Buka also names firewood.
cards.answer: Yes. Buka can refer to the fuel before it burns; context also allows a fire sense.

cards.question: The flames are rising and more wood is added. Which form makes the burning state clearer?
cards.incorrectHint: The longer recorded word is the more specific live-fire label.
cards.answer: Bukawaqa. A Fiji Bible Week text distinguishes a burning bukawaqa from the buka added to feed it.

cards.question: If the fire goes out but a pile of fuel remains, has every bit of buka vanished?
options: Yes, buka can only mean flames
cards.incorrectHint: The shorter word has a fuel sense too.
cards.answer: No. Buka can still be the unburnt wood. Bukawaqa names the fire in action; the distinction helps you follow what is happening in the scene.

link.label: Read a Fijian account of a beach fire

bukawaqa.title: Wood ready to burn, or fire burning?
bukawaqa.intro: Buka can name firewood or fire. Bukawaqa points more specifically to a fire that is actively burning.

cards.question: A family stacks wood at the beach before lighting it. Can that fuel already be called buka?
cards.incorrectHint: Buka also names firewood.
cards.answer: Yes. Buka can refer to the fuel before it burns; context also allows a fire sense.

cards.question: The flames are rising and more wood is added. Which form makes the burning state clearer?
cards.incorrectHint: The longer recorded word is the more specific live-fire label.
cards.answer: Bukawaqa. A Fiji Bible Week text distinguishes a burning bukawaqa from the buka added to feed it.

cards.question: If the fire goes out but a pile of fuel remains, has every bit of buka vanished?
options: Yes, buka can only mean flames
cards.incorrectHint: The shorter word has a fuel sense too.
cards.answer: No. Buka can still be the unburnt wood. Bukawaqa names the fire in action; the distinction helps you follow what is happening in the scene.

link.label: Read a Fijian account of a beach fire

bulabula.title: Healthy, flourishing, or a species name?
bulabula.intro: Bulabula can describe health or flourishing. It also appears in the scientific name of one Fijian banded iguana.

cards.question: In a discussion of people's wellbeing, what does bulabula contribute to this expression?
cards.incorrectHint: The topic is people's health.
cards.answer: Tiko bulabula is used for living in good health. Bula is related to life and health, but bulabula in this phrase describes a healthy condition.

cards.question: If bulabula is part of this iguana's scientific name, does it prove that every individual iguana is healthy?
options: No, it is a species name
Yes, the name diagnoses each animal
cards.correct: No, it is a species name
cards.incorrectHint: A scientific name identifies a kind of animal, not its medical condition.
cards.answer: No. Researchers chose bulabula as the name of a Fijian banded-iguana lineage. The familiar word travels into science, but the species name is not a health report on every animal.

link.label: Read the research that named the iguana

qito.title: Playing, or the game itself?
qito.intro: Qito can refer to play and to a game or sport. The surrounding words reveal which use is meant.

cards.question: In a Fiji sports report, which sport does rakavi specify after qito?
cards.incorrectHint: Rakavi narrows the kind of sport.
cards.answer: Rugby. Qito is the broader play or sport word; rakavi tells you which game the report concerns.

cards.question: When a coach urges players to perform well, does qito here name a game as an object or what the players do?
cards.incorrectHint: The coach is telling the team how to act.
cards.answer: What they do: play. The Fiji Times uses me ratou na qito in advice to players, while na qito in a sports report can name the game itself.

link.label: Read qito in Fiji rugby reporting

dua.title: One, then one more than ten
dua.intro: Dua counts one. In a longer number, it can contribute the extra one after ten.

cards.question: How many fish does this recorded counting phrase indicate?
cards.incorrectHint: Dua is the number one.
cards.answer: One fish. The phrase shows the number with na and ika, rather than leaving dua as a word on a number chart.

cards.question: If tini is ten, what does the added dua make in this recorded number?
cards.incorrectHint: Start at ten and add one.
cards.answer: Eleven. The longer expression retains dua's one while ka joins it to ten.

link.label: See Fijian number examples

rua.title: Counting two and referring to two
rua.intro: Rua counts two things. Rau is a pronoun meaning 'the two of them'; one word does not simply replace the other.

cards.question: Which word gives the number of fish in this phrase?
cards.incorrectHint: Ika tells you what is being counted.
cards.answer: Rua gives the count: two fish. Ika names the fish, and na introduces it in the counting phrase.

cards.question: A story says 'the two of them' and no longer counts fish. Which form refers to the people?
cards.incorrectHint: Rua is the numeral; the pronoun has a different order of vowels.
cards.answer: Rau. The swapped vowels matter: rua is the number two, while rau points to two people already in the story.

link.label: See e rua na ika in a Fijian phrase guide

tolu.title: A count of three and a group of 'we'
tolu.intro: Tolu is three. Keitou is a pronoun for a small 'we' that excludes the listener; counting and including people are separate decisions.

cards.question: In the sequence dua, rua, tolu, what count does tolu complete?
cards.incorrectHint: It follows two.
cards.answer: Three. Te Papa's Fijian number activity lists tolu as the third count.

cards.question: Three friends tell you 'we went', but you stayed behind. Which pronoun makes their membership clear?
cards.incorrectHint: Kedatou includes the listener.
cards.answer: Keitou for a small group that excludes you. Tolu counts exactly three; keitou marks a small speaker group and whether you are in it, rather than functioning as the numeral itself.

link.label: Try Te Papa's Fijian counting activity

tini.title: Ten on its own and inside a number
tini.intro: Tini counts ten. Another ten element, sagavulu, appears in longer numbers rather than replacing tini in every position.

cards.question: At the end of counting from dua upward, which word is ten by itself?
cards.incorrectHint: Rua is only two.
cards.answer: Tini is ten. The distinct form matters before you learn numbers built beyond ten.

cards.question: In the recorded form for twenty, which piece signals two tens?
cards.incorrectHint: Tini ka dua is eleven.
cards.answer: Rua with sagavulu makes twenty. Tini is ten on its own, while sagavulu is used within this larger number.

link.label: Read a Fijian numeral list

sucu.title: Born, birthday, or Christmas?
sucu.intro: Sucu means to be born. Siga ni sucu adds a day, and context determines whether it means a person's birthday or Christmas Day.

cards.question: A form asks for your personal date of birth. Which meaning of this phrase fits?
cards.incorrectHint: The form asks about your own birth.
cards.answer: Your birthday or date of birth. A Fiji government form asks for a person's siga ni sucu alongside their name and contact details.

cards.question: A newspaper writes about celebrations in late December. Could the same words now point to Christmas?
cards.incorrectHint: Look at the calendar and public setting.
cards.answer: Yes. Siga ni Sucu can refer to Christmas Day in that context. The shared sucu idea is birth, but the occasion must be read from the whole setting.

link.label: See siga ni sucu on a Fiji government form

taubale.title: A few steps or a long walk?
taubale.intro: Taubale is travel on foot. The distance and destination come from the rest of the account.

cards.question: In an account of a parked car, did Saiasi drive away or move out on his feet?
cards.incorrectHint: The vehicle had already stopped.
cards.answer: He walked out. Taubale names the walking, while yani ki tuba gives the direction in this recorded account.

cards.word: taubaletaka kina sivia e dua na drau tolusagavulu vakacaca na maile
cards.question: What makes the second recorded walk much more than a few steps?
cards.incorrectHint: Look at the quantity following the walking form.
cards.answer: The distance. In this historical account, the walk exceeded 130 miles. The longer form and distance show how much ground was covered; do not assume taubale itself means a long journey.

link.label: Read the account of a long walk in Fiji

bula.title: A greeting with life in it
bula.intro: Bula is heard as a greeting, but its meanings also touch on life and health. The situation decides which one is foremost.

cards.question: When someone welcomes a visitor with Bula!, is a medical diagnosis being made?
options: Yes, it confirms the visitor is healthy
cards.incorrectHint: The encounter is a welcome.
cards.answer: No. It greets the visitor, while carrying a wish associated with life and good health. Fiji's tourism guide records both layers.

cards.question: A conversation turns from greeting to a person's continuing wellbeing. Which related word especially describes being healthy?
cards.incorrectHint: Pae names a pie.
cards.answer: Bulabula can describe a healthy state. Bula is also a greeting and can mean life; the repeated form is useful in a health phrase such as tiko bulabula.

link.label: See Tourism Fiji's explanation of bula

vava.title: Carrying on a back, or wearing on feet?
vava.intro: Vava is recorded for carrying a person on one's back. Ivava is a different whole word for footwear.

cards.question: A baby is carried against an adult's back. Which meaning of vava fits?
options: Carry a person on the back
cards.correct: Carry a person on the back
cards.incorrectHint: The person being carried is on the back.
cards.answer: To carry a person on the back, especially a child in the recorded description.

cards.question: A school list asks children to bring ivava. Does that mean they should carry someone on their backs?
options: Yes, it is the same action
cards.incorrectHint: The added i- belongs to another recorded whole word.
cards.answer: No. Ivava refers to shoes or footwear; vava here is the carrying action. Their similar shape is a clue to inspect, not a licence to guess that they mean the same thing.

link.label: See vava in a Pacific comparative wordlist

biau.title: What moves beyond the reef?
biau.intro: Biau names a wave; cakau names the reef. A wave may break near a reef, but the two words name different things.

cards.question: In a Fiji Times description of white foam behind the reef, what is producing the foam?
cards.incorrectHint: Biau is the moving water.
cards.answer: The waves. Vuso ni biau evokes their foam; the phrase gives biau a visible coastal scene.

cards.question: Which word names the fixed reef, rather than the water breaking near it?
cards.incorrectHint: Biau moves across the water.
cards.answer: Cakau is the reef. Biau is the wave. A navigator may have to watch both, but knowing one does not tell you the other's meaning.

link.label: Read the coastal description in the Fiji Times

duru.title: Find the supporting pieces
duru.intro: A duru works alongside a yavu inside a phrase; its position and job matter.

cards.question: In Au sa lako, which pieces support the base lako?
cards.answer: Au identifies the speaker and sa marks time or aspect; lako is the yavu they accompany.

cards.question: Must every duru come before the base?
cards.answer: No. A durumuri such as mai can follow lako. Duruliu and durumuri name different positions.

duruliu.title: Before the base
duruliu.intro: Duruliu names the supporting position before a predicate's yavu.

cards.question: In Au sa lako, where are au and sa relative to lako?
cards.answer: They are duruliu in this phrase. Their separate jobs are not erased by their shared position.

cards.question: In Au sa lako mai, is mai another duruliu?
cards.answer: Mai follows the base, so examine it as a durumuri rather than moving it into the earlier slot.

durumuri.title: After the base
durumuri.intro: A durumuri follows the main base and can add direction or another nuance.

cards.question: Which word follows lako in Au sa lako mai?
cards.answer: Mai comes after the base and adds direction. Sa precedes the base.

cards.question: In Oni bula vinaka sara, which final word comes after vinaka?
cards.answer: The analyzed phrase places sara after vinaka as a following duru; Oni refers to the addressee.

durusau.title: Who is doing it?
durusau.intro: Durusau points to the participant by person and number within a matavu.

cards.question: In Au sa lako, which word points to the speaker?
cards.answer: Au is durusau in this matavu. Lako supplies the predicate base.

cards.question: In Era lade e na marau, does Era point to one speaker or a group?
cards.answer: Era points to several people in this phrase. Compare au in Au sa lako before choosing the actor marker.

dewa.title: What changes on the predicate?
dewa.intro: A dewa is an attached ending on certain predicate bases; the affected participant helps choose the form.

cards.question: Which form stands before the personal name Jo: raici or raica?
cards.answer: Au raici Jo tiko has -i with the personal name immediately after the predicate. The whole phrase determines the choice.

cards.question: Which form occurs in Au raica tiko na gone?
cards.answer: Raica appears with na gone in the contrast. Do not swap the endings from English object order alone.

isema.title: What joins the phrase?
isema.intro: An isema connects a clause or predicate phrase to another part of a sentence.

cards.question: In me da tekivu, which opening is the connector?
cards.answer: Me connects the clause; da refers to the inclusive group. Their jobs differ although both stand before tekivu.

cards.question: In se ra sa yaco mai, which word introduces the connected clause?
cards.answer: Se is the connector. Ra refers to the participants; its shorter shape after se follows a durusau pattern.

mata.title: Open the noun phrase
mata.intro: A mata introduces the whole matanauni; it is not an attached beginning of the noun.

cards.question: In na vale, which piece introduces the phrase?
cards.answer: Na is the mata; vale is the nominal base. Together they form a matanauni.

cards.question: Would you expect the same mata before a personal name such as Mere?
cards.answer: The pattern uses o Mere. The marker changes with the kind of phrase; na is not a universal translation of 'the'.

matanauni.title: A word or a whole phrase?
matanauni.intro: Matanauni names the whole nominal phrase, which may refer to a person, place, thing, or time.

cards.question: In na vale, is the matanauni vale alone or na vale together?
cards.answer: The whole na vale is the matanauni. Vale is its yavu.

cards.question: Can a matanauni lack na, as in kei Jone?
cards.answer: Kei Jone is a matanauni toka built around a personal name. Do not require na in every nominal phrase.

matavu.title: Read the predicate phrase
matavu.intro: A matavu gathers a predicate base and its relevant supporting pieces.

cards.question: Which group is a matavu: Au sa lako mai or na vale?
cards.answer: Au sa lako mai expresses going with its speaker and direction. Na vale is a nominal phrase.

cards.question: In Oni bula vinaka sara, is bula the yavu of a predicate phrase here?
cards.answer: Bula is the base of this matavu. In na nona bula taucoko, the same form has a nominal use; the phrase decides.

nauni.title: Find the nominal base
nauni.intro: Nauni points to the base, not automatically to the whole phrase around it.

cards.question: In na vale, which part names the building?
cards.answer: Vale is the nauni base; na introduces the whole phrase.

cards.question: Does calling vale a nauni also make na vale a single word?
cards.answer: Na vale is a matanauni with more than one piece. Keep the word's role and the phrase's role separate.

vu.title: Follow the predicate base
vu.intro: A vu carries the central predicate meaning in a matavu; one form can have another role elsewhere.

cards.question: In Au sa lako, which word carries the going?
cards.answer: Lako is the predicate base; sa is a time or aspect marker before it.

cards.question: Does bula keep a vu role in na nona bula taucoko?
cards.answer: There bula has a nominal use meaning life. In Oni bula vinaka sara it is a vu. Read the phrase before labeling the word.

iyatuvosa matanauni.title: A sentence of nominal phrases
iyatuvosa matanauni.intro: Fijian can put nominal phrases together without an overt predicate word.

cards.question: In [o yau] [na vunivai], must a word for English 'is' be inserted?
cards.answer: The nominal-sentence pattern places two nominal phrases side by side; English may translate the relation with 'is'.

cards.question: What does [nikua] [na soqo] show about a time expression?
options: It can be one nominal phrase in the sentence
It must be a predicate verb
cards.correct: It can be one nominal phrase in the sentence
cards.answer: Nikua stands as a time phrase beside na soqo in the nominal sentence.

matanauni raraba.title: Notice the na
matanauni raraba.intro: MNR is the nominal-phrase type that includes na in its marker pattern.

cards.question: Which phrase fits MNR: na vale or kei Jone?
cards.answer: Na vale has na. Kei Jone belongs to a na-less matanauni pattern.

cards.question: Can an MNR have another marker before na, as in e na marau?
cards.answer: The analysis has both e and na before marau. The presence of na still matters to the MNR classification.

matanauni toka.title: A nominal phrase without na
matanauni toka.intro: MNT groups nominal phrases whose structure does not use na; inspect what comes after their marker.

cards.question: Why can kei Jone count as MNT?
cards.answer: Kei Jone is a na-less phrase built around a person's name; its narrower type is MNY.

cards.question: Is vei koya also a na-less matanauni even though it points to a pronoun?
cards.answer: Vei koya is an MNT with a pronoun. Its more specific type is matanauni sosomi.

matanauni yatuvosa.title: A whole clause in a nominal role
matanauni yatuvosa.intro: MNYt is a clause that fills a nominal-phrase position; it is not merely a clause describing one noun.

cards.question: In a pattern such as ni via kana, what can the whole ni-clause do?
cards.answer: The analysis treats the whole clause as one nominal unit when a suitable predicate takes it.

cards.question: Does the clause after kaloko in na kaloko [au a solia vei iko enanoa] have that same whole-phrase role?
cards.answer: That bracketed clause is kilanauni yatuvosa: it describes kaloko. MNYt instead occupies the nominal slot itself.

matanauni gauna.title: Time as a whole phrase
matanauni gauna.intro: MNG can place a time expression where a nominal phrase belongs without adding na.

cards.question: Which form can stand as an MNG meaning today?
cards.answer: Nikua is a whole time expression in the nominal-sentence pattern.

cards.question: Is na siga qo the same no-na pattern as nikua?
cards.answer: Na siga qo contains na and a nominal base. Compare its structure with standalone nikua before assigning the MNG label.

matanauni yaca.title: A person's name in the phrase
matanauni yaca.intro: MNY is the na-less nominal-phrase type built around a personal name.

cards.question: Which part makes kei Jone a name phrase?
cards.answer: Jone is the personal name; kei introduces the phrase in this pattern.

cards.question: Would i Viti be MNY merely because Viti has a capital letter?
cards.answer: Viti names a place, so inspect matanauni yacanivanua rather than the personal-name type.

matanauni sosomi.title: A pronoun in the whole phrase
matanauni sosomi.intro: MNS names a marked phrase built around a nauni sosomi; it does not label the pronoun alone.

cards.question: In o yau, which is the whole MNS?
cards.answer: O is the marker and yau the pronoun. Together they make the phrase being classified.

cards.question: Does kei Jone become MNS because it also starts with a marker?
cards.answer: Jone is a personal name, so kei Jone belongs to MNY. The type depends on the base as well as the marker.

matanauni yacanivanua.title: A place name in the phrase
matanauni yacanivanua.intro: MNYV is a na-less nominal phrase built around the name of a place.

cards.question: In i Viti, what makes the phrase a place-name type?
cards.answer: I Viti contains the place name Viti after its marker.

cards.question: Would i tuba also be MNYV?
cards.answer: I tuba gives a location without naming a particular place; compare matanauni vanua.

matanauni vanua.title: Where, but not which named place?
matanauni vanua.intro: MNV locates or directs without building the phrase around a place name.

cards.question: Which expression gives a location without a proper place name: e ke or i Viti?
cards.answer: E ke points to a location. I Viti names a particular place and belongs to MNYV.

cards.question: In i tuba, is tuba functioning as a place name such as Lautoka?
cards.answer: I tuba locates something outside without naming a particular town or village.

matanauni sema.title: Two nominal phrases, one role
matanauni sema.intro: A sema links or places nominal phrases together so they serve one part of the sentence.

cards.question: If two phrases refer to different things, which connection should you inspect?
cards.answer: Sosoqoni groups different referents. Check whether the phrase uses kei, se, or no spoken linker in its context.

cards.question: If two phrases identify the same person, which connection should you inspect?
cards.answer: Veitokoni places two descriptions of one referent side by side in the pattern.

sosoqoni.title: Different people or things together
sosoqoni.intro: Sosoqoni joins nominal expressions for distinct referents in one sentence role.

cards.question: If na sabutu and na kawago name two different things, which relation fits?
cards.answer: Different referents are grouped in sosoqoni. Veitokoni is for descriptions of the same referent.

cards.question: Does every sosoqoni require an audible kei?
cards.answer: The patterns can use kei, se, or no spoken link. Their meanings are not interchangeable; read the whole sentence.

veitokoni.title: Two descriptions, one person
veitokoni.intro: Veitokoni puts nominal phrases for the same referent side by side.

cards.question: In na turaga na rātū, do the two phrases identify one person or two?
cards.answer: The contrast uses the second phrase to identify the same person further.

cards.question: Would inserting kei preserve that same side-by-side identification pattern?
cards.answer: The veitokoni pattern has no kei. Kei can instead link distinct referents in sosoqoni.

kilanauni dusi.title: Point to the one you mean
kilanauni dusi.intro: A kilanauni dusi follows a nominal base and identifies which one is meant.

cards.question: In na siga qo, which word points to this day?
cards.answer: Qo follows siga and narrows which day the phrase names.

cards.question: Is standalone oqori in Kauta mai oqori serving that same after-the-base role?
cards.answer: Oqori stands as a whole pointing phrase there; qo after siga qualifies a base. The position changes the analysis.

kilanauni nauni.title: Which kind of thing?
kilanauni nauni.intro: A nauni base can qualify another nominal base inside one phrase.

cards.question: In na kali vesi levu qori, which word tells what kind of kali?
cards.answer: Vesi qualifies kali with a material or kind; qori points to the item.

cards.question: Which word in that phrase tells size rather than material?
cards.answer: Levu is a kilanauni vu in this analysis. Vesi supplies the nauni-based qualifier.

kilanauni vu.title: Add a property to the noun
kilanauni vu.intro: A vu base can qualify a nominal base without becoming the head of the phrase.

cards.question: In na kali vesi levu qori, which word tells you the kali is large?
cards.answer: Levu supplies the size description after the base and nauni-based qualifier.

cards.question: In na vale levu, has levu replaced vale as the main nominal base?
cards.answer: Vale remains the base; levu qualifies it. Compare the unqualified na vale.

kilanauni.title: What describes the nominal base?
kilanauni.intro: Kilanauni is the wider family of qualifiers inside a matanauni.

cards.question: In na kali vesi levu qori, is kali itself the kilanauni?
cards.answer: Kali is the nominal base. Vesi, levu, and qori give different kinds of added information after it.

cards.question: Does the pointing word qori have the same subtype as size word levu?
cards.answer: Qori is a kilanauni dusi; levu is a kilanauni vu. Both qualify the base, but they do different jobs.

matanauni dusi.title: Can the pointing form stand alone?
matanauni dusi.intro: MND lets a pointing form fill the whole nominal phrase rather than merely describe a noun.

cards.question: In Kauta mai oqori, is oqori standing as the whole pointing phrase?
cards.answer: Oqori supplies the whole nominal expression in this example.

cards.question: In na siga qo, does qo fill the whole nominal-phrase role by itself?
cards.answer: Qo follows siga to point out which day; here it is a kilanauni dusi, not a standalone MND.

nauni sosomi.title: A pronoun as the base
nauni sosomi.intro: The nauni sosomi chart lists independent pronouns by person, group size, and listener inclusion.

cards.question: In o yau, is yau the pronoun or the marker?
cards.answer: Yau is the independent pronoun; o introduces the whole matanauni sosomi.

cards.question: If 'we two' includes the listener, does the chart choose kedaru or keirau?
cards.answer: Kedaru includes the listener. Keirau names two people while leaving the listener out.

drua.title: Spot the repeated piece
drua.intro: Drua names repetition in a word, but a repeated-looking shape needs a checked base and meaning.

cards.question: Which part repeats in the word ilakolako?
cards.answer: Ilakolako shows i- together with repeated lako. Its meaning is a journey; repetition alone would not tell you that meaning.

cards.question: Can every doubled-looking word be analyzed safely by repeating an imagined base?
cards.answer: No. First find the actual base, repeated span, and use. Drua is a pattern to investigate, not a licence to invent a word.

durugauna.title: Now or later?
durugauna.intro: Durugauna helps place a predicate in time or aspect; read the whole phrase to see its force.

cards.question: In Au sa lako, which word adds current relevance to going?
cards.answer: Sa is the durugauna in this phrase. Au points to the speaker.

cards.question: If Au na lako points ahead, would replacing na with sa leave the same time reading?
cards.answer: Na points ahead in that comparison; sa presents the going differently. Both belong beside the predicate, but they are not interchangeable.

ikurau.title: A word set apart
ikurau.intro: Ikurau can stand as an expressive call rather than filling a slot inside an ordinary phrase.

cards.question: Does Isa! need a nauni after it to be an expressive call?
cards.answer: Isa! can stand as its own exclamation; its feeling depends on the situation.

cards.question: Is Sobo! doing the same job as au in Au sa lako?
cards.answer: Sobo! is an expressive form. Au serves as durusau within the predicate phrase.

ikuriliu.title: Attached before the base
ikuriliu.intro: Ikuriliu is an addition to a word, unlike a separate mata opening a phrase.

cards.question: In ilakolako, is i- attached to the word or a separate na before it?
cards.answer: The word joins i- with the repeated base lako. Na in na vale is a different, phrase-level marker.

cards.question: In veivosaki, which beginning invites a word-building analysis?
cards.answer: Vei- is attached in this form. Check what the complete derived word means before generalizing from the prefix.

ikurimuri.title: Attached after the base
ikurimuri.intro: Ikurimuri follows a word base; the ending's job must be checked in that word and phrase.

cards.question: In batiqu, is -qu attached to bati or a separate mata?
cards.answer: The possessor ending -qu is attached to bati. A phrase can still need its own mata, as in na batiqu.

cards.question: Can you identify a dewa just by seeing a final -i on any word?
cards.answer: No. Compare a complete pair such as raica and raici and the participant that follows it.

kilavu.title: What narrows the action?
kilavu.intro: Kilavu qualifies the predicate inside a matavu; its base can come from different word families.

cards.question: In Oni bula vinaka sara, which word qualifies bula?
cards.answer: Vinaka adds a quality to the predicate base bula; this is a kilavu vu use.

cards.question: In au gunu yaqona tiko, is yaqona an affected object or a noun-based qualifier in the analysis?
cards.answer: Yaqona narrows the drinking event as kilavu nauni here. Do not assign its role from the English translation alone.

matavosa.title: What kind of phrase is it?
matavosa.intro: A matavosa has a meaning-bearing yavu and any supporting pieces it needs.

cards.question: What is the yavu in na vale?
cards.answer: Vale carries the building meaning; na opens the matanauni.

cards.question: Can Au sa lako also be analyzed as a matavosa?
cards.answer: Yes. Its base is lako and its supporting pieces include au and sa; the phrase is a matavu.

qali.title: Who or what is affected?
qali.intro: Qali names the affected participant as a meaning role; it is not the label for every nominal phrase after a predicate.

cards.question: In Au raici Jo tiko, who is affected by the seeing?
cards.answer: Jo is the affected person. Au identifies the one doing the seeing.

cards.question: Does na gone in Au raica tiko na gone have to be inside the same narrow matavu slot as Jo?
cards.answer: Jo is nauni qali within the matavu, while na gone is a separate matanauni raraba. Both can name someone affected.

sau.title: Follow the actor
sau.intro: Sau identifies the actor-like participant in the event, separately from a word's position.

cards.question: In Au raica na gone, which participant does the seeing?
cards.answer: Au is the actor-like participant here. Na gone names the one seen.

cards.question: In the cici / ciciva contrast, does the runner cease to be the actor when the longer form is used?
cards.answer: The same runner remains the sau in that contrast. Compare this with sogo / sogota, where a participant's role shifts.

nauni raraba.title: A common nominal base
nauni raraba.intro: Nauni raraba names a general kind of thing, unlike a personal name; the whole phrase has another label.

cards.question: In na vale, is vale the common nominal base or the phrase marker?
cards.answer: Vale names a type of building; na is its marker in this phrase.

cards.question: Is Mere in o Mere a nauni raraba just because it fills a nominal phrase?
cards.answer: Mere is a personal name. The distinction is between kinds of base, not between whole phrases and isolated words.

mata ni wiliwili.title: Open the number
mata ni wiliwili.intro: A counted phrase may have a marker for its number and another marker for its nominal base.

cards.question: In E rua na toa, which word introduces the quantity rua?
cards.answer: E is the mata ni wiliwili here; na introduces toa as the nominal base.

cards.question: In kei na dua na yalewa, are both occurrences of na doing exactly the same job?
cards.answer: The first na introduces the quantity; the second na introduces the nominal base yalewa.

taukeni sosomi.title: When the owner is understood
taukeni sosomi.intro: The possessor can be expressed by a form before the nominal base instead of a named person after it.

cards.question: In na noqu vale, is the owner named as Luke is in na vale nei Luke?
cards.answer: Noqu points to the speaker without naming an owner. Nei Luke supplies a name after vale.

cards.question: In noqu, which piece identifies the person?
cards.answer: The attached -qu identifies the speaker; no- helps mark the kind of possessive relation.

ikuri taukeni.title: Choose the relationship
ikuri taukeni.intro: The first element of a preposed possessive form helps show how the possessor is related to what follows.

cards.question: In noqu vale, which piece comes before the person ending -qu?
cards.answer: No- is the ikuri taukeni of noqu. Vale remains the thing named.

cards.question: Would the relationship marker before tea in memudou ti be no- simply because it has an owner?
cards.answer: The drinking-related form uses me-. The kind of relationship matters as well as who is involved.

ikuri sosomi.title: Who is connected?
ikuri sosomi.intro: The attached person-and-number piece of a possessive form is different from a free pronoun.

cards.question: In noqu, which attached piece means 'my'?
cards.answer: The -qu ending points to the speaker. The no- piece gives the possessive relation.

cards.question: Does -itou in neitou include the listener just because tou can be an inclusive short form elsewhere?
cards.answer: Neitou is exclusive; the attached -itou must be read in its own word, not confused with separate tou.

kilavu nauni.title: A noun that narrows the action
kilavu nauni.intro: A nauni can follow a predicate to say what kind of activity is taking place.

cards.question: What does yaqona add in au gunu yaqona tiko?
cards.answer: Yaqona narrows the drinking action in the analysis; it is kilavu nauni here.

cards.question: Does its being a nauni automatically make yaqona a nauni qali in that phrase?
cards.answer: The phrase treats it as a qualifier of gunu. Compare nauni qali, which occupies an affected-participant slot in another construction.

kilavu vu.title: A predicate qualifying another
kilavu vu.intro: The qualifier can itself be a vu-like base, with a later particle still following.

cards.question: In Oni bula vinaka sara, which word qualifies bula?
cards.answer: Vinaka is kilavu vu in this analysis. Sara follows later as durumuri.

cards.question: In keitou gunu yaqona butā toka, which of yaqona and butā is the vu-based qualifier?
cards.answer: Butā is the kilavu vu; yaqona is a nauni-based qualifier and toka follows later.

vucoko.title: Can the ending come off?
vucoko.intro: A vucoko has a dewa form bound into the predicate; do not invent an unattested bare base.

cards.question: Nanuma and nanumi both occur. Does that make *nanu a word too?
cards.answer: No. *Nanu is an invented base; keep the complete forms nanuma and nanumi.

cards.question: Could a learner decide vucoko from the English word 'think' alone?
cards.answer: The Fijian form family and complete phrase matter. An English gloss cannot tell whether a dewa is permanently attached.

vusaumaki.title: Who changes role?
vusaumaki.intro: Some base/dewa contrasts change the relationship of a participant to the event.

cards.question: In the sogo / sogota contrast, does the thing that closes keep exactly the same role?
cards.answer: The analysis moves the thing that closes from the sole participant to the affected participant of the longer form.

cards.question: Is this the same participant pattern as cici / ciciva?
cards.answer: The cici runner remains the actor-like participant across that contrast. Vusaumaki points to the different role shift shown by sogo / sogota.

wiliwili.title: Number or whole counted phrase?
wiliwili.intro: Wiliwili can name counting itself or a number expression inside a larger phrase.

cards.question: In E rua na toa, which word gives the count?
cards.answer: Rua says how many. Toa names what is counted; the phrase does more than name a number in isolation.

cards.question: Does changing rua to tolu change the count or the kind of thing counted?
cards.answer: Rua is two and tolu is three. The counted thing remains toa in this comparison.

ciwa.title: One before ten
ciwa.intro: Ciwa counts nine; try it against the nearby numerals.

cards.question: Which number follows walu when counting toward tini?
cards.answer: Walu is eight, ciwa is nine, and tini is ten.

cards.question: If one is added to ciwa, which number is reached?
cards.answer: Nine plus one is ten. The Fijian counting words are ciwa and tini.

lima.title: Count to five
lima.intro: Lima is five, a useful pivot between four and six.

cards.question: Which word names the number between va and ono?
cards.answer: Va is four, lima is five, and ono is six.

cards.question: Two groups of lima make which number?
cards.answer: Two fives make ten: lima and tini are different count words.

ono.title: Count to six
ono.intro: Ono is six; notice how it sits between two number words.

cards.question: Which comes straight after lima?
cards.answer: Ono is six, following lima, five.

cards.question: Two groups of tolu make how many?
cards.answer: Tolu is three; two groups of three make ono, six.

va.title: Four in the count
va.intro: Va is four in the number list; the same spelling needs context in other uses.

cards.question: Two groups of rua make which count?
cards.answer: Rua is two; two pairs make va, four.

cards.question: Which number follows va in the sequence?
cards.answer: The counting sequence moves from va (four) to lima (five).

vitu.title: Count to seven
vitu.intro: Vitu sits after six and before eight.

cards.question: If you have ono and add dua, which number follows?
cards.answer: Six plus one makes seven: ono, then vitu.

cards.question: Which word comes after vitu?
cards.answer: Walu is eight, the next count after vitu.

walu.title: Four pairs make eight
walu.intro: Walu names eight; compare it with other counts rather than translating a whole sentence from English.

cards.question: Four groups of rua make which number?
cards.answer: Four pairs make eight, which is walu.

cards.question: If you add one to walu, which count word follows?
cards.answer: Walu is eight; ciwa is nine, one step before tini.

iyatuvosa.title: What makes the whole sentence?
iyatuvosa.intro: An iyatuvosa can contain a predicate phrase or place nominal phrases side by side.

cards.question: In E lako mai o Mere, which group tells what happens?
cards.answer: E lako mai is the matavu; o Mere identifies the person outside that predicate phrase.

cards.question: Do [o yau] [na vunivai] need a separate word for English 'is'?
cards.answer: The iyatuvosa matanauni puts two nominal phrases together without an overt vu.

nauni qali.title: The affected participant inside the phrase
nauni qali.intro: Nq identifies a named or pronominal participant immediately after the relevant predicate form in this analysis.

cards.question: In au raici Jo tiko, which word is the nauni qali?
cards.answer: Jo follows raici inside the matavu and names the person seen; au identifies the one seeing.

cards.question: Does na gone in au raica tiko na gone occupy the same narrow slot as Jo?
cards.answer: Na gone forms a separate matanauni raraba, although the child is still the person seen.

taukeni.title: How is the person connected?
taukeni.intro: Taukeni can be shown by a named person after the base or by a possessive form before it.

cards.question: In na vale nei Luke, which part identifies the person connected to the house?
cards.answer: Nei Luke names the person after vale; na introduces the whole phrase.

cards.question: If Luke himself says na noqu vale, is Luke named inside that phrase?
cards.answer: Noqu identifies the speaker without repeating the name. The relationship is expressed before vale.

vosa tuvai.title: One word, different jobs
vosa tuvai.intro: A vosa tuvai gets its role from the phrase it helps build.

cards.question: Is bula a vu in Oni bula vinaka sara?
cards.answer: Bula is the predicate base here; vinaka qualifies it. Read the whole matavu before naming the role.

cards.question: In na nona bula taucoko, does bula keep that same vu role?
cards.answer: Here bula names life as a nominal base. Its spelling stays the same while its phrase role changes.

kilanauni yatuvosa.title: A clause describes which one
kilanauni yatuvosa.intro: A whole clause can follow a nominal base and tell the reader which item is meant.

cards.question: In na kaloko [au a solia vei iko enanoa], does the bracketed clause identify which kaloko?
cards.answer: The clause describes the kaloko; it is a kilanauni yatuvosa attached to that nominal base.

cards.question: Does that clause replace the whole nominal phrase the way an MNYt clause can?
cards.answer: It qualifies kaloko inside the phrase. An MNYt clause occupies a nominal-phrase position itself.

isosomi.title: Refer back without repeating the name
isosomi.intro: An isosomi can stand for an already identifiable participant.

cards.question: After Oqo o Jale, who does koya point to in Na tagane mamakutu o koya?
cards.answer: Koya refers back to Jale; the listener can identify the person without hearing his name again.

cards.question: In o koya, is o part of the pronoun itself?
cards.answer: Koya is the pronoun; o is the mata of the whole matanauni sosomi.

tiko.title: Staying or keeping on?
tiko.intro: Tiko can be the predicate base or a following continuation marker; the phrase shows which.

cards.question: In e gole tiko yani, does tiko stand as the main base or follow gole?
cards.answer: Gole is the base; tiko follows it as a durumuri while the movement continues.

cards.question: In ena tiko mai nodratou, is tiko still merely following another base?
cards.answer: Here tiko itself is the predicate base, with mai following it. Its role has changed with the construction.

vinaka.title: Good, and doing well
vinaka.intro: Vinaka can express a quality; in a predicate phrase it may qualify another base.

cards.question: In Oni bula vinaka sara, which word says how the living or well-being is going?
cards.answer: Vinaka qualifies bula in this phrase; sara follows later to strengthen the expression.

cards.question: Is sara the same kind of qualifier as vinaka in that analysis?
cards.answer: Vinaka is kilavu vu here, while sara occupies a later durumuri position. The two words do different jobs.

mai.title: Which way is the movement?
mai.intro: Mai can point movement toward the speaker; its phrase role changes in other constructions.

cards.question: In Au sa lako mai, is the movement presented toward here or away from here?
cards.answer: Mai gives the toward-speaker direction after lako in this phrase.

cards.question: In era yabe vata yani, would yani point the same direction as mai?
cards.answer: Yani presents movement away or onward. Compare the two directions before choosing a word for a journey.

yani.title: Away and onward
yani.intro: Yani follows a moving predicate in the phrase and points away or onward.

cards.question: In era yabe vata yani, which final word gives the direction?
cards.answer: Vata says they move together; yani points the movement onward or away.

cards.question: Could you switch the order to era yabe yani vata here?
cards.answer: For this meaning, vata comes before yani. Their order matters; they cannot simply be moved like two English adverbs.

tani.title: Away, or a different one?
tani.intro: Tani changes role with its phrase: direction after a predicate, description after a nominal base.

cards.question: In wasea tani na duka, does tani follow the action or describe a named object inside na duka?
cards.answer: Tani is the following direction or separation word in this phrase.

cards.question: In na kā tani qori, which word distinguishes this thing from another?
cards.answer: Tani qualifies kā inside the nominal phrase; it is not a direction marker in this use.

sobu.title: Downward in two positions
sobu.intro: Sobu can follow another predicate or itself be the central predicate base.

cards.question: In sā vakarōrō sobu mai, does sobu come before or after vakarōrō?
cards.answer: Sobu follows the base here, before the later mai.

cards.question: In sā vakarau sobu na kākō, does sobu merely add direction after a different movement base?
cards.answer: Sobu is the predicate base here. The same spelling need not always have the same phrase role.

makawa.title: Long ago or an old building?
makawa.intro: Makawa can follow a predicate in a time reading or describe a nominal base.

cards.question: In ratou sā moce makawa, does makawa describe a house?
cards.answer: It follows moce with a time-related reading; no house is named in this phrase.

cards.question: In na vale makawa, what is old?
cards.answer: Makawa qualifies vale inside the nominal phrase rather than following a sleeping predicate.

wale.title: Only, or without a further reason?
wale.intro: Wale has several phrase roles; its position and context decide the reading.

cards.question: In au via taroga wale gā, which word limits the asking to 'just asking'?
cards.answer: Wale follows taroga as a durumuri; gā further limits the expression.

cards.question: In e sega ni kā wale, is wale still following a predicate as in the first phrase?
cards.answer: Here wale qualifies kā inside the nominal expression. In another context it can also qualify a predicate.

cake.title: Upward, but check the order
cake.intro: Cake can add upward direction after a movement predicate.

cards.question: In sā curuma cake tiko, which word gives the upward direction?
cards.answer: Cake adds upward direction; tiko marks continuation after it here.

cards.question: Would sā curuma tiko cake keep the same word order?
cards.answer: The upward direction cake precedes the continuation tiko in this construction.

vakatotolo.title: Where can quickly go?
vakatotolo.intro: This particular vaka- form is shown in two positions around mai; that flexibility is not a rule for every qualifier.

cards.question: In Drau lako mai vakatotolo, is vakatotolo before or after mai?
cards.answer: The quick manner follows the direction word mai, in the later kilavu tale position.

cards.question: Can you also say Drau lako vakatotolo mai?
cards.answer: Vakatotolo can take this earlier position too. Similar looking words do not all move so freely; check each phrase.

oti.title: Has it finished?
oti.intro: Oti can mark completion after a predicate; it is not the same as a marker of ongoing action.

cards.question: In Au nanuma de o sa kana oti, does oti point to completed or continuing eating?
cards.answer: Oti follows kana and presents the eating as finished in the clause.

cards.question: Does tiko in e gole tiko yani give the same completed reading as oti?
cards.answer: Tiko presents continuation there; oti supplies completion after kana in the other phrase.

vuwale.title: A predicate without dewa
vuwale.intro: A vuwale is a predicate base that has no dewa form in that use.

cards.question: In its predicate use, does levu itself take a dewa?
cards.answer: Levu is a vuwale in that use: its own form has no dewa.

cards.question: Does the existence of vakalevutaka make bare levu a vu dewa?
cards.answer: Vakalevutaka is a different derived form. Do not transfer its ending to levu itself.

vu dewa.title: Read the base with its ending
vu dewa.intro: This family has dewa forms, but the suffix and the following participant still need phrase-level checking.

cards.question: Which form stands immediately before Jo in Au raici Jo tiko?
cards.answer: Raici has the -i form before a personal name here.

cards.question: Does the pair nanuma / nanumi allow an invented bare *nanu?
cards.answer: Nanuma and nanumi are complete forms; *nanu is an invented base.

matanauni taukeni.title: Which relationship is inside the phrase?
matanauni taukeni.intro: A matanauni taukeni connects what is named with a person or another thing; the connection can be expressed in more than one place.

cards.question: In na vale nei Luke, does the phrase name the house or Luke alone?
cards.answer: Vale names the house; nei Luke identifies the person connected to it.

cards.question: If Luke says na noqu vale, where is the possessor signaled?
cards.answer: Noqu points to the speaker before the base. The phrase can express the relationship without repeating Luke's name.

taukeni dina.title: Owned, made, or performed?
taukeni dina.intro: Nei can connect a named person to a house, a song they sing, or another thing associated with them.

cards.question: In na vale nei Luke, is Luke the named person linked to the house?
cards.answer: Nei Luke identifies the person associated with the house; the phrase does not say who built it.

cards.question: In na sere nei Mere, is Mere the subject of the song or the one singing it?
cards.answer: Nei presents Mere as the performer in this example. Na sere kei Lia instead makes Lia the person the song is about.

taukeni bale.title: About someone, or intended for them
taukeni bale.intro: Kei can point to a person whom a song concerns or for whom something is intended.

cards.question: In na sere kei Lia, is the song about Lia or sung by Lia?
cards.answer: Kei Lia makes Lia the person the song is about here; nei Mere in another phrase marks the performer.

cards.question: In na dai kei Leone, is Leone named as the trap's maker?
cards.answer: The trap is intended for Leone in this phrase. The same kei marker takes its precise reading from dai and the situation.

taukeni kana.title: Who is meant to eat it?
taukeni kana.intro: Kei can link food or another consumable to the person meant to consume it.

cards.question: In na dalo kei Sami, does kei say Sami grew the taro?
cards.answer: Here the dalo is for Sami to eat. Ownership or growing would be a different relationship.

cards.question: Would na yaqona mei Tui use the same drinking relationship as na dalo kei Sami?
cards.answer: Mei marks a drink for Tui; kei marks food for Sami in these phrases. What is consumed guides the form.

taukeni gunu.title: A drink for whom?
taukeni gunu.intro: Mei points to the person who will drink what the phrase names.

cards.question: In na yaqona mei Tui, who is the intended drinker?
cards.answer: Mei Tui names the person for whom the yaqona is to drink.

cards.question: Does na yaqona nei Jo say exactly the same thing as na yaqona mei Jo?
cards.answer: Nei can link Jo to yaqona as an owner or preparer. Mei makes Jo the intended drinker.

taukeni kuri.title: A close part or family link
taukeni kuri.intro: The named person can follow a body part or close relation after the separate linker i.

cards.question: In na luve i Jo, does i Jo identify a parent or the child?
cards.answer: Luve names the child; i Jo supplies the person to whom the child is related.

cards.question: In na balu i Sisi dakoba, can dakoba be moved before i Sisi without changing this construction?
cards.answer: The relationship to Sisi is completed before dakoba qualifies balu. Read the full phrase before moving a description.

nei.title: Whose house, whose song?
nei.intro: Nei before a name marks a general association; context tells you whether it is ownership, making, or performing.

cards.question: In na vale nei Luke, which piece introduces the named person?
cards.answer: Nei introduces Luke after the nominal base vale. Na opens the whole phrase.

cards.question: Would na sere kei Lia necessarily mean Lia sings it, as na sere nei Mere does?
cards.answer: Kei Lia makes the song about Lia; nei Mere presents Mere as its singer. The same English 'of' would hide this difference.

kei.title: The same marker, different links
kei.intro: Kei before a name can mark what concerns a person or what they are meant to consume.

cards.question: In na sere kei Lia, what is Lia's connection to the song?
cards.answer: The phrase is about Lia. A singer can be expressed with nei in a different construction.

cards.question: In na dalo kei Sami, what changes from the song example?
options: The person is to eat it
The person becomes a place name
cards.correct: The person is to eat it
cards.answer: Dalo is food for Sami. The base and situation distinguish taukeni kana from taukeni bale even though both use kei.

mei.title: A drink set aside
mei.intro: Mei before a named person marks a drink intended for that person.

cards.question: In na yaqona mei Tui, which piece points to Tui as the drinker?
cards.answer: Mei Tui follows yaqona and names who is meant to drink it.

cards.question: If Jo instead owns the yaqona, would mei still be the clear choice?
cards.answer: For ownership, na yaqona nei Jo uses nei. Mei Jo would change the relationship to an intended drinker.

i.title: A small linker, a close relationship
i.intro: I can link a body part or family member to the named person after it; check the full phrase before assigning that role.

cards.question: In na luve i Jo, which separate word links luve to Jo?
cards.answer: I stands before Jo in this taukeni kuri phrase; na introduces the larger nominal phrase.

cards.question: Does i Jo in na luve i Jo have the same relationship as nei Luke in na vale nei Luke?
cards.answer: I links a close relation here, while nei expresses a general association with Luke's house.

ni.title: A common noun follows
ni.intro: Ni can join one nominal base to another common-noun base, but it does not give one fixed English relationship.

cards.question: In na ulu ni vuaka, is vuaka a personal name like Jo?
cards.answer: Vuaka is the common nominal base for pig. Ulu names its head; ni links the two bases.

cards.question: Does ni mean exactly the same relation in na vale ni koli and na ulu ni vuaka?
cards.answer: A house can belong to a dog; a head is a body part of a pig. Ni is the same visible linker, but the nouns determine the relationship.

no-/ne-.title: A general possessive link
no-/ne-.intro: No- and ne- join person endings in forms for a general ownership or related action.

cards.question: In noqu vale, which piece says what kind of possessive link precedes -qu?
cards.answer: No- is the relationship element; -qu identifies the speaker. Vale names the house.

cards.question: Does neitou include the listener merely because it ends in -itou?
cards.answer: Neitou points to the speaker's few-person group excluding the listener. An attached ending is not the same as free tou in another phrase.

ke-.title: What is the person meant to do with it?
ke-.intro: Ke- can appear in possessive forms for something about a person or food meant for them.

cards.question: In kemu uvi, is the food meant for the listener to eat or drink?
cards.answer: Uvi is food. Ke- in kemu fits the eating relationship; -mu identifies the listener.

cards.question: In keda vere, does the same ke- have to mean food?
cards.answer: Vere is a plan or plot concerning the group; ke- also appears in a taukeni bale relationship.

me-.title: When the item is a drink
me-.intro: Me- appears before person endings in possessive forms for a drink intended for someone.

cards.question: In memudou ti, which part marks the drinking relationship?
cards.answer: Me- marks the relationship to tea as a drink; -mudou identifies the listeners.

cards.question: Would ke- in kemu uvi be the same drinking marker as me-?
cards.answer: Kemu uvi concerns food to eat. Memudou ti concerns tea to drink; the first element differs.

-qu.title: Where is 'my' attached?
-qu.intro: The ending -qu can attach directly to a body-part noun, while a house uses a different possessive form.

cards.question: In na batiqu, is -qu attached to bati or standing before it as a separate word?
cards.answer: Batiqu puts the speaker ending on bati, the teeth.

cards.question: Can you normally make 'my house' by writing *valequ on the pattern of batiqu?
cards.answer: For the house use na noqu vale; direct -qu attachment belongs to a different relationship class here.

vica.title: A question or a small number
vica.intro: Vica can ask for a count or state an indefinite small number; the sentence tells you which.

cards.question: In E vica na roti o kania?, is the speaker asking how many or saying several?
cards.answer: The question asks how many roti were eaten. Vica asks for the number here.

cards.question: In E vica na koro, does vica name an exact count like rua?
cards.answer: It gives a few or several villages without specifying an exact number.

vuqa.title: Many, but how many?
vuqa.intro: Vuqa expresses a large number without giving an exact count.

cards.question: Does vuqa tell you an exact number as ciwa does?
cards.answer: Ciwa is nine; vuqa leaves the amount open while saying there are many.

cards.question: Which is the closer contrast to vuqa: vica as 'a few' or rua as 'two'?
cards.answer: Vica and vuqa can both give inexact quantities, but one suggests a few and the other many.

levu.title: Size or quantity?
levu.intro: Levu may describe a large thing or contribute a large-quantity reading; inspect what it qualifies.

cards.question: In na vale levu, is levu about the house's size or a count of houses?
cards.answer: Levu follows vale and describes a large house in this nominal phrase.

cards.question: In E levu na koro, does levu mean one large village?
cards.answer: The phrase concerns a large number of villages. The same form can contribute quantity rather than the size of one building.

vei-.title: Together, toward each other, or a group
vei-.intro: Vei- is a clue to more than one word-building pattern; check the full derived word.

cards.question: In rau sā veidomoni, does the action involve the two people toward each other?
cards.answer: Veidomoni expresses a mutual relationship here. The whole word, not vei- alone, carries this reading.

cards.question: Does veidogo, a stand of mangroves, mean two mangroves acting on each other?
cards.answer: Here vei- helps form a collective or place-related noun from dogo. The prefix has different effects in different words.

vaka-.title: One beginning, several effects
vaka-.intro: Vaka- can help form a causative action or a manner word; a complete word decides which.

cards.question: In vakalevutaka, does the longer form make something become large or merely name a large thing?
cards.answer: Vaka- participates in a causative formation with levu here; the complete form matters.

cards.question: Does vakatotolo express that same 'make large' effect?
cards.answer: Vakatotolo expresses quick manner. Compare whole derived words before giving vaka- a meaning.

i-.title: A noun built from an action
i-.intro: I- can help form a noun from a predicate base, but the result needs its own checked meaning.

cards.question: In ilakolako, which part is the attached beginning before repeated lako?
cards.answer: The word combines i- with repeated lako and can name a journey.

cards.question: Is i- inside ilakolako the same as separate i before Jo in na luve i Jo?
cards.answer: The first is attached to a derived word; the second links a family relation to a name inside a phrase.

veitabui.title: Which orders are blocked?
veitabui.intro: A veitabui restriction applies to a particular combination or order; check the two forms together.

cards.question: Can era yabe vata yani be reordered as era yabe yani vata here?
cards.answer: For this meaning, vata precedes the direction word yani.

cards.question: In sā curuma cake tiko, can tiko move before cake without changing this construction?
cards.answer: Cake gives upward direction before tiko marks continuation. Their order matters here.

vūtū.title: Does the actor stay the same?
vūtū.intro: In this vu class, the base can stand without dewa and the actor remains the actor when a dewa form is used.

cards.question: Across cici and ciciva, does the runner stop being the actor?
cards.answer: The runner remains the actor-like participant in both constructions.

cards.question: Is that the same participant shift illustrated by sogo and sogota?
cards.answer: Sogo and sogota illustrate a different class, vusaumaki, where the closing thing can shift to the affected role.

druabalavu.title: Which part repeats?
druabalavu.intro: Druabalavu repeats a longer part of a base; the new word's meaning still needs its own context.

cards.question: In culacula, which complete part is repeated?
cards.answer: Cula repeats as a whole: cula + cula. This is the longer repetition pattern.

cards.question: Does lelewa show the same whole-base repetition as culacula?
cards.answer: Lelewa repeats a shorter opening part instead. Compare its shape with the full cula repeat.

drualeka.title: A short repeat at the start
drualeka.intro: Drualeka repeats a shorter part rather than the whole base.

cards.question: In kekeli, which opening part is repeated?
cards.answer: Ke repeats before keli; this is a shorter repeated span.

cards.question: Is cula + cula in culacula another drualeka?
cards.answer: It repeats the whole base and belongs to the longer druabalavu pattern.

dranu.title: Fresh water or a lake?
dranu.intro: Dranu describes water without the saltiness of the sea. Drano, with a different final vowel, names a lake or inland body of water.

cards.question: In wai dranu (‘freshwater’), what does dranu tell you about the water?
options: It is certainly safe to drink
cards.answer: The phrase distinguishes fresh water from seawater. It does not by itself certify drinking safety.

cards.question: Does drano name the same thing as dranu?
cards.answer: Drano names a lake or inland body of water. Dranu gives a water quality, as in wai dranu. The final vowel matters.

link.label: Explore dranu in a Pacific linguistics study

bu.title: Which coconut is ready to drink?
bu.intro: Bu names a green coconut at a particular useful stage, not every coconut on the palm.

cards.question: Which part is still soft when a bu is ready to drink?
cards.answer: Its water is drinkable while the flesh remains soft; a mature niu is a different stage.

cards.question: If a seller offers bu and niu, do those words necessarily specify the same stage?
cards.answer: Bu selects the drinkable green stage. Niu names the coconut more generally, especially a mature one in this dictionary.

link.label: Explore a study of Fijian coconut stages

buru.title: Count the coconuts
buru.intro: Buru is a traditional unit of ten coconuts; the same counted-unit name is also recorded for bottles of coconut oil.

cards.question: If there are two buru of coconuts, how many coconuts are counted?
cards.answer: Each buru counts ten, so two count twenty. It is a unit, not the name of a coconut stage.

cards.question: In the recorded oil example, what does one buru count?
cards.answer: Traditional counting can group different related goods; this example groups ten bottles of oil.

link.label: Read about traditional Fijian counted units

kavika.title: An apple by name, a different tree
kavika.intro: Kavika is the Malay apple, Syzygium malaccense; the English common name can mislead someone expecting a temperate apple.

cards.question: Is kavika the same botanical fruit as the ordinary temperate apple?
cards.answer: Malay apple belongs to Syzygium, while the familiar temperate apple belongs to Malus.

cards.question: In a Fiji plant survey, was kavika recorded as an introduced cultivated plant or as a sea animal?
cards.answer: The Fiji survey lists kavika among cultivated introduced plants; its Fijian name still belongs in a Fiji dictionary.

link.label: Read the Fiji plant survey

duruka.title: A crop with an edible shoot
duruka.intro: Duruka is a cultivated sugarcane relative. The tender flower shoot is the part commonly prepared as food.

cards.question: When duruka is served as a vegetable, which part is being used?
cards.answer: The crop is grown for that edible shoot, which is why English descriptions sometimes call it Fiji asparagus.

cards.question: Does Fiji's crop guide list only one named duruka variety?
cards.answer: It lists several varieties, including Duruka leka and Baribari; the broad word duruka is not one cultivar name.

link.label: Open Fiji's crop guide for duruka

baka.title: A banyan in a Fiji forest
baka.intro: Baka names a large banyan fig; a Fiji vegetation survey uses the word for more than one Ficus identification.

cards.question: In the Monuriki survey, is baka treated as a single fixed scientific species?
cards.answer: The survey records baka or baka ni Viti with Ficus names, and also uses Ficus spp. for banyans.

cards.question: Would you expect a baka's spreading branches and hanging roots to resemble a coconut palm?
cards.answer: Banyan figs spread a broad crown and aerial roots. The familiar niu is a palm with a different form.

link.label: Read the Monuriki vegetation survey

balolo.title: A seasonal visitor from the reef
balolo.intro: Balolo is an edible marine worm, not a fish, and its appearance is seasonal.

cards.question: If balolo appears around a reef, should it be counted as an ika species?
cards.answer: The reported Fiji balolo is a marine worm. Ika names fish, even when fish are prepared as food.

cards.question: Does a balolo gathering depend on a seasonal appearance or a constant daily catch?
cards.answer: The worms emerge in seasonal swarms, a feature of the word's local food context.

link.label: See a scientific report on Fiji balolo

vonu.title: Which turtle?
vonu.intro: Vonu names a sea turtle. Vonu dina names the green sea turtle in Fiji's conservation writing.

cards.question: Does vonu dina narrow vonu to a particular sea turtle?
cards.answer: The added dina identifies the green sea turtle; vonu alone is the broader turtle name.

cards.question: Which animal appears as vonu dina on Fiji's five-dollar banknote design?
cards.answer: The Reserve Bank uses the species name beside the image, linking a familiar word to conservation.

link.label: See the Reserve Bank's turtle design

kawakawa.title: One fish name, several levels of precision
kawakawa.intro: Kawakawa refers to grouper; a Fiji conservation guide uses it specifically for the camouflage grouper.

cards.question: In the WCS Fiji guide, which scientific name goes with kawakawa?
cards.answer: That is the camouflage grouper in the guide. Xiphias gladius is the swordfish called saku vorowaqa.

cards.question: Why might a spawning group of kawakawa be especially vulnerable to fishing?
options: Many gather at one place and time
cards.correct: Many gather at one place and time
cards.answer: WCS reports predictable spawning aggregations, so a single fishing event can affect many breeding fish.

link.label: Explore WCS Fiji's grouper guide

saku vorowaqa.title: A bill like a sword
saku vorowaqa.intro: Saku vorowaqa is the Fiji name recorded for Xiphias gladius, the swordfish.

cards.question: Which feature helps distinguish this fish from a reef grouper?
cards.answer: The bill gives swordfish their English name; kawakawa is a grouper, not this species.

cards.question: Does FishBase describe this species as oceanic or as a coral-reef grouper?
cards.answer: The species is listed as pelagic-oceanic; its habitat contrasts with reef-associated kawakawa.

link.label: See the Fiji swordfish record

yaqona.title: The plant and the drink
yaqona.intro: Yaqona can name the kava plant or the drink prepared from its root. The phrase tells you which sense is active.

cards.question: If yaqona is growing in a field, which sense is intended?
cards.answer: A growing yaqona is the plant. In a serving context the same word can refer to the prepared drink.

cards.question: In na yaqona mei Tui, does mei Tui name the plant's owner or the intended drinker?
cards.answer: The phrase uses taukeni gunu. Na yaqona nei Jo would point to another relationship, such as ownership or preparation.

link.label: Read Fiji's kava information

ika.title: A broad food word, a precise species
ika.intro: Ika can mean a fish or fish as food. A more specific name can identify which animal is meant.

cards.question: Is saku vorowaqa a more specific fish name than ika?
cards.answer: It names swordfish; ika does not identify a species on its own.

cards.question: Can you call edible balolo an ika merely because it comes from the sea?
cards.answer: Balolo is a marine worm. Being edible and marine does not make it a fish.

dau-.title: A person formed from an activity
dau-.intro: Attached dau- can help make a word for someone who habitually does or knows an activity.

cards.question: In dauqoli, which part points to a habitual or skilled person?
cards.answer: Dau- is attached to the base; dauqoli names a person associated with fishing.

cards.question: Is attached dau- in dauqoli the same written construction as a separate dau before a predicate?
cards.answer: The attached form builds a word for a person. Separate dau can indicate that an action happens habitually; the whole phrase decides its role.

dauqoli.title: One catch or a fisher?
dauqoli.intro: Dauqoli names a person associated with fishing as an occupation, habit, or skill.

cards.question: If someone catches one fish once, does that single event by itself establish that they are a dauqoli?
cards.answer: The word suggests a habitual or skilled fisher, not merely one completed catch.

cards.question: In dauqoli, does the whole word name the person or the fish?
cards.answer: The attached dau- helps form a person word; ika is a broad word for fish.

kuri sosomi.title: Who is attached to the noun?
kuri sosomi.intro: A kuri sosomi identifies the related person or group in an attached form.

cards.question: In na yavaqu, which ending identifies the speaker?
cards.answer: The ending attaches to yava. Na introduces the larger nominal phrase.

cards.question: In na luveikeimami, is -ikeimami placed before luve as a separate possessive word?
cards.answer: It follows the base as an attached form. Na neimami gone uses a different, preposed possessive pattern.

ikurisosomi.title: An ending or a separate word?
ikurisosomi.intro: Ikurisosomi concerns a person ending attached directly to a suitable nominal base.

cards.question: In batiqu, is the speaker ending part of the written word?
cards.answer: Bati and -qu are written together. Na noqu vale expresses a different possessive pattern.

cards.question: Does na neirau dra put the same ending directly on dra as na dakuikeirau puts on daku?
cards.answer: Neirau stands before dra; -ikeirau follows daku in a directly suffixed form. Similar ownership does not erase the different construction.

yavu ni matavu.title: Find the predicate's core
yavu ni matavu.intro: The yavu carries the central meaning of a matavu; it is identified in the complete phrase.

cards.question: In Au sa lako mai, which word is the yavu?
cards.answer: Au and sa precede it; mai follows it. Lako is the meaning-bearing base of this predicate phrase.

cards.question: Must every yavu ni matavu be a vu rather than a nauni?
cards.answer: A photographed teacher example places qasenivuli, a nominal base, in the yavu position. Read the phrase before naming its role.

kilavu tale.title: A later place for some qualifiers
kilavu tale.intro: Some qualifiers can follow the durumuri; another qualifier may be restricted to an earlier place.

cards.question: In Drau lako mai vakatotolo, which word is the later qualifier?
cards.answer: Mai supplies direction; vakatotolo follows it and describes the manner of going.

cards.question: Can you move butako after tiko merely because vakatotolo can appear after mai?
cards.answer: The photographed contrast permits two positions for vakatotolo here but rejects that later position for butako. Check each word and phrase.

mataqali vu.title: Two tests for a predicate class
mataqali vu.intro: The class depends on whether a dewa form occurs and what happens to the participants.

cards.question: Which pair keeps the runner as the actor-like participant?
cards.answer: The cited analysis uses this pair for vūtū, where the runner stays the runner across the contrast.

cards.question: Which pair illustrates a shift in the closing thing's role?
cards.answer: The photographed vusaumaki contrast changes how the closing thing participates. The suffix alone cannot tell you the class.

lawa cocoko.title: A restricted order
lawa cocoko.intro: Some word combinations allow only a tightly limited arrangement in a given construction.

cards.question: In the cited contrast e rairai via lako, is *e via rairai lako offered as the same acceptable order?
cards.answer: The asterisk marks the rejected rearrangement in that teaching example. It is a specific contrast, not a universal ban on via.

cards.question: Does a restricted pair justify treating every Fijian phrase as fixed in the same way?
cards.answer: The position of vakatotolo around mai is more flexible in another cited phrase. A lawa cocoko applies where the actual construction restricts it.

lawa cicila.title: Where does the order have room?
lawa cicila.intro: A lawa cicila permits variation in a particular phrase pattern; the permission is not automatic for every word.

cards.question: Are both Drau lako mai vakatotolo and Drau lako vakatotolo mai offered in the cited example?
cards.answer: The qualifier vakatotolo can occur on either side of mai in that recorded contrast.

cards.question: Does that mean butako can also move after tiko in its own example?
cards.answer: The source restricts butako in its own construction. Variation has to be checked with the actual qualifier.

semavosa.title: Inside a word or between words?
semavosa.intro: Semavosa studies how bases and additions combine; a similar-looking piece may instead be a separate phrase word.

cards.question: In ilakolako, is i- attached to the repeated lako base?
cards.answer: The beginning is part of the derived word. The repetition must be examined with the whole form's meaning.

cards.question: Is the separate i in na luve i Jo attached to luve in the same way?
cards.answer: That i links a family relation to a name in a phrase; it is not the word-forming i- of ilakolako.

vosa veibasai.title: A contrast in meaning
vosa veibasai.intro: Vosa veibasai are words with opposed meanings in a given use.

cards.question: In a Fijian school exercise, which answer contrasts with lelevu?
cards.answer: The teacher's guide gives lelevu and lalai as an opposite pair. The words still need their sentence for precise use.

cards.question: If a task instead seeks a near meaning of vuqa, should you use vosa veibasai?
cards.answer: A near meaning belongs under vosa tautauvata; the guide pairs vuqa with levu for that task.

link.label: See a Fijian teacher's contrast and similarity exercises

vosa tautauvata.title: Near meaning, not automatic substitution
vosa tautauvata.intro: Vosa tautauvata are words with similar meanings; the phrase still decides whether either fits.

cards.question: Which pair does a Fijian teacher's guide place together as near in meaning?
cards.answer: The guide offers vuqa and levu as a similarity pair; lelevu and lalai are an opposite pair.

cards.question: Does that exercise prove vuqa and levu are interchangeable in every sentence?
cards.answer: A similarity exercise identifies a relation in meaning, not a licence to swap the words in every Fijian construction.

link.label: Read the teacher's similarity examples

veitacini.title: A relationship, not an action
veitacini.intro: Veitacini names siblings in a particular kin relation; its vei- does not by itself mean that they are acting on each other.

cards.question: In Rau tawase na veitacini ena rakavi, is veitacini naming one person alone?
cards.answer: The news heading speaks of siblings on different sides in rugby. The word supplies the kin relationship.

cards.question: Does the vei- in veitacini automatically give the same mutual-action reading as in every vei- predicate?
cards.answer: Here the whole word names a kin relationship. The attached beginning has several uses across Fijian words.

link.label: Read veitacini in a Fiji news heading

taucoko.title: Many or the whole total?
taucoko.intro: Taucoko says complete or whole; in a count it can make clear that a number is the total.

cards.question: In e 105 taucoko na koro, is 105 presented as the total or as an extra 105?
cards.answer: The iTaukei Affairs account counts the province's villages in all.

cards.question: If vuqa says there are many villages, does it also tell you the set is complete?
cards.answer: Vuqa says the number is large; taucoko speaks to completeness. The words answer different questions.

link.label: See taucoko in an iTaukei Affairs account

drano.title: An inland place, not a water quality
drano.intro: Drano names an inland lake or related standing-water place. Dranu, with a different final vowel, describes freshwater.

cards.question: If a story leads you to a drano, are you looking for an inland water place or simply a glass without salt?
cards.answer: The word names a lake, pond, or freshwater swamp depending on the variety; dranu describes the water's fresh quality.

cards.question: Bauan drano can include a freshwater swamp; Wayan drano can include a pond. What stays shared?
cards.answer: The comparative record shows related but not identical ranges in the two Fijian varieties.

link.label: See drano across Fijian varieties

buta.title: When is it ready?
buta.intro: Buta can describe food that is cooked; other recorded senses concern removing cooked food or heat affecting skin.

cards.question: In Sa buta na kakana? (‘Is the food cooked?’), what is being checked?
cards.answer: Buta concerns the food's cooked state in this question. A different construction can use buta for taking cooked food out.

cards.question: If a description says skin is buta, would you read it as a meal ready to eat?
cards.answer: The historical skin sense concerns scorching or blistering. The surrounding noun changes which sense of buta fits.

link.label: See the cooked-food question in use

ca.title: Bad in which way?
ca.intro: Ca can judge damage, poor condition, or moral wrong; context tells you how strong the judgment is.

cards.question: In the public phrase e ca na nomu basikeli (‘your bicycle is damaged’), is the bicycle being called morally evil?
cards.answer: Here ca describes something wrong with the bicycle. Moral judgment is another use, not the reading forced by every object.

cards.question: If ca names badness or harm itself, is that the same use as describing a damaged bicycle?
cards.answer: The dictionary keeps the quality or harm sense apart from the descriptive use. A complete phrase shows which one is active.

link.label: Read ca with basikeli in a Fiji speech

cadra.title: A sunrise and a new beginning
cadra.intro: Cadra can describe a heavenly body rising; it can also evoke something new appearing.

cards.question: In na cadra ni dua na matanisiga vou (‘the dawn of a new sun’), is cadra about an arrival or a sunset?
cards.answer: A Fiji report uses the rising-sun image for a new beginning. The astronomical meaning makes the metaphor work.

cards.question: Does cadra only apply to the sun, never to the moon or an emerging tooth?
cards.answer: The recorded meaning includes other things coming into view or through a surface. The phrase identifies what is emerging.

link.label: See the rising-sun image in a Fiji report

dredre.title: The task, or the time?
dredre.intro: Dredre says something is difficult; it can describe a job to do or a hard period of life.

cards.question: If a report calls a year yabaki dredre (‘a difficult year’), is it weighing the year on a scale?
cards.answer: Dredre describes hardship or difficulty. Bibi can mean physically heavy or serious; that is a different starting image.

cards.question: When a task is dredre, does the word by itself say that the task is impossible?
cards.answer: Difficult is not the same as impossible. Rawa concerns whether something can be done.

link.label: Read yabaki dredre in a Fiji annual report

yawa.title: Distance, or a fish?
yawa.intro: Yawa can express distance. A separate recorded sense uses the same spelling for a coastal fish.

cards.question: In a question about the yawa between a village and Suva, which sense fits?
