cards.answer: The question asks how far the village is from Suva; it does not identify a fish.

cards.question: If a speaker names an animal as yawa, can the distance meaning identify its species?
cards.answer: The fish sense has its own identification questions. One spelling can carry unrelated senses, and the complete context matters.

link.label: See a Fijian question about distance

lade.title: A leap is more specific than travel
lade.intro: Lade focuses on jumping or leaping; lako can speak more broadly of going.

cards.question: If someone moves by leaving the ground in a leap, which word captures that movement?
cards.answer: Lade identifies the leap. Lako can say someone goes without telling you that they jump.

cards.question: Does lade alone tell you where a person lands?
cards.answer: The landing place has to come from more context. A motion word need not specify a destination.

tale.title: Returning, or doing it again?
tale.intro: Tale adds a return or repetition idea in context; its precise reading depends on the surrounding action.

cards.question: In Au na qai lesu tale mai nimataka (‘I will come back tomorrow’), what does tale reinforce?
cards.answer: Lesu mai already points to returning; tale makes the return idea explicit in this sentence.

cards.question: If tale accompanies a different action, must it always mean physical travel back?
cards.answer: With another predicate it can mark doing something again. Read the action beside it.

link.label: Read a return-tomorrow sentence

rawa.title: Possible is not completed
rawa.intro: Rawa can concern ability or possibility after a predicate. It does not itself report a finished event.

cards.question: If a plan says it can be done, does rawa by itself prove it has already happened?
cards.answer: Rawa expresses possibility or ability; another marker or context is needed for a completed event.

cards.question: Which word better tests whether a difficult task is achievable: rawa or dredre?
cards.answer: Dredre says it is hard; rawa addresses whether it can be done. Both can be true of one task.

link.label: Read rawa in a Fiji audit report

sara.title: Very, or a fish name?
sara.intro: Sara can strengthen an expression. A separate fish entry shares the spelling; the setting tells you which one is meant.

cards.question: In a statement saying an issue is bibi sara (‘very serious’), which sara sense fits?
cards.answer: The issue is being described as very serious. The fish sense belongs to a different context.

cards.question: If a catch list includes sara beside other fish, should you read it as ‘very’?
cards.answer: In a fish list the separate animal sense may be intended. The nearby words disambiguate the spelling.

nanoa.title: Look one day back
nanoa.intro: Nanoa locates an event yesterday. It is a time expression, not a hidden na- prefix plus a separate base.

cards.question: In Au a yaco mai nanoa (‘I arrived yesterday’), when did the arrival happen?
cards.answer: The time word nanoa locates the arrival before today.

cards.question: Does the written start of enanoa prove that nanoa begins with the noun-phrase marker na?
cards.answer: The Tuvavosa time analysis treats enanoa or nanoa as a whole time expression, rather than splitting its letters into invented markers.

link.label: Read a yesterday sentence

edaidai.title: Today, or the present time
edaidai.intro: Edaidai can point to today or, in context, the present period. It is grouped with Fijian time expressions.

cards.question: If edaidai contrasts with nanoa, which time is on the current side?
cards.answer: Nanoa means yesterday; edaidai points to today or the present.

cards.question: Does the initial e in edaidai automatically make e a separate noun-phrase marker?
cards.answer: The recorded Tuvavosa analysis treats edaidai as a whole matanauni gauna without a separately identified mata.

link.label: See the paired time words in a Fijian text

nikua.title: Today is the reference point
nikua.intro: Nikua is today. Comparing it with nanoa and nimataka creates a useful three-day sequence.

cards.question: In the recorded contrast nimataka, sega ni nikua (‘tomorrow, not today’), which word identifies today?
cards.answer: The clause explicitly rejects today and chooses tomorrow.

cards.question: If an event is put at nikua, has the word alone told you whether it happened earlier or later in this day?
cards.answer: Nikua locates the day, not the exact hour or completion status. More of the sentence must supply those.

link.label: Read the today–tomorrow contrast in a USP study

nimataka.title: A day ahead
nimataka.intro: Nimataka points to tomorrow. It does not itself say that a future plan is certain.

cards.question: In Au na kania na apolo nimataka (‘I will eat the apple tomorrow’), which word sets the day?
cards.answer: Nimataka supplies tomorrow; the other words tell you what is planned.

cards.question: In the contrast nimataka, sega ni nikua, are both words names for the same day?
cards.answer: The speaker contrasts tomorrow with today. The words are distinct time expressions.

link.label: Read a tomorrow sentence

bibi.title: Weight can be physical or serious
bibi.intro: Bibi can describe something heavy in weight or important and serious in discussion.

cards.question: When Parliament speaks of an ulutaga bibi (‘important topic’), is it weighing a physical object?
cards.answer: The topic is serious or weighty in importance, not heavy on a scale.

cards.question: If an object is bibi to carry, is that the same use as calling an issue bibi?
cards.answer: The first concerns physical weight; the second concerns significance. The shared word invites a metaphor, but the contexts remain different.

link.label: Read ulutaga bibi in Fiji parliamentary debate

ilavo.title: Money, or an amount?
ilavo.intro: Ilavo names money; a phrase may then specify who holds it, earns it, or uses it.

cards.question: In a public discussion of ilavo votai (‘allocated money’), has ilavo itself told you the amount?
cards.answer: The word names money; the allocation and amount come from surrounding words and figures.

cards.question: If a sentence says someone has ilavo, can you infer whether it was earned, donated, or borrowed from ilavo alone?
cards.answer: Ilavo identifies the resource, not its history. The action and context establish that relationship.

link.label: See ilavo votai in a Fiji audit report

vuaka.title: The animal and its food sense
vuaka.intro: Vuaka names a pig; in a food setting it can also refer to pork.

cards.question: If a vuaka is running in a yard, which sense fits?
cards.answer: The animal is alive in that context. A meal setting can select the meat sense.

cards.question: Does a record of vuaka among Fijian food taboos automatically mean every community treats pigs identically?
cards.answer: The research records local food knowledge and variation; the word for the animal does not dictate a universal custom.

link.label: Explore research on Fiji food knowledge

basikeli.title: A bicycle in a Fijian sentence
basikeli.intro: Basikeli is a bicycle. Its final vowel belongs to the adapted Fijian word.

cards.question: In kevaka e ca na nomu basikeli (‘if your bicycle is damaged’), what does basikeli name?
cards.answer: Ca describes its bad condition; basikeli names the vehicle.

cards.question: Would the English spelling bicycle be the same written Fijian word as basikeli?
cards.answer: The borrowing has been adapted to Fijian sound and spelling patterns; the dictionary keeps the Fijian form.

link.label: See basikeli in a Fiji public statement

bebe.title: A flying insect, not one species
bebe.intro: Bebe can name a butterfly and in some regional speech a moth; the word is broader than one scientific species.

cards.question: Does bebe alone identify Fiji's endemic swallowtail, Papilio schmeltzii?
cards.answer: The Fiji study identifies that particular species; bebe is a broader insect word and does not give a species name by itself.

cards.question: If a speaker uses bebe for a night-flying moth, must that invalidate the butterfly sense?
cards.answer: Some regional usage covers moths too. Ask which insect the speaker means instead of assuming one English label everywhere.

link.label: Explore a Fiji butterfly study

drokadroka.title: A green word in the landscape
drokadroka.intro: Drokadroka names green, especially of vegetation; a green plant is a good place to test the colour sense.

cards.question: If a leaf is described as drokadroka, is the word pointing to colour or the leaf's size?
cards.answer: It gives the green colour. Levu or lailai can instead describe size in a suitable phrase.

cards.question: Can you prove that drokadroka simply means ‘twice as green’ by its repeated shape?
cards.answer: A repeated-looking word needs its own checked meaning. Here the whole word means green; drua does not supply a fixed multiplication rule.

link.label: See green in a Fijian word list

bukete.title: A person and a condition
bukete.intro: Bukete can describe a pregnant person and can also name pregnancy as a condition.

cards.question: If bukete describes a person, is it naming the person’s condition or a food?
cards.answer: The descriptive sense is about pregnancy. A full phrase is needed to identify the person involved.

cards.question: If a sentence discusses bukete as a state, does that force every occurrence to be the same phrase role?
cards.answer: The same spelling has both a descriptive and a nominal use in the reviewed entries. The complete Fijian phrase settles the role.

moku.title: A hit is not a blame
moku.intro: Moku concerns striking or hitting. Beitaka concerns laying blame on someone.

cards.question: If someone is physically struck, which word is closer: moku or beitaka?
cards.answer: Moku names a physical hit; beitaka assigns blame. They are different actions.

cards.question: Does moku alone identify the exact body part hit or the way the blow was delivered?
cards.answer: A fuller phrase would need to provide the target and manner. Do not turn the broad word into a specific slap without that context.

caga.title: Measure with your hand
caga.intro: Caga is a hand span, a length measured between the outstretched thumb and little finger.

cards.question: If a mat is two caga wide, are you counting two hand spans or two whole hands laid flat?
cards.answer: The unit uses the distance between fingertips when the hand is stretched.

cards.question: Would one person's caga necessarily equal another person's in centimetres?
cards.answer: The unit is based on a person's hand, so its physical length can vary. It is a traditional measure, not a fixed centimetre value.

link.label: Explore the comparative record for caga

bite.title: Dew is not a rainfall
bite.intro: Bite is dew: moisture that forms on a surface overnight, especially when it cools.

cards.question: If grass is wet with bite at dawn, must rain have fallen in the night?
cards.answer: Dew can form by condensation on a cool surface without rainfall.

cards.question: Is bite a time word like nanoa, or the moisture you might notice in the morning?
cards.answer: Nanoa places an event yesterday; bite names a physical substance or condition on a surface.

vumatua.title: When vaka- strengthens an action
vumatua.intro: Vumatua labels a vaka- use that strengthens the action or quality of its base.

cards.question: In this Tuvavosa use, does vaka- intensify the base or make someone else cause it?
cards.answer: The latter is the vuvakavu pattern. The whole recorded word and phrase decide which use applies.

cards.question: Can you label every new vaka- word vumatua solely because it begins with those letters?
cards.answer: Vaka- has several functions. A complete attested form and phrase are needed before assigning this stronger-action reading.

link.label: Read a Fijian grammar on vaka- uses

vuvakavu.title: When vaka- brings about a result
vuvakavu.intro: Vuvakavu labels a vaka- use that makes an event or state happen.

cards.question: Does this use of vaka- point to causing a result or simply making a base more intense?
cards.answer: Strengthening is the separate vumatua use. Neither label follows automatically from the prefix alone.

cards.question: Before calling a whole word vuvakavu, what should you inspect?
cards.answer: The added prefix is a clue; the recorded word and its participants show whether causation is involved.

link.label: Read a Fijian grammar on causative vaka-

baigani.title: The crop behind the name
baigani.intro: Baigani is eggplant or aubergine. Fiji's food-growing guide groups it with transplanted vegetables, rather than starchy staples.

cards.question: A grower raises baigani seedlings before moving them into the garden. Is that the guide's approach for this crop or for tavioka?
cards.answer: Baigani is listed among transplanted vegetables. Tavioka is listed among starchy crops planted from cuttings.

cards.question: If a market table has baigani and kumala, which one is the eggplant?
cards.answer: Kumala is sweet potato. The two names point to different plants and different parts of a meal.

link.label: Explore Fiji's home-gardening guide

tavioka.title: Cassava in a Fiji garden
tavioka.intro: Tavioka names cassava. The Fiji guide groups it with starchy staples and lists cuttings as planting material.

cards.question: A family plants tavioka from stem cuttings. Which crop is it growing: cassava or sweet potato?
cards.answer: Tavioka is cassava; kumala is sweet potato, whose vine cuttings are used for planting.

cards.question: The guide names tavioka and uvi as resilient starchy crops. Does that make them two names for the same plant?
cards.answer: Tavioka is cassava and uvi is yam. They share a food-crop group without becoming synonyms.

link.label: Explore Fiji's home-gardening guide

uvi.title: Which root crop?
uvi.intro: Uvi is yam. Fiji's food guide lists it beside tavioka and kumala but keeps the three crop names separate.

cards.question: A recipe asks for uvi. Would replacing it with tavioka keep the same crop name?
cards.answer: Uvi names yam; tavioka names cassava. A cook may substitute ingredients, but the words do not name one crop.

cards.question: The garden guide gives cuttings or toppings for planting uvi. Does that instruction identify baigani seedlings?
cards.answer: The guide treats uvi as a starchy crop; baigani is an eggplant raised as a transplanted vegetable.

link.label: Explore Fiji's home-gardening guide

kumala.title: Sweet potato has its own name
kumala.intro: Kumala names sweet potato. A Fiji crop guide recommends planting healthy vine cuttings and describes several cultivated varieties.

cards.question: If a grower sets healthy vine cuttings for kumala, is the crop sweet potato or cassava?
cards.answer: Kumala is sweet potato; tavioka is cassava. The crop guide describes planting kumala from its vine.

cards.question: Does kumala identify just one named variety, such as Vulatolu?
cards.answer: Kumala is the crop name. Vulatolu is one variety listed in Fiji's crop guide, so the broader word does not identify a cultivar by itself.

link.label: See kumala varieties and planting advice

dovu.title: From cane field to sugar
dovu.intro: Dovu is sugarcane. Fiji's public reports use musu dovu for cane cutting, an activity tied to the sugar industry.

cards.question: In the recorded phrase musu dovu, what is being cut?
cards.answer: Dovu is the cane crop; tavioka is cassava. The Fiji Corrections Service uses musu dovu for its cane-cutting programme.

cards.question: A report discusses the price paid per tonne of dovu. Does dovu name the harvested cane or the white sugar on a table?
cards.answer: The report measures harvested sugarcane by weight. Dovu names the plant and its stalks, not every sweet food.

link.label: See musu dovu in a Fiji cane-growing report

dewaleka.title: Look at the ending
dewaleka.intro: Dewaleka is the short dewa family: -a or -i in the recorded forms. A whole predicate decides which ending is actually used.

cards.question: In mokuta and mokuti, which part is the short ending?
cards.answer: Moku is the base. The recorded short forms end with -a and -i; the preceding t belongs to the connecting material.

cards.question: Would mokulaka be another example of dewaleka just because it begins with moku?
cards.answer: Mokulaka carries the longer -aka family. Compare dewabalavu and check what the full phrase means before choosing a form.

dewabalavu.title: A longer ending can change the relationship
dewabalavu.intro: Dewabalavu covers the longer -aka and -aki forms. The examples mokulaka and mokulaki should be read as complete forms.

cards.question: Which recorded form carries the longer dewa ending: mokulaki or mokuti?
cards.answer: Mokulaki ends in -aki, from the longer family; mokuti belongs to the short -i family.

cards.question: Can you replace -aka with -aki in any predicate and assume the same participant relationship?
cards.answer: The longer forms are not a free spelling choice. Their meaning and affected participant need the attested base and phrase.

koso dewa.title: Find the connecting consonant
koso dewa.intro: Koso dewa is the consonant between a base and its dewa ending. It varies by word; a list of consonants is not a rule for inventing forms.

cards.question: In the recorded pair moku → mokuta, what stands between moku and the final -a?
cards.answer: The t is the connecting consonant. The base is moku and -a is the short ending in this analysis.

cards.question: If another base uses a different connecting consonant, may we write a new form by copying t from mokuta?
cards.answer: The consonant depends on the actual word and construction; find a recorded whole form before teaching it.

druadina.title: How much is repeated?
druadina.intro: Druadina is another name for druabalavu, where a longer stretch is repeated. The effect still depends on the particular word.

cards.question: In the recorded boroboro example, is a longer stretch repeated than in a drualeka pattern?
cards.answer: The classification is about the span repeated, not a promise that every repeated word means 'many'.

cards.question: Can a word's repeated shape alone prove a productive drua analysis?
cards.answer: Yavu drua names a base that already looks repeated. Check the lexical base before explaining a new formation.

yavu drua.title: A repeated look can mislead
yavu drua.intro: Yavu drua is a whole base with a repeated-looking shape. Totoka is the recorded illustration, not an invitation to invent a shorter base.

cards.question: Does totoka's visible pattern alone prove that a productive drua rule made it?
cards.answer: The source treats totoka as a lexical base. Its spelling is not enough to reconstruct a shorter word.

cards.question: What would make a stronger word-building claim: a guessed split, or a checked base plus related attested forms?
cards.answer: Druadina describes a repeat process; yavu drua reminds us that a similar-looking base may already be a word in its own right.

draki.title: What is the weather doing?
draki.intro: Draki names the weather or outdoor conditions. A fishing question asks whether the draki is suitable; a forecast can describe draki suasua, wet weather.

cards.question: In O na laki siwa ke vinaka na draki? (‘Will you go fishing if the weather is good?’), what does draki refer to?
cards.answer: The recorded question makes the trip conditional on good weather. It does not name a boat.

cards.question: A Fiji forecast mentions draki suasua. Is that the same as saying cagi alone?
cards.answer: Draki concerns the weather conditions as a whole; cagi specifically names wind, one possible part of the weather.

link.label: Read draki suasua in Fiji's climate advice

bulumakau.title: Cattle in life and in food
bulumakau.intro: Bulumakau names cattle. Food context can select beef, while a list of living farm animals selects the animal sense.

cards.question: In a public list of bulumakau, vuaka, ose and farm goods being sold, is bulumakau the living cattle or a prepared beef dish?
cards.answer: The listed animals are being sold for a journey; bulumakau identifies the cattle among them.

cards.question: In a food discussion, can bulumakau refer to beef without changing its spelling?
cards.answer: The recorded animal and meat readings share a form. The surrounding phrase tells you which is meant, just as vuaka can name pig or pork.

link.label: Read bulumakau beside vuaka in a Fijian account

akaude.title: The account and the money in it
akaude.intro: Akaude can name a bank account. A Fiji form writes akaude ni baqe, while ilavo is the money that may be kept in it.

cards.question: In akaude ni baqe, what does baqe tell you about the akaude?
cards.answer: Baqe identifies the bank relationship. Akaude names the account; the phrase does not give a balance.

cards.question: If money is paid into an akaude, does akaude itself tell you how much ilavo arrived?
cards.answer: Ilavo is money, and a figure would give its amount. Akaude is the account that can receive or hold it.

link.label: See akaude ni baqe in a Fiji public notice

taukeni nauni.title: Which relationship does the marker show?
taukeni nauni.intro: A noun-based taukeni phrase links one base to another. Nei, kei, mei and ni do different work in the recorded examples; the base and context matter.

cards.question: In na vale nei Luke and na sere kei Lia, which marker is used with Luke's house?
cards.answer: Nei marks the recorded house relationship; kei in the song example points toward Lia as its subject or addressee.

cards.question: The recorded na ulu ni vuaka links a body part to an animal. Would replacing ni with nei Luke keep that same related base?
cards.answer: Ni vuaka relates the head to a pig. Nei Luke would relate a phrase to the named person Luke; a new phrase needs its own meaning and context.

nauni taukeni kuri.title: Direct possession belongs to particular bases
nauni taukeni kuri.intro: Some kin and body-related bases accept possessive material directly; others use a preposed owner form. Check the whole word.

cards.question: In na dakuikeirau, does -ikeirau attach within the nominal word or appear before it as neirau?
cards.answer: The recorded dakuikeirau is a directly suffixed form. Na neirau dra is the contrasting preposed construction.

cards.question: The record accepts noqu qāvokavoka but rejects *qāvokavokaqu. Can every related body or kin base take a direct -qu?
cards.answer: Some bases use a preposed form such as noqu. The word class has to be checked base by base.

link.label: Explore a linguistic account of Fijian possession

balavu.title: Length can belong to time
balavu.intro: Balavu can describe physical length or height, and a Fiji public text also uses balavu ni gauna for a length of time.

cards.question: In balavu ni gauna, is the length measured along a road or across time?
cards.answer: Gauna means time. The public text discusses how long an order remains in force, not the length of an object.

cards.question: If a person is balavu, does that by itself mean the person is broad or numerous?
cards.answer: Balavu can describe height; levu concerns size, amount, or largeness. A full phrase resolves the intended reading.

link.label: Read balavu ni gauna in a Fiji legal summary

baravi.title: Where land meets the sea
baravi.intro: Baravi is coastal land or seashore. A Fiji building guide sets it beside bati ni uciwai, the edge of a river, as two places needing care.

cards.question: A building guide asks whether a house is e baravi. Is it asking about a coastal site or the middle of a river?
cards.answer: Baravi points to land along the shore; the same guide separately mentions a river's edge.

cards.question: Would bati ni uciwai and baravi name exactly the same kind of edge?
cards.answer: The first is the edge of a river; baravi is the seashore or coastal land. Both can matter for choosing a safe building site.

link.label: See the coastal and river-edge questions in Fiji's building guide

gade.title: Going for a visit
gade.intro: Gade suggests an outing for pleasure or a visit. Lako says someone goes without necessarily telling us why.

cards.question: A village report says visitors gade yani to see a local cave. Are they going for a visit or being described as commuters?
cards.answer: The context is visitors entering the village to see a place. Gade carries the outing sense in that passage.

cards.question: If a sentence says only that someone lako, can you infer the trip is a leisure gade?
cards.answer: Lako is a general going word. Gade adds the recreational or visiting purpose when context supports it.

link.label: Read gade in a Fiji village-visit report

basi.title: A ride and its fare
basi.intro: Basi is a bus. Fiji's public transport texts use vodo basi for riding one and discuss assistance with the fare.

cards.question: In vodo basi, which word names the vehicle rather than the action of boarding?
cards.answer: Basi is the bus. Vodo supplies the riding or boarding action in this recorded expression.

cards.question: A budget mentions ivodovodo ni Basi assistance. Is the help about passenger fares or about buying a whole bus?
cards.answer: The budget explains a subsidy on people's bus travel costs. The bus and the fare are related, but they are not the same thing.

link.label: See bus-fare assistance in Fiji's budget guide

uto-.title: Inside the word, around the word
uto-.intro: Uto- names the core of a matavosa: its yavu with any attached ikuri. A separate duru can sit around that core in the phrase.

cards.question: In an analysis written yavu + ikuri, do the attached ikuri belong inside the uto- or in a separate surrounding duru?
cards.answer: The core includes its base and attached word-building material. Duru is a distinct phrase element.

cards.question: If an analysis identifies a mata before a matanauni, does that alone tell us the lexical core of the predicate?
cards.answer: Mata marks a phrase boundary or relation; uto- concerns the central word form inside a matavosa. They answer different questions.

lau-.title: Look for the affected participant
lau-.intro: Lau- can bring the affected person or thing forward while the actor is left unstated. Laukana is a recorded example with an eaten or edible reading.

cards.question: In laukana, does the form itself name who did the eating?
cards.answer: The affected food is in focus; the eater is not named by the form. Context may add that information.

cards.question: If two people act on each other, is that the same relationship as lau- leaving an actor unstated?
cards.answer: Reciprocal vei- can express an exchanged action. Lau- in the cited construction focuses the affected participant instead.

link.label: Read an older recorded laukana analysis

gauna.title: A day is one measure of time
gauna.intro: Gauna can mean a time, period or occasion. A phrase such as balavu ni gauna asks about duration; siga names a day.

cards.question: A form asks Vakaevei na balavu ni gauna e taura? (‘How long does it take?’). Is it asking for a duration or a place?
cards.answer: Balavu ni gauna asks about the length of time an action takes.

cards.question: If a notice says an answer takes five siga, which word supplies the day as a unit rather than time in general?
cards.answer: Gauna is the broader time word; siga counts days in the notice.

link.label: Read a Fiji form about processing time

siga.title: Day, daylight and night
siga.intro: Siga can identify a day or the light of day; bogi points to night. Context decides which siga sense is active.

cards.question: A Fiji form says the process takes five siga. Is it counting days or five flashes of sunlight?
cards.answer: Here siga is the day as a unit of time.

cards.question: If a story contrasts light during siga with darkness at bogi, which side is night?
cards.answer: Siga can point to daylight in this contrast, while bogi names night.

link.label: See siga counted in a Fiji public form

kakana.title: Food in an ordinary meal or a feast
kakana.intro: Kakana is food. Magiti brings food into a feast or ceremonial presentation; mamau is the feeling of having eaten enough.

cards.question: If a plate holds kakana, is mamau the food on the plate or the feeling after enough of it?
cards.answer: Kakana names the food; mamau describes the satisfied person.

cards.question: Does calling food magiti add a feast or presentation setting beyond the broad word kakana?
cards.answer: Magiti is the more situated food word. Kakana alone does not announce a feast.

mamau.title: Enough food, a particular feeling
mamau.intro: Mamau is being full and satisfied after eating. It is a state of the eater, not the name of the meal.

cards.question: After a meal, which word names the satisfied state rather than the meal itself?
cards.answer: Kakana is food; mamau is how someone feels after enough food.

cards.question: Someone can be marau about a visit without having eaten. Does that automatically make them mamau?
cards.answer: Marau is happiness or delight; mamau is fullness from food. The feelings can coincide but do not mean the same thing.

makete.title: Going to the market
makete.intro: Makete is a market. Ki na makete means ‘to the market’; sitoa is a shop.

cards.question: In Ki na makete (‘to the market’), is makete the destination or the item bought?
cards.answer: Ki na introduces the destination; makete names the marketplace.

cards.question: Would sitoa give exactly the same setting as makete in every sentence?
cards.answer: Sitoa names a shop; makete names a market. Both involve trade, but the place differs.

link.label: See the market phrase in a Fijian lesson

sitoa.title: A shop is a place, not its stock
sitoa.intro: Sitoa is a shop or store. Makete names a market, another kind of trading place.

cards.question: If someone names the sitoa, have they named the building or place, or every item on its shelves?
cards.answer: The word names the shop. The goods need their own words.

cards.question: Does the spelling sitoa copy every letter of English store?
cards.answer: The borrowed shop word has been adapted to Fijian spelling and ends in a vowel.

raraba.title: Wide is a direction of measurement
raraba.intro: Raraba concerns breadth. Qiqo points toward narrowness; balavu concerns length or height.

cards.question: A path has room for several people side by side. Which description addresses that width: raraba or balavu?
cards.answer: Raraba looks across the path. Balavu would say how long it is.

cards.question: If the same path becomes too narrow for two people abreast, which word gives the opposite direction?
cards.answer: Qiqo is narrow; raraba is broad or wide.

qiqo.title: A narrow route
qiqo.intro: Qiqo describes narrowness, especially where a path or road has little room across. Its opposite is raraba.

cards.question: Two people cannot walk side by side on a qiqo path. Is the problem its width or its length?
cards.answer: Qiqo concerns little room across. Balavu would concern length.

cards.question: If a route is qiqo but also balavu, must it be short because it is narrow?
cards.answer: Width and length are separate. A narrow route can still run a long way.

marau.title: Happiness is not fullness
marau.intro: Marau describes happiness or delight. Mamau concerns being full after eating; rarawa points toward sadness.

cards.question: A visitor is glad to see a friend but has eaten nothing. Which feeling can still fit: marau or mamau?
cards.answer: Marau is the happy feeling; mamau requires the food-related sense of satisfaction.

cards.question: If the story turns from joy to sorrow, which word marks the change away from marau?
cards.answer: Rarawa names sorrow. Totoka praises beauty, which is a different kind of judgment.

totoka.title: Beauty, goodness and a doubled-looking base
totoka.intro: Totoka praises what is pleasing or beautiful. Vinaka is a broader word for good; totoka is also treated as a whole yavu drua base.

cards.question: If you praise a view because it looks beautiful, which word is the more specific choice?
cards.answer: Vinaka can mean good in many ways; totoka focuses on beauty or pleasing appearance.

cards.question: Does totoka's doubled-looking shape prove that you may remove a piece to make its true base?
cards.answer: This word is recorded as a yavu drua, a lexical base already shaped that way. A visual pattern is not enough to invent a shorter form.

mate.title: The phrase tells which mate
mate.intro: Mate can concern illness or death. A full phrase is needed before deciding which reading a speaker intends.

cards.question: In mate rerevaki (‘a feared disease’), is mate about an illness or the time of day?
cards.answer: Rerevaki describes the disease as feared. The phrase is used in Fiji public health writing.

cards.question: If a brief account says only mate, can we safely decide whether it means an illness or a death?
cards.answer: The same spelling has both readings. Ask for the whole phrase before treating one English gloss as fixed.

link.label: Read mate rerevaki in a Fiji health guide

qase.title: Age, respect and a whole phrase
qase.intro: Qase can identify an older person. Turaga may be a chief or a respectful address; qase ni vuli names a teacher.

cards.question: If someone is called qase, does that word alone establish that they hold a chiefly title?
cards.answer: Qase points to age or seniority. A chiefly title must be established separately; turaga also has respectful uses.

cards.question: In qase ni vuli, is the whole phrase simply any older person or a teaching role?
cards.answer: The whole expression names a schoolteacher; its meaning cannot be read by stopping at qase.

lekaleka.title: Short in space or time
lekaleka.intro: Lekaleka can make a route short or a visit brief. Balavu points the other way.

cards.question: If a trip covers little distance, which word fits the route: lekaleka or balavu?
cards.answer: Lekaleka describes its short length; balavu would describe a long one.

cards.question: A visit is lekaleka. Is that about how long the visit lasts or how small the visitor is?
cards.answer: The word can extend from length to a brief period. Gauna is the broader word for time.

buto.title: Darkness is not a clock
buto.intro: Buto can name or describe darkness. Bogi is night, a time during which it is often dark.

cards.question: A room has no light at midday. Can it be buto even though it is not bogi?
cards.answer: Buto concerns darkness, not the hour. A place can be dark during the day.

cards.question: In a story that begins at bogi, does bogi itself name the quality of darkness or the night-time setting?
cards.answer: Bogi identifies night; buto describes darkness. The two often coincide but are distinct words.

matanitu.title: A political level in a wider place
matanitu.intro: Matanitu names a state or government. Vanua has a wider range of meanings, including land and the community connected with it.

cards.question: In a public document about a state decision, which word names the governing authority: matanitu or vanua?
cards.answer: Matanitu points to state authority; vanua can include land, place and its connected community.

cards.question: In the community sequence matanitu, yasana, tikina and koro, which level is above yasana?
cards.answer: Matanitu is the wider political level in that sequence. The levels help locate a place but do not replace its local relationships.

vanua.title: More than a patch of soil
vanua.intro: Vanua may name land, a place, territory or people connected with it. The surrounding phrase decides how much is included.

cards.question: If a speaker means the people and place connected through a shared territory, is nuku broad enough to carry all of that?
cards.answer: Nuku is sand. Vanua can have a wider place and community sense.

cards.question: Would matanitu always replace vanua in a phrase about ancestral land and community?
cards.answer: Matanitu names political authority; vanua can carry land and community relationships beyond that institution.

toba.title: A bay along the coast
toba.intro: Toba is a bay or sheltered inlet. Baravi is coastal land; waitui is sea water more broadly.

cards.question: A place is named na toba o Laucala. Are you being directed to a bay or to an inland mountain?
cards.answer: Toba names a coastal inlet in this recorded place expression.

cards.question: If a map shows a toba inside the shoreline, does waitui name only that sheltered inlet?
cards.answer: Waitui can name sea water or the sea more broadly; toba narrows the place to a bay.

uciwai.title: The river and its edge
uciwai.intro: Uciwai is a river or stream. Bati ni uciwai is its edge; waitui refers to sea water.

cards.question: In bati ni uciwai, which part names the river rather than its edge?
cards.answer: Bati names the edge in this phrase; uciwai names the watercourse.

cards.question: If a boat leaves the river for open salt water, which word is the sea-water side of the contrast?
cards.answer: Uciwai identifies the river or stream; waitui identifies sea water or the sea.

link.label: See bati ni uciwai in Fiji's building guide

baqe.title: A bank, its accounts and its name
baqe.intro: Baqe is a bank. Akaude ni baqe names an account at one; Fiji's Reserve Bank has a longer institutional name.

cards.question: In akaude ni baqe, which word names the bank rather than the customer's account?
cards.answer: Baqe names the institution; akaude is the account held with it.

cards.question: Would Baqe ni Lavo Maroroi ni Matanitu ko Viti mean every ordinary branch bank?
cards.answer: That longer expression names Fiji's Reserve Bank. Baqe by itself is the broader word for a bank.

bia.title: A drink and a purpose for possession
bia.intro: Bia names beer. In Oqo na mequ bia, mequ identifies the drink as the speaker's to consume.

cards.question: In Oqo na mequ bia (‘This is my beer to drink’), does mequ tell us the beer is for the speaker to drink or to wear?
cards.answer: The attested mequ construction marks a consumable for the speaker. English 'my' alone hides that relationship.

cards.question: Would replacing bia with yaqona keep the same drink?
cards.answer: Bia is beer; yaqona is kava, a different beverage with different social settings.

link.label: See the bia example in a Fijian lesson

isele.title: A cutting tool
isele.intro: Isele is a knife. The particular knife may be identified by its work, such as gardening; moto is a spear.

cards.question: Someone needs a blade for a gardening task. Which broad tool name can fit: isele or moto?
cards.answer: Isele is a knife and can be a gardening knife in context. Moto names a spear.

cards.question: If a description calls an isele gata, which part names the tool and which gives its sharpness?
cards.answer: Gata can describe a sharp point or blade; isele names the knife.

moto.title: The spear and its edge
moto.intro: Moto is a spear. Isele is a knife; gata can describe a sharp point on either suitable tool.

cards.question: An older account names a moto among weapons. Is it naming a spear or a basket?
cards.answer: Moto names the spear; kato names a basket or box.

cards.question: If a moto is described as gata, does gata replace the name of the spear?
cards.answer: Gata adds the sharp quality. Moto still names the object.

kato.title: A container for things, not a cup for a drink
kato.intro: Kato can be a basket or box. Bilo is a cup or small drinking vessel.

cards.question: A person carries several pieces of produce in one container. Which word can name the basket: kato or bilo?
cards.answer: Kato can carry or hold goods; bilo is a drinking cup.

cards.question: Does kato by itself say whether this container is woven as a basket or made as a box?
cards.answer: The checked meaning covers both; the surrounding description or an image would identify the material and shape.

benisini.title: Fuel with a borrowed name
benisini.intro: Benisini means petrol or gasoline used as motor fuel. Its spelling resembles English benzine, but the English solvent name is not a safe everyday translation.

cards.question: A driver puts benisini in a motoka. Is the word naming the fuel or the car?
cards.answer: Benisini is petrol; motoka is the vehicle using it.

cards.question: Would an English label 'benzine solvent' safely explain every Fijian use of benisini?
cards.answer: Here benisini is the motor fuel. Similar-looking English technical terms can mislead a reader.

gata.title: Sharp describes the edge
gata.intro: Gata can describe a sharp point or blade. It does not itself name the knife or spear that has the edge.

cards.question: If an isele is gata, which word gives the sharp quality?
cards.answer: Isele identifies the knife; gata tells you its edge is sharp.

cards.question: Can a moto be gata without becoming an isele?
cards.answer: Sharpness can apply to a spear's point too. Moto and isele remain different tools.

koli.title: A dog and its owner
koli.intro: Koli is a dog. Manumanu is a wider animal word; noqu can tell whose dog is meant.

cards.question: If a story names a koli, have we learned that the animal is a dog or only that it is some manumanu?
cards.answer: Koli is the specific dog word; manumanu covers a wider range of animals.

cards.question: In the attested phrase na noqu koli, which word tells you the dog belongs to the speaker?
cards.answer: Koli names the dog. Noqu expresses the owner's relationship to it.

link.label: Read na noqu koli in a Fijian text

macala.title: Clear does not mean solved
macala.intro: Macala can say that something is clear or understood. A leqa can be clearly explained while remaining a problem.

cards.question: If the cause of a leqa is now macala, has the problem necessarily been fixed?
cards.answer: Macala concerns clarity or understanding. Leqa names the difficulty, which may still need action.

cards.question: Two answers are duidui but both are easy to understand. Can both still be macala?
cards.answer: Duidui marks their difference; macala concerns how clear each answer is.

motoka.title: Vehicle, person and fuel
motoka.intro: Motoka is a car. Draiva names the person driving; benisini names its fuel.

cards.question: In advice that mentions a motoka and a draiva, which word names the vehicle?
cards.answer: The motoka is the car; the draiva is a person who drives it.

cards.question: If a car needs benisini, is the missing item another vehicle or its fuel?
cards.answer: Benisini is petrol. It belongs in the vehicle but does not name the vehicle.

link.label: Read motoka and draiva in Fiji health advice

maqo.title: A mango in the seasonal calendar
maqo.intro: Maqo names a mango. Fiji's traditional calendar places the mango season alongside the maturing of other fruit, including vudi.

cards.question: The calendar says via oti na maqo while vudi is maturing. Which named fruit is nearing the end of its season?
cards.answer: The recorded phrase says the mango season is nearly over; it separately describes vudi maturing.

cards.question: Could maqo and vudi be translated as the same fruit just because both appear in that calendar entry?
cards.answer: Maqo is mango and vudi is plantain. A shared season does not make the plants identical.

link.label: Explore Fiji's traditional seasonal calendar

duidui.title: Different without changing
duidui.intro: Duidui says things are distinct from one another. Veisau concerns change, which is another relationship.

cards.question: Two already existing designs are duidui. Must either design have changed?
cards.answer: Duidui compares difference between them; it does not by itself report a change over time.

cards.question: If one design later becomes different from its earlier version, which word draws attention to the change?
cards.answer: Veisau points to change. Duidui can describe the difference between the two versions.

ibe.title: A mat with local stories
ibe.intro: Ibe names a mat. Some forms have their own local histories, such as the ibe vaNamuka associated with Namuka in Macuata.

cards.question: The name ibe vaNamuka identifies a tradition tied to Namuka. Does ibe alone name every local style?
cards.answer: Ibe is the broad mat word; the longer name identifies one local weaving tradition.

cards.question: A public account lists yaqona, ibe and tabua among customary items. Which one is the mat?
cards.answer: Ibe is the mat; tabua is a whale tooth. Their ceremonial contexts can overlap without the objects being alike.

link.label: Read about the ibe vaNamuka tradition

isulu.title: Clothing and whose it is
isulu.intro: Isulu is clothing or a garment. Its name alone does not say who wears or owns it.

cards.question: Would a woven ibe used on a floor normally be called isulu just because both involve fibres?
cards.answer: Isulu names clothing; ibe names a mat. Their uses matter more than the shared material.

cards.question: If a sentence only gives isulu, can you tell whose garment it is?
cards.answer: An owner needs more context or possessive material. The clothing word alone leaves that relationship open.

kuro.title: The vessel, not the meal
kuro.intro: Kuro is a cooking pot. Kato can hold or carry things; kakana is the food itself.

cards.question: A family cooks a meal in a kuro. Does kuro name the pot or the cooked kakana?
cards.answer: Kuro is the vessel used in cooking; kakana is the food.

cards.question: Someone carries uncooked produce in a kato. Has the word kato named the same vessel as kuro?
cards.answer: Kato is a basket or box; kuro is a cooking pot. Both hold things but serve different tasks.

leqa.title: Knowing the problem is one step
leqa.intro: Leqa is a problem or difficulty. Macala can describe an explanation that makes the problem clear.

cards.question: If someone says the leqa is macala, do you know the problem has gone away?
cards.answer: A clear explanation may identify a problem without resolving it.

cards.question: Can a person feel madua because of a leqa while the two words still name different things?
cards.answer: Leqa is the difficulty; madua is embarrassment or shame a person may feel about it.

levulevu.title: A body description, not every large thing
levulevu.intro: Levulevu concerns a stout or fat build. Levu is the broader word for large; raraba concerns width.

cards.question: For a person's stout build, which word is the specific description: levulevu or raraba?
cards.answer: Levulevu describes bodily build; raraba describes breadth or width.

cards.question: Would levulevu be the safe general translation for large eyes just because levu can mean large?
cards.answer: Levulevu has the body-build meaning. Levu can describe size more generally; the whole phrase decides the best form.

madua.title: A feeling after an event
madua.intro: Madua is feeling ashamed or embarrassed. The situation that causes the feeling needs its own description.

cards.question: A person is madua about a leqa. Which word names the feeling?
cards.answer: Madua is the feeling; leqa is the difficulty being discussed.

cards.question: Could someone feel madua without the word itself telling us what happened?
cards.answer: The adjective reports embarrassment or shame, not its cause. Ask for the surrounding story.

mamaqi.title: Reluctance to share
mamaqi.intro: Mamaqi describes someone unwilling to give or share freely. It does not measure how much money that person has.

cards.question: A person has plenty of ilavo but refuses to share any. Which word speaks to the unwillingness?
cards.answer: Ilavo is money; mamaqi describes the person's reluctance to give.

cards.question: Can you infer someone's bank balance solely because they are called mamaqi?
cards.answer: The word judges a habit or attitude toward giving, not the amount in an akaude.

manumanu.title: The broad animal word
manumanu.intro: Manumanu names an animal and can refer especially to a bird in some contexts. The rest of the phrase helps narrow it.

cards.question: If a speaker says only manumanu, have they identified a dog as precisely as koli would?
cards.answer: Koli specifies a dog. Manumanu leaves the kind of animal open.

cards.question: If a family records its neitou manumanu, does the word alone reveal which bird or animal is connected with them?
cards.answer: The family or village must supply the actual name. Manumanu only tells you the broad kind of living thing being asked about.

matua.title: Fully developed depends on the fruit
matua.intro: Matua describes something mature or fully developed. A Fiji seasonal account uses it for vudi; a nearly ripe fruit can be described differently.

cards.question: In the traditional calendar, matua na vudi concerns a plantain's stage. Is this about maturity or the colour of the sky?
cards.answer: The calendar records the vudi as mature at that time of year.

cards.question: If a fruit is only carawabobota, nearly ripe, has it reached the fully mature or ready stage implied by matua in every context?
cards.answer: Carawabobota marks a near-ripe stage; matua is broader and needs the crop and sentence for its exact reading.

link.label: See matua na vudi in Fiji's seasonal calendar

turaga.title: Respect is wider than a title
turaga.intro: Turaga can name a chief or address a man respectfully. A sentence or title must show which sense is intended.

cards.question: If an account calls someone turaga, can you conclude from that word alone that he holds a chiefly title?
cards.answer: Turaga is also respectful address. The office, if any, needs separate evidence.

cards.question: Does cauravou describe the same thing as a chiefly title when it identifies a young man?
cards.answer: Cauravou concerns a young man's life stage or social description; turaga may be a respectful address or chiefly term.

uca.title: Rain within the wider weather
uca.intro: Uca is rain. Draki is the broader weather or climate, and a report may describe weather without saying it rained.

cards.question: If a forecast discusses draki, does it necessarily promise uca?
cards.answer: Draki covers weather more broadly; uca specifically names rain.

cards.question: A seasonal calendar says tau bi na uca. Which word identifies what is falling?
cards.answer: The phrase describes heavy rain. Uca is the rain; siga is a day or daylight.

link.label: Read tau bi na uca in Fiji's seasonal calendar

vudi.title: Plantain and the season
vudi.intro: Vudi is a plantain, often cooked as food. Fiji's traditional calendar records when it matures alongside other fruit.

cards.question: The calendar says matua na vudi. Which word names the plantain: vudi or matua?
cards.answer: Vudi names the crop; matua describes its mature stage.

cards.question: If a basket has vudi and maqo, are both names for the same fruit?
cards.answer: Vudi is plantain and maqo is mango. Their preparation and use differ.

link.label: Explore Fiji's traditional seasonal calendar

bisinisi.title: Trade as an activity
bisinisi.intro: Bisinisi is business or commercial activity. A sitoa may be one place where business happens, but the two words do different jobs.

cards.question: A family runs a bisinisi from several places. Does bisinisi name the activity or one particular sitoa?
cards.answer: Bisinisi is the enterprise or trade; sitoa names a shop.

cards.question: If a business keeps an akaude at a baqe, which word names the business itself?
cards.answer: A baqe is a bank and an akaude is an account; neither is automatically the business.

cauravou.title: A young man in a village account
cauravou.intro: Cauravou describes a young man; in some contexts it also carries the sense that he is not yet married.

cards.question: An account mentions cauravou ni koro. Does cauravou identify young men or chiefly titles?
cards.answer: The phrase speaks about young men of a village, not the title of its chief.

cards.question: Would qase be the more likely word for an elder in a contrast between generations?
cards.answer: Qase concerns an older person; cauravou points toward youth. Context and local usage still matter.

link.label: Read cauravou ni koro in Fiji Focus

draiva.title: The person, not the car
draiva.intro: Draiva is a driver. Motoka is the car; benisini is its fuel.

cards.question: A health notice mentions pasidia and draiva. Is the draiva a person travelling in the vehicle or the vehicle itself?
cards.answer: Draiva names the driver; motoka names a car.

cards.question: Does draiva end in the same consonant as English driver?
cards.answer: The borrowed form follows Fijian spelling and ends in a vowel, unlike the English word.

link.label: Read draiva in Fiji health advice

dravuisiga.title: The sun's effect on land
dravuisiga.intro: Dravuisiga describes land parched or scorched by sun. Uca is rain, which would change the conditions rather than name the dryness.

cards.question: A field has become dravuisiga. Is the land wet from uca or parched by the sun?
cards.answer: The word describes sun-scorched land; uca is rain.

cards.question: Does dravuisiga by itself tell us which crop was growing in the field?
cards.answer: It describes the land's condition. A separate crop name, such as tavioka, would identify what grew there.

icurucuru.title: Paying to enter
icurucuru.intro: Icurucuru is an admission fee. Ilavo is money more generally; the entrance purpose makes this payment specific.

cards.question: A notice asks for icurucuru before someone enters an event. Is it a fee for entry or the whole amount in their akaude?
cards.answer: Icurucuru names the admission payment, not every sum of money someone owns.

cards.question: If an entrance is free, is there necessarily an icurucuru to pay?
cards.answer: The word identifies a charge for admission; an entry without a charge has no fee of that kind.

idabedabe.title: The place to sit
idabedabe.intro: Idabedabe names a seat or chair. An ibe can also be used under a seated person, but it is a mat, not the same named object.

cards.question: Someone brings an idabedabe into a room. Have they brought a seat or a cooking kuro?
cards.answer: Idabedabe names the seating object; kuro is a pot.

cards.question: Can an ibe serve as a place to sit without becoming the same kind of object as an idabedabe?
cards.answer: Ibe is a mat; idabedabe is a seat or chair. Similar use does not erase the difference.

ikatalau.title: The first meal, whenever the clock says
ikatalau.intro: Ikatalau names breakfast. A Fiji account places an ikatalau at eight in the morning, but the word names the meal rather than one fixed hour.

cards.question: A Fiji account says ikatalau ena walu na kaloko. Is ikatalau the breakfast or the number eight?
cards.answer: The phrase puts the meal at eight o'clock; ikatalau itself names breakfast.

cards.question: If a household eats breakfast at a different hour, must the meal stop being ikatalau?
cards.answer: The word names the morning meal, not a particular clock time.

link.label: Read the breakfast account in Fiji Focus

itau.title: A friend in a real phrase
itau.intro: Itau names a friend. Fijian writing also uses itokani for a friend, but the surrounding words may give the relationship more detail.

cards.question: In the attested phrase noqu itau, which word names the friend and which marks the relationship to the speaker?
cards.answer: Itau is the friend word; noqu identifies the speaker's relationship to that friend.

cards.question: A passage uses noqu itau and noqu itokani. Must those phrases name two different people?
cards.answer: The words can both refer to a friend. The whole passage decides whether it is the same person or two people.

link.label: Read noqu itau beside noqu itokani

kateni.title: Which kind of container?
kateni.intro: Kateni is a carton or cardboard box. Kato is broader for a basket or box, and tavaya names a bottle.

cards.question: A parcel arrives in a cardboard carton. Which word picks out that packaging: kateni or tavaya?
cards.answer: Kateni names a carton; tavaya is a bottle.

cards.question: Could a woven kato be useful without being a kateni?
cards.answer: Kato can be a basket or box. Kateni is specifically the carton or cardboard-box kind.

keba.title: A camp is a setting, not a building type
keba.intro: Keba is an organised camp, such as a military or scouting camp. An otela is a hotel, which offers another kind of stay.

cards.question: A scouting group stays together at a keba. Is the word naming the camp or an otela?
cards.answer: Keba names the organised camp; otela names a hotel.

cards.question: Can the same word keba cover a military camp and a scouting camp without making them the same activity?
cards.answer: The headword identifies the camp setting. The people and purpose tell which kind of camp it is.

kemesi.title: Medicine has a place and a person
kemesi.intro: Kemesi is a pharmacy or chemist's shop. A vuniwai is a doctor; sitoa is the broader shop word.

cards.question: A person goes to a kemesi for medicine. Is kemesi the pharmacy or the vuniwai who treats them?
cards.answer: Kemesi names the shop; vuniwai names a medical practitioner.

cards.question: If an account says only sitoa, does that already tell us it is a kemesi?
cards.answer: Sitoa is a shop in general. Kemesi narrows it to a pharmacy.

lase.title: Coral is not every grain of sand
lase.intro: Lase can name coral or coral sand. Nuku is sand more generally, while cakau is a reef.

cards.question: Someone points to nuku on a beach. Can you conclude every grain is coral-based lase?
cards.answer: Nuku is sand; lase is the more specific coral or coral-sand reading.

cards.question: A map marks a cakau offshore. Does that name the whole reef or a loose piece of lase?
cards.answer: Cakau identifies a reef structure; lase can identify coral material.

lesoni.title: A lesson can use a book
lesoni.intro: Lesoni is a lesson or teaching unit. Ivola may hold its written material; qase ni vuli names a teacher.

cards.question: A qase ni vuli prepares a lesoni. Which expression names the teacher rather than the teaching unit?
cards.answer: The teacher leads the learning; the lesoni is what is being taught.

cards.question: If a lesoni appears in an ivola, must the whole book consist of only that one lesson?
cards.answer: Ivola is a book or written record. It may contain one lesson, many lessons, or other writing.

lovo.title: Cooking under the ground
lovo.intro: A lovo is a Fijian earth oven: hot stones heat food in a covered pit. A kuro is a cooking pot, a different vessel.

cards.question: In a lovo, is the heat held in a covered pit with hot stones or inside a portable kuro?
cards.answer: The earth oven uses heated stones and covering to cook food; kuro is a pot.

cards.question: A visitor enjoys the kakana from a lovo. Does lovo name the cooking method and oven or each food item by itself?
cards.answer: The cooked foods still have their own names. Lovo tells how they were prepared.

link.label: See how a Fijian lovo is prepared

lululu.title: A greeting by hand
lululu.intro: Lululu is shaking hands or a handshake. It is a physical greeting, not the relationship of friendship itself.

cards.question: Can two people lululu when they first meet, before they are itau?
cards.answer: A handshake is an action. Itau names a friend, a relationship that is not established by the gesture alone.

cards.question: Fiji health guidance once advised people to avoid lululu. Was it asking them to stop shaking hands or to stop being friends?
cards.answer: The advice addressed physical contact during a health emergency, not the existence of friendship.

link.label: Read lululu in Fiji health guidance

maile.title: Distance without a clock
maile.intro: Maile is a mile, a distance unit. Miniti measures time; raraba can describe how wide a route is.

cards.question: A road is two maile long. Does that tell you the distance or the number of miniti needed to travel it?
cards.answer: Maile measures distance. Miniti measures elapsed time, which depends on the journey.

cards.question: A path has a length in maile. Has that number also told you whether the path is raraba?
cards.answer: Length and width are separate measures. Raraba concerns breadth.

masese.title: What lights the fire?
masese.intro: Masese is a match or matches for lighting a fire. Waqaca is the action of lighting it.

cards.question: Someone uses a masese to waqaca a fire. Which word names the match?
cards.answer: Masese is the small lighting item; waqaca names the lighting action.

cards.question: Would calling a cooking kuro masese tell you what the pot is?
cards.answer: Kuro is the vessel for cooking; masese can help start the fire but does not name the pot.

matasawa.title: Where land meets a landing
matasawa.intro: Matasawa is a beach or shore used as a landing place. Baravi names coast more broadly; waitui names sea water.

cards.question: A boat reaches a matasawa. Does the word direct you to a landing shore or to open waitui?
cards.answer: Matasawa identifies the shore or landing place; waitui is the sea-water side.

cards.question: If a route follows baravi for miles, must every part of that coast be a matasawa?
cards.answer: Baravi is coastal land broadly; matasawa is a shore associated with landing.

nuku.title: Sand is a material, not a whole place
nuku.intro: Nuku is sand. Baravi is coastal land, and lase can refer specifically to coral sand.

cards.question: A handful of nuku comes from a baravi. Which word names the material in the hand?
cards.answer: Nuku is sand; baravi is the coast where it may be found.

cards.question: Can someone know a beach has nuku without knowing whether that sand is coral lase?
cards.answer: The broad sand word does not identify what the grains are made from.

ivava.title: Footwear and an action built from it
ivava.intro: Ivava is footwear. Fiji health guidance uses vakaivava when telling people to wear shoes outdoors.

cards.question: In the advice nomu vakaivava, is the action about wearing footwear or washing an isulu?
cards.answer: The advice concerns shoes on the feet; isulu is the broader clothing word.

cards.question: Does ivava name every kind of isulu, or the part worn on the feet?
cards.answer: Ivava narrows the item to shoes or other footwear.

link.label: Read Fiji health advice about wearing footwear

masi.title: Cloth and mat are different crafts
masi.intro: Masi is Fijian barkcloth. Ibe is a woven mat; their materials and uses can be discussed together without merging the words.

cards.question: A heritage report lists Masi Vulavula and Ibe Draukekua separately. Which broad word is barkcloth?
cards.answer: Masi is barkcloth; ibe is a mat. The longer names identify particular local traditions.

cards.question: If a visitor sees a piece of masi displayed beside an ibe, can the visitor assume they were made by the same technique?
cards.answer: Barkcloth and woven mat involve different materials and making methods. Ask about the maker and place for the specific tradition.

link.label: Read a Fiji heritage report on masi and ibe

miniti.title: Minutes measure how long
miniti.intro: Miniti is a minute, a time unit. Aua is an hour; maile measures distance instead.

cards.question: A journey takes twenty miniti. Have you learned its time or its distance in maile?
cards.answer: Miniti measures duration; maile measures distance along the route.

cards.question: How many miniti make one aua?
cards.answer: One hour has sixty minutes. Aua is the hour word, while miniti is the smaller unit.

moli.title: A citrus fruit in a seasonal account
moli.intro: Moli often names an orange or another citrus fruit. It is distinct from a maqo, a mango.

cards.question: The traditional calendar says dreu na moli. Which fruit is ripening there: citrus or mango?
cards.answer: Moli identifies the citrus fruit; maqo would identify a mango.

cards.question: Does moli on its own tell you the exact citrus variety in the speaker's hand?
cards.answer: The word has a range of citrus uses, with orange especially common. A more detailed context identifies a variety.

link.label: See moli in Fiji's seasonal calendar

namu.title: A mosquito in the changing season
namu.intro: Namu is a mosquito. Fiji's traditional calendar records a time when mosquitoes are fewer as bad weather eases.

cards.question: A household notices fewer namu. Has it counted mosquitoes or qasikalolo?
cards.answer: Namu are mosquitoes; qasikalolo are ants.

cards.question: The calendar says lailai tale ga na namu after draki ca eases. Does that report a seasonal observation or say mosquitoes can never appear then?
cards.answer: The text records fewer mosquitoes in that period; it does not promise none in every place.

link.label: Read namu in Fiji's seasonal calendar

ose.title: A horse is not the car that travels beside it
ose.intro: Ose is a horse. It is a manumanu, while a motoka is a vehicle made by people.

cards.question: A traveller rides an ose. Has the word named an animal or a motoka?
cards.answer: Ose names the horse; motoka names a car.

cards.question: Would the broad word manumanu identify that animal as specifically as ose does?
cards.answer: Manumanu leaves the animal kind open. Ose narrows it to a horse.

otela.title: A place for visitors to stay
otela.intro: Otela is a hotel. A vulagi is a visitor or guest, who may stay in a hotel or somewhere else.

cards.question: A vulagi checks into an otela. Which word names the place to stay?
cards.answer: Otela is the hotel; vulagi is the visitor.

cards.question: If a group stays at a keba, must the place also be an otela?
cards.answer: Keba is an organised camp, a different setting from a hotel.

vulagi.title: The visitor and the welcome
vulagi.intro: Vulagi is a visitor or guest. The place they stay or the way hosts receive them is a separate part of the story.

cards.question: If someone is a vulagi, does that word tell you they are staying at an otela?
cards.answer: Vulagi identifies the visitor, not their accommodation. A guest may stay with hosts or elsewhere.

cards.question: When a vulagi arrives in a village, which expression names a customary presentation that may introduce visitors?
cards.answer: I sevusevu is a customary presentation; icurucuru is an admission fee and should not be substituted for it.

qase ni vuli.title: The whole phrase names the teacher
qase ni vuli.intro: Qase ni vuli names a schoolteacher. Qase alone can mean an older person; lesoni is what a teacher may prepare.

cards.question: If someone is a qase ni vuli, does the whole phrase name any elder or a teacher?
cards.answer: The complete expression is the teaching role; qase alone has a wider age-related sense.

cards.question: A qase ni vuli prepares a lesoni. Which expression identifies the teaching unit?
cards.answer: Lesoni is the lesson; qase ni vuli is the teacher.

qasikalolo.title: The insect, not its mound
qasikalolo.intro: Qasikalolo is an ant. Buri can name an anthill; namu is a mosquito.

cards.question: A qasikalolo comes out of a buri. Which word names the ant itself?
cards.answer: Qasikalolo names the insect; buri is its mound or nest.

cards.question: If someone complains of namu, have they named the same insect as qasikalolo?
cards.answer: Namu is a mosquito; qasikalolo is an ant.

rarawa.title: Sorrow among other feelings
rarawa.intro: Rarawa is sorrow or sadness. Marau is joy; rere is fear, which is another feeling again.

cards.question: A reunion turns from rarawa to marau. What has changed?
cards.answer: Rarawa names sorrow; marau names happiness or delight.

cards.question: Someone is rere about what may happen but rarawa about what already happened. Do the two words name exactly the same feeling?
cards.answer: Rere is fear; rarawa is sadness. The same event can cause both, but they are not interchangeable.

rere.title: Fear and courage
rere.intro: Rere is fear. Yaloqaqa is courageous; rarawa is sadness rather than fear itself.

cards.question: A person acts while still feeling rere. Does acting yaloqaqa require that no fear exists?
cards.answer: Courage concerns how one faces a situation; rere names the feeling of fear.

cards.question: A loss brings rarawa but no threat. Which word names sadness rather than fear?
cards.answer: Rarawa is sorrow; rere is fear of danger or what may happen.

sote.title: A shirt within clothing
sote.intro: Sote names a shirt. Isulu is the broader clothing word; ivava is footwear.

cards.question: A person puts on a sote. Has the word told you the garment is a shirt or any kind of isulu?
cards.answer: Sote is the particular garment; isulu covers clothing more broadly.

cards.question: Someone also puts on ivava. Does ivava name another shirt?
cards.answer: Ivava is footwear. A complete outfit can include both a sote and shoes.

sovu.title: Soap and the result of washing
sovu.intro: Sovu is soap. Fiji health guidance pairs it with water for washing hands; savasava describes a clean state.

cards.question: The guidance says sovu kei na wai. Which word names the soap?
cards.answer: Sovu is the substance used in washing. Savasava describes cleanliness.

cards.question: If someone's hands are savasava, must the word itself say which brand or kind of sovu was used?
cards.answer: The result and the cleaning material have different names; the description does not specify a product.

link.label: Read sovu kei na wai in Fiji health advice

senikau.title: A flower and a garland
senikau.intro: Senikau names a flower. In a Fijian account of welcoming visitors, different senikau are used in a salusalu, a flower garland.

cards.question: If you admire a senikau on a plant, have you named the flower or its fruit?
cards.answer: Senikau is the flower; a plant may later bear fruit, but that is a different part.

cards.question: A welcome garland is made with several senikau. Which word names the finished garland?
cards.answer: Senikau are the flowers; salusalu is the garland made from them.

link.label: Read about senikau in a Fijian welcome garland

tagane.title: Which person?
tagane.intro: Tagane specifies a male person. Tamata can refer to a person without making that distinction.

cards.question: A report says tamata but gives no other clue. Can you conclude that the person is a tagane?
cards.answer: Tamata alone does not specify male; tagane does.

cards.question: A story contrasts a tagane with a yalewa. Which word names the woman?
cards.answer: Yalewa is the woman; tagane is the man.

tamata.title: One person or the people?
tamata.intro: Tamata can name a person or people, according to the phrase. Tagane adds a male distinction; a Fiji government speech uses nomuni tamata when referring to a community's people.

cards.question: If a sentence names a tamata but gives no further detail, is the person's sex already stated?
cards.answer: Tamata names the person; it does not itself say tagane or yalewa.

cards.question: A speaker addresses leaders about nomuni tamata. Does the phrase refer to just one person or their people together?
cards.answer: In that speech the phrase points to the community's people. The wider context helps show the collective reading.

link.label: Read nomuni tamata in a Fiji government speech

tavaya.title: A vessel for carrying liquid
tavaya.intro: Tavaya is a bottle. Bilo is a drinking cup, while vokete is a bucket.

cards.question: You pour from a tavaya into a bilo. Which one is the bottle?
cards.answer: Tavaya names the bottle; bilo names the cup used to drink.

cards.question: A household carries a large amount of water in a vokete. Is vokete simply another word for a bottle?
cards.answer: Vokete is a bucket or pail. Tavaya is a bottle.

teveli.title: A surface, a seat, a meal
teveli.intro: Teveli is a table. Idabedabe is a seat; kakana is food that may be set on a table.

cards.question: A person pulls up an idabedabe beside a teveli. Which one is the seat?
cards.answer: Idabedabe names a seat; teveli is the table.

cards.question: Kakana is placed on the teveli. Does teveli name the food?
cards.answer: Kakana is food; teveli is the surface it is placed on.

uto.title: Breadfruit among Fiji's food crops
uto.intro: Uto is breadfruit. Fiji's traditional seasonal calendar mentions uto beside vudi, a distinct food crop.

cards.question: A seasonal list mentions uto and vudi together. Does that make them two names for breadfruit?
cards.answer: Uto is breadfruit; vudi is plantain or cooking banana.

cards.question: A recipe replaces uto with tavioka. Has it kept the same crop?
cards.answer: Tavioka is cassava, a different plant and food from breadfruit.

link.label: See the Fiji seasonal calendar

oca.title: Feeling tired
oca.intro: Oca describes being tired. Waiting may contribute to fatigue, but waraka itself names the act of waiting.

cards.question: Someone has been waiting a long time and now feels oca. Which word names the tired feeling?
cards.answer: Oca describes tiredness; waraka means to wait.

cards.question: Can a person be oca after work without being rarawa?
cards.answer: Oca is tiredness and rarawa is sorrow. They can occur together, but one does not imply the other.

polo.title: The object in the game
polo.intro: Polo is a ball. Qito can name play or a game, and imau refers to cards or other game pieces.

cards.question: Children start a qito by passing a polo. Which word names the ball?
cards.answer: Polo is the object; qito is the playing or game.

cards.question: A game uses imau rather than a polo. Must every qito involve a ball?
cards.answer: Imau can be cards or game pieces; a ball is only one possible object used in play.

ramusu.title: What kind of break?
ramusu.intro: Ramusu can describe a broken limb, branch or other long part. Cabola is used for something split or cracked open; mavoa concerns injury or damage.

cards.question: A long branch snaps across its length. Which word fits that kind of break?
cards.answer: Ramusu fits the broken branch; cabola foregrounds splitting or cracking open.

cards.question: A person is mavoa after an accident. Does mavoa by itself say a limb is ramusu?
cards.answer: Mavoa means injured or wounded. Ramusu is a more specific description of a break.

vakabauta.title: Belief, evidence and permission
vakabauta.intro: Vakabauta concerns believing or trusting. Vakadinata concerns accepting something as true; vakadonuya concerns approving it.

cards.question: Someone trusts a person before seeing proof. Which word puts that trust in focus?
cards.answer: Vakabauta can express belief or trust. Vakadonuya is approval or permission.

cards.question: A claim is checked and then accepted as true. Which related word makes that acceptance explicit?
cards.answer: Vakadinata is to acknowledge or accept the truth of a claim; vakabauta can be broader belief or trust.

vakadinata.title: Accepting a claim as true
vakadinata.intro: Vakadinata concerns agreement that something is true. Belief and official permission are related but different acts.

cards.question: A witness examines evidence and accepts a statement as true. Which word points to that acceptance?
cards.answer: Vakadinata concerns accepting the statement as true; vakadonuya concerns approval or permission.

cards.question: Can someone vakabauta a friend yet still ask for proof before they vakadinata a particular claim?
cards.answer: Trust in a person and acceptance of a specific claim are separable; the complete Fijian phrase determines the precise use.

vakadonuya.title: Permission is a decision
vakadonuya.intro: Vakadonuya is to approve or permit something. A decision to allow an action differs from accepting a statement as true.

cards.question: A group asks to hold an event and receives approval. Which word names the approval?
cards.answer: Vakadonuya concerns permission; vakadinata concerns accepting a claim as true.

cards.question: Someone wants to join, but the organiser has not agreed. Is vinakata alone the organiser's permission?
cards.answer: Vinakata names wanting; vakadonuya names the separate act of approval.

vakalailai-taka.title: Make it smaller
vakalailai-taka.intro: Vakalailai-taka describes reducing something. Levu describes largeness; the two words do different work in an account of change.

cards.question: A pile was levu, then someone reduced it. Which word names the act of reduction?
cards.answer: Levu describes the quantity or size; vakalailai-taka describes making it smaller.

cards.question: If a task says vakalailai-taka, is it describing a finished small size or asking for a change?
cards.answer: The word expresses making or reducing, not merely a fixed measurement.

vakaloloma.title: A response to distress
vakaloloma.intro: Vakaloloma describes something pitiful or distressing. Rarawa names sorrow; the two may occur together without being identical.

cards.question: A difficult situation is vakaloloma. Does that word identify a distressing situation or only the feeling of fear?
cards.answer: Vakaloloma can characterise a pitiful or distressing state; rere names fear.

cards.question: Someone feels rarawa while hearing about a vakaloloma event. Which word names the sorrow they feel?
cards.answer: Rarawa is sadness; vakaloloma describes the distressing or pitiable state.

varada.title: Part of a building
varada.intro: Varada is a veranda or balcony attached to a building. Vale names a house; an otela is a hotel that may also have a veranda.

cards.question: A home has an open, attached veranda. Which word names that part rather than the whole house?
cards.answer: Varada is the veranda; vale is the house or building.

cards.question: If an otela has a varada, has varada become another name for the hotel?
cards.answer: A veranda is a part of the building. Otela names the hotel as a whole.

veiliutaki.title: Leading and taking part
veiliutaki.intro: Veiliutaki names leadership. Vakaitavi names participation; a participant need not be the leader.

cards.question: A community project has many helpers but one person directing it. Which word names the work of leading?
cards.answer: Veiliutaki is leadership; vakaitavi is taking part.

cards.question: A group works together on a task. Does each person's vakaitavi automatically mean that each holds veiliutaki?
cards.answer: Taking part and holding a leadership role are distinct, even when many people contribute.

link.label: See veiliutaki and vakaitavi in Fiji's Constitution

veimau.title: Play without a ball
veimau.intro: Veimau is used for playing a nonphysical game, such as cards. Polo names a ball; qito is a wider play or game word.

cards.question: Players sit around a table with imau. Which word can name the kind of game they play?
cards.answer: Veimau concerns a game such as cards; polo is a ball.

cards.question: Could qito describe play more generally without telling you that it is veimau?
cards.answer: Qito is broader play or game; veimau gives the more particular nonphysical game context.

vinakata.title: Wanting is not waiting
vinakata.intro: Vinakata expresses wanting or wishing for something. Waraka is waiting; vakadonuya is approving.

cards.question: A person wants a reply but has not received it. Which word names the wanting?
cards.answer: Vinakata names the wish; waraka names waiting for the reply.

cards.question: A child vinakata an outing. Does that by itself mean a parent has vakadonuya it?
cards.answer: Wanting an outing and receiving permission are separate matters.

vinivo.title: A particular garment
vinivo.intro: Vinivo names a dress or pinafore. Sote names a shirt; isulu is a wider clothing word.

cards.question: A garment is identified as a vinivo. Does that tell you a particular kind of clothing or only that it is isulu?
cards.answer: Vinivo is the dress or pinafore; isulu can refer to clothing more generally.
