cards.question: A shopper asks for a sote rather than a vinivo. Which garment have they asked for?
cards.answer: Sote is a shirt; vinivo is a dress or pinafore.

vokete.title: Three kinds of container
vokete.intro: Vokete is a bucket or pail. Tavaya is a bottle, while kuro is a cooking pot.

cards.question: A family carries water in a vokete and pours some into a tavaya. Which word names the bucket?
cards.answer: Vokete is the bucket; tavaya is the bottle.

cards.question: A cook heats food in a kuro. Is that the same kind of vessel as a vokete?
cards.answer: Kuro is a cooking pot; vokete is a bucket or pail.

vuniwai.title: Who treats the patient?
vuniwai.intro: Vuniwai names a doctor or medical practitioner. Kemesi names the pharmacy or chemist's shop; mate can name illness.

cards.question: A patient consults a vuniwai about a mate. Which word names the practitioner?
cards.answer: Vuniwai is the practitioner; mate can mean illness or disease in this context.

cards.question: Someone visits a kemesi after seeing a vuniwai. Which word names the place, not the person?
cards.answer: Kemesi is a pharmacy; vuniwai is the doctor.

link.label: See vuniwai in Fiji health advice

waqavuka.title: The aircraft and the airfield
waqavuka.intro: Waqavuka is an aeroplane, distinct from a motoka. An official Fiji account uses rara ni waqavuka for the place where aircraft land.

cards.question: An itinerary uses a waqavuka for the long journey. Which vehicle is named?
cards.answer: Waqavuka is an aeroplane; motoka is a car.

cards.question: In rara ni waqavuka, is the whole expression naming the aircraft or the airfield?
cards.answer: The official passage uses rara ni waqavuka for the place; waqavuka alone names the aircraft.

link.label: Read rara ni waqavuka in a Fiji government statement

waraka.title: The wait and the wish
waraka.intro: Waraka means to wait for someone or something. Vinakata names wanting; lako names going.

cards.question: A visitor wants to leave but stays until a friend arrives. Which word names the staying and waiting?
cards.answer: Waraka is the wait; vinakata is the wish or desire.

cards.question: When the friend finally arrives, the visitor begins to lako. Which word names the earlier action?
cards.answer: Waraka is waiting; lako is going or travelling.

weleti.title: Papaya in Fiji's fields and markets
weleti.intro: Weleti is papaya. A Fiji parliamentary account names weleti as a crop in a small-scale export trade; maqo is a different fruit, mango.

cards.question: A fruit seller labels one pile weleti and another maqo. Are both names for papaya?
cards.answer: Weleti is papaya; maqo is mango.

cards.question: A grower speaks of sending weleti to a market overseas. Which crop is being discussed?
cards.answer: The parliamentary account explicitly pairs weleti with papaya; vudi is plantain.

link.label: Read the Fiji parliamentary account of weleti growing

yabaki.title: A year in a longer calendar
yabaki.intro: Yabaki names a year. Vula can name a month, and siga a day.

cards.question: A record covers several vula but less than one yabaki. Which unit is the year?
cards.answer: Yabaki is a year; vula can be a month.

cards.question: A notice gives one siga for an event. Has it named a whole yabaki?
cards.answer: Siga can name a day. Yabaki is the longer yearly unit.

mamada.title: Light in the hand
mamada.intro: Mamada describes light weight. Bibi can describe heaviness; levu describes size or quantity, which is a different measure.

cards.question: Two identical vokete are lifted; one is mamada because it contains less. Which other word would describe the heavier one?
cards.answer: Mamada concerns light weight; bibi can mean heavy.

cards.question: An empty bag is levu but mamada. Is there a contradiction?
cards.answer: Levu describes its size; mamada describes its light weight. A large object need not be heavy.

matata.title: Clear does not always mean true
matata.intro: Matata can describe an explanation or situation that is clear. A clear claim can still need checking before someone vakadinata it.

cards.question: A statement is easy to understand but has not yet been checked. Which word speaks to its clarity?
cards.answer: Matata concerns clarity; vakadinata concerns accepting a statement as true.

cards.question: A plan is matata but its details are not titobu. Must a clear plan also be deep or detailed?
cards.answer: Matata concerns clarity; titobu concerns depth, including depth of thought in a suitable phrase.

meimei.title: Care for a child
meimei.intro: Meimei is someone who looks after a child, such as a babysitter or nursemaid. It identifies a caregiving role, not necessarily a family relationship.

cards.question: A child is looked after by a meimei while tata is away. Which word names the caregiver rather than the father?
cards.answer: Meimei names the childcare role; tata is a familiar way to say dad.

cards.question: Does calling someone a meimei automatically mean that the person is the child's momo?
cards.answer: Momo is a maternal uncle; meimei describes care for a child, whether or not the caregiver is related.

yalewa.title: A woman, a person, a form of respect
yalewa.intro: Yalewa specifies a woman. Tamata is broader, while marama can be a respectful way to refer to a lady.

cards.question: A description says tamata and nothing more. Does it yet tell you that the person is a yalewa?
cards.answer: Tamata names a person without specifying woman or man.

cards.question: A speaker addresses a marama. Is that respectful term merely another way of saying tagane?
cards.answer: Marama is a respectful term for a lady; tagane names a man.

yaloqaqa.title: What courage describes
yaloqaqa.intro: Yaloqaqa describes courage. Rere is fear; veiliutaki is the work of leading people.

cards.question: Someone acts despite feeling rere. Could the action still be yaloqaqa?
cards.answer: Courage is compatible with feeling fear; rere names the fear itself.

cards.question: If someone holds veiliutaki, does the role alone prove that every action is yaloqaqa?
cards.answer: Veiliutaki is leadership as a role or activity; yaloqaqa describes courage in how someone faces difficulty.

yasana.title: Province, island, or country?
yasana.intro: Yasana is a province of Fiji. An island is a yanuyanu; matanitu can name a state or government. These labels describe different ways of grouping places.

cards.question: A visitor asks which Fiji province a place belongs to. Which word names that administrative level?
cards.answer: Yasana names the province. Yanuyanu names an island, which is a geographical feature.

cards.question: In the community sequence, is a yasana the same level as a whole matanitu?
cards.answer: Matanitu is the wider state or government level; yasana names a province within Fiji.

link.label: See koro, tikina and yasana in a Fiji place record

boso.title: A boss is a role, not a skill
boso.intro: Boso is an informal word for a boss or person in charge. Matai can describe someone skilled at a task; turaga can be a respectful address or title.

cards.question: A skilled worker is called matai but is not managing anyone. Must that person also be the boso?
cards.answer: Matai concerns skill; boso concerns being in charge.

cards.question: If someone uses turaga as a respectful address, have they necessarily called the person their workplace boso?
cards.answer: Turaga and boso have different uses; respect does not by itself identify an employer.

imau.title: What the players hold
imau.intro: Imau can name cards or other game pieces. Polo is a ball, and veimau is the activity of playing a nonphysical game.

cards.question: Players deal imau rather than pass a polo. Which word can name the cards?
cards.answer: Imau refers to cards or pieces; polo is a ball.

cards.question: Two people sit at a table and veimau. Is veimau the game activity or another name for the pieces they hold?
cards.answer: Veimau names playing this kind of game; imau can name the pieces used.

matai.title: Skill and the person who directs work
matai.intro: Matai may describe someone skilled at a task; another recorded sense names a skilled craft worker. Boso instead concerns being in charge.

cards.question: A carpenter is respected for careful work but supervises no one. Is matai or boso the clearer clue to skill?
cards.answer: Matai points to expertise. Boso points to a person in charge.

cards.question: Does calling someone matai tell you that the person works only in one craft in every context?
cards.answer: The word has a broader skilled-person use as well as a more specific craft-worker sense; the surrounding phrase matters.

matanivanua.title: Who speaks in formal protocol?
matanivanua.intro: Matanivanua is a herald or spokesperson in formal communication. Turaga names a chief or respected man; i sevusevu names a customary presentation, not the spokesperson.

cards.question: During a formal welcome, which word identifies the herald rather than the presentation itself?
cards.answer: Matanivanua is the spokesperson; i sevusevu is a customary presentation.

cards.question: If a speaker is a matanivanua, does the role alone tell you that the person is the turaga being addressed?
cards.answer: The herald's communication role and the chief's title are distinct.

link.label: Read about the matanivanua role in Fiji Parliament

momo.title: A relative on the mother's side
momo.intro: Momo names a maternal uncle, the mother's brother. Tata names a father; veiwekani is a wider word for kinship ties.

cards.question: A child introduces their mother's brother. Which family word identifies him?
cards.answer: Momo is a maternal uncle; tata is dad or father.

cards.question: A family describes its wider veiwekani. Does that broad term specify that every relative is a momo?
cards.answer: Veiwekani covers relationships more broadly; momo identifies one particular family relation.

sigalevu.title: The middle of the day
sigalevu.intro: Sigalevu refers to midday or the early afternoon. Siga can refer to a day; karobo is dusk or twilight.

cards.question: An appointment is at sigalevu. Has it named the middle of the day or the whole siga?
cards.answer: Sigalevu narrows the time; siga can refer to a day more generally.

cards.question: If the light is fading at karobo, is that the same time as sigalevu?
cards.answer: Karobo is dusk; sigalevu is around midday or early afternoon.

tata.title: Dad and other people who care
tata.intro: Tata is a familiar way to say father or dad. Momo names the mother's brother; meimei names someone caring for a child.

cards.question: A child calls their father tata. Would momo identify that same relationship?
cards.answer: Momo is a maternal uncle, a different family relation.

cards.question: A meimei looks after the child while tata works. Does the childcare role itself make the meimei the father?
cards.answer: Meimei describes care for a child; tata names the father.

tea.title: From planting to selling
tea.intro: Tea means to plant something so it grows. Tavioka is one crop that can be planted; volitaka means to sell something after it has been produced.

cards.question: Someone puts tavioka cuttings into the ground. Which word names the planting action?
cards.answer: Tea is the action of planting; tavioka is the cassava crop.

cards.question: A farmer grows a crop and later volitaka it. Which action came first?
cards.answer: Tea is planting; volitaka is selling. They describe different stages of growing and trading food.

tukuna.title: A thought, a telling, a record
tukuna.intro: Tukuna means to tell or say something. Nanuma is to think or remember; ivola can be a written record.

cards.question: A person remembers a story but has not yet shared it. Which word names the act of telling it aloud?
cards.answer: Nanuma is remembering or thinking; tukuna is telling or saying it.

cards.question: The story is preserved in an ivola. Is the book itself the same thing as the act of tukuna?
cards.answer: Ivola is a book or written record; tukuna is an act of telling.

yanuyanu.title: Land surrounded by sea
yanuyanu.intro: Yanuyanu is an island. Wasawasa is the sea or ocean around it; yasana is a province, an administrative grouping.

cards.question: A boat crosses the wasawasa and reaches a yanuyanu. Which word names the land it reaches?
cards.answer: Yanuyanu names the island; wasawasa names the sea.

cards.question: A map gives a yasana for an island. Are yasana and yanuyanu two labels for the same kind of feature?
cards.answer: Yasana is a province; yanuyanu is a landform. A province and an island are different kinds of grouping.

yadra.title: Awake is not a clock time
yadra.intro: Yadra can describe being awake or waking up. Karobo is dusk; siga is a day. A person may be awake at different times.

cards.question: A person yadra before anyone calls them. Is the word describing their waking or the hour of the day?
cards.answer: Yadra concerns the person's state or change to wakefulness; it is not a clock time.

cards.question: Someone is still yadra at karobo. Must yadra mean morning?
cards.answer: Karobo is dusk; yadra can describe wakefulness then too.

mavoa.title: An injury may need more detail
mavoa.intro: Mavoa describes an injury or wound. Ramusu is more specific to a break, and mate can name an illness in context.

cards.question: Someone's arm is mavoa. Can you conclude from that word alone that it is ramusu?
cards.answer: Mavoa says injured; ramusu would specify a break.

cards.question: A doctor sees someone with a mate but no wound. Does mate necessarily describe the same thing as mavoa?
cards.answer: Mate can refer to illness; mavoa points to injury or damage.

niusiveva.title: A newspaper with an English origin
niusiveva.intro: Niusiveva names a newspaper and was adapted from the English word newspaper. Ivola is a wider book or record word; tukuna is the act of telling something.

cards.question: Which English word can you hear behind the Fijian form niusiveva?
cards.answer: Niusiveva is a borrowing from newspaper, reshaped to fit Fijian sounds. Ivola has a wider written-record sense.

cards.question: A neighbour tukuna the same news aloud. Has the news necessarily been printed in a niusiveva?
cards.answer: Tukuna is telling; niusiveva names the printed newspaper.

savasava.title: The result and the cleaning material
savasava.intro: Savasava describes something clean. Sovu is soap used in cleaning; maca describes a different state, such as a container being empty or liquid used up.

cards.question: A washed cup is savasava. Which word names the soap that might have been used?
cards.answer: Sovu is soap; savasava describes the clean result.

cards.question: A clean vokete is empty. Does savasava itself tell you that the bucket is maca?
cards.answer: Cleanliness and emptiness are separate properties; maca can refer to an empty or used-up supply.

katakata.title: Heat in two settings
katakata.intro: Katakata can describe high heat and, in a food context, spicy heat. Masima is salt, a different taste clue.

cards.question: A pot is katakata after cooking. Is the heat from temperature or necessarily from chilli?
cards.answer: Katakata can describe something physically hot; the context tells you which kind of heat is meant.

cards.question: A dish tastes katakata but not masima. Which contrast fits?
cards.answer: Katakata can describe spicy heat in food; masima is salt.

maca.title: Empty, dry or simply clean?
maca.intro: Maca can describe a supply of liquid that has run out or dried up. A clean container is savasava, which is a separate idea.

cards.question: The last water has been poured from a tavaya. Which word points to the supply being used up?
cards.answer: Maca can describe a liquid supply that is empty or used up; savasava would concern cleanliness.

cards.question: A vokete is washed and clean but still full of water. Must it also be maca?
cards.answer: Maca concerns emptiness or drying up in this use. A full bucket can be savasava without being empty.

nanuma.title: Remembering before speaking
nanuma.intro: Nanuma can mean thinking about or remembering. Tukuna is telling; ivola is a written record that may preserve something for later.

cards.question: You nanuma a person's name but have not said it. Which word names speaking it to someone?
cards.answer: Nanuma concerns thought or memory; tukuna is the telling.

cards.question: An ivola preserves an event that you no longer nanuma clearly. Is the written record the same as your remembering?
cards.answer: Ivola can be the record; nanuma is the act of thinking or remembering.

yali.title: Gone does not always mean dead
yali.intro: Yali can mean missing, absent or gone; in some contexts it can refer to death. Mate can name death or illness, depending on its phrase.

cards.question: A friend has not arrived and is yali for now. Does that word alone prove the friend has died?
cards.answer: Yali can simply mean missing or absent; context is needed before reading it as death.

cards.question: You waraka someone who is still away. Which word names your waiting, rather than their absence?
cards.answer: Waraka is waiting; yali describes the person's absence or disappearance.

osooso.title: Busy is not automatically tired
osooso.intro: Osooso means occupied with many things. Galala is free or available; oca describes tiredness.

cards.question: A worker has many tasks and is osooso. Which word would say that the worker is available instead?
cards.answer: Galala can describe being free or available; osooso means busy.

cards.question: A person finishes an osooso day but still feels energetic. Must they be oca?
cards.answer: Osooso is busyness; oca is tiredness. One does not necessarily follow from the other.

ceva.title: A direction, not the whole forecast
ceva.intro: Ceva points south. Cagi names wind; draki names weather. The direction can describe where a wind comes from without naming all the weather.

cards.question: A chart points ceva on the compass. Does it point north or south?
cards.answer: Ceva is the southern direction; vualiku points north.

cards.question: If someone reports a wind from the south, which word names the wind itself?
cards.answer: Cagi is wind; ceva supplies a direction.

daveta.title: A way through the reef
daveta.intro: Daveta is a passage through a reef that boats can use. The recorded place-name Davetalevu refers to a particular passage, while daveta can describe a reef opening more generally.

cards.question: A boat crosses a reef through its daveta. What feature is the word pointing to?
cards.answer: Daveta names the passage, whereas wasawasa names the sea.

cards.question: Does the name Davetalevu mean that every daveta is the same passage?
cards.answer: Daveta can be a general reef-passage word; Davetalevu names a particular passage in a recorded place-name.

link.label: Read about the named Davetalevu

duna.title: Which eel is being named?
duna.intro: Duna names a freshwater eel. One Fiji fisheries list identifies a duna with the marbled eel, Anguilla marmorata; local names may cover more than one identification.

cards.question: A duna is caught in a river. Which habitat matches the dictionary meaning?
cards.answer: Duna is recorded as a freshwater eel; tunatuna names a conger eel.

cards.question: Would the English word eel by itself tell you whether a fish is duna or tunatuna?
cards.answer: The broad English label is not enough. Habitat and local identification matter; diria is another recorded freshwater eel name.

link.label: See duna in a Fiji fish-name list

iloilo.title: A surface that shows you yourself
iloilo.intro: Iloilo can name a mirror or glass. Bilo is a drinking vessel, so the shared English word glass needs the object in view.

cards.question: You see your face in an iloilo. Which English meaning fits?
cards.answer: Iloilo can be a mirror; bilo is a cup or drinking vessel.

cards.question: If someone says 'glass' in English, can you always choose iloilo without knowing whether they mean a mirror or a cup?
cards.answer: The object matters. English glass can name different things, while iloilo and bilo separate this contrast.

laga.title: Starting the song
laga.intro: Laga can mean beginning or leading a song. The word points to a singer's role in starting it, not merely to any listener hearing it.

cards.question: One singer laga a song before others join. Which action is being described?
cards.answer: The recorded sense of laga is to begin or lead a song.

cards.question: If three people hear a song, has that fact alone told you which one laga it?
cards.answer: Hearing a song does not identify the person who began or led it.

lalai.title: Small things in a group
lalai.intro: Lalai describes more than one small person or thing. Lailai is the related form for a single one in this contrast.

cards.question: A group of objects is described as lalai. Is the word pointing to one object or several?
cards.answer: The reviewed meaning of lalai specifies more than one; lailai is the related singular form.

cards.question: Several objects change from lelevu to lalai. What has changed: their size or their number?
cards.answer: Both words can describe several things. Lelevu says large; lalai says small.

tovolea.title: Trying is a step, not a result
tovolea.intro: Tovolea means to try or attempt something. The word tells you there was an effort, not that the aim was achieved.

cards.question: A person tovolea a task but cannot finish it. Was there still an attempt?
cards.answer: Tovolea names the attempt; success is a separate question.

cards.question: Which statement needs more evidence than tovolea alone gives: 'they tried' or 'they succeeded'?
cards.answer: The meaning establishes the effort. It does not settle the outcome.

vualiku.title: North and the northerly wind
vualiku.intro: Vualiku can point north and can also refer to a northerly wind. Compare ceva for south and cagi for wind itself.

cards.question: On a compass, which word opposes vualiku?
cards.answer: Vualiku points north; ceva points south. Cagi means wind.

cards.question: A report speaks of vualiku as a wind. What has the northern direction helped specify?
cards.answer: In this sense the direction is part of naming a northerly wind; draki is the broader weather word.

galala.title: Room in a schedule
galala.intro: Galala can mean free or available. Osooso points to being occupied; galala need not mean that a person has no responsibilities at all.

cards.question: A person has time to meet today. Which word fits that availability?
cards.answer: Galala can mean available; osooso means busy.

cards.question: A worker is galala this afternoon but busy tomorrow. Does galala have to describe their whole life?
cards.answer: Availability can belong to a particular time or situation; gauna is a time or period.

soqo.title: People gathered for a purpose
soqo.intro: Soqo is a gathering or meeting. Bose more specifically points to a discussion or council meeting; magiti brings food into a feast setting.

cards.question: People assemble for an event. Which word can name the gathering itself?
cards.answer: Soqo names a gathering of people; wasawasa is the sea.

cards.question: If the gathering is described specifically as a discussion meeting, which related word is useful?
cards.answer: Bose points to a meeting or deliberation, while soqo is a broader gathering word.

wasawasa.title: The sea around an island
wasawasa.intro: Wasawasa names the sea or ocean. Yanuyanu is land surrounded by it; waitui can draw attention to sea water.

cards.question: A boat travels between two yanuyanu across the wasawasa. What does it cross?
cards.answer: Wasawasa names the sea; yanuyanu names an island.

cards.question: If someone is talking about salty sea water itself, which related word makes that water more explicit?
cards.answer: Waitui can mean sea water; wasawasa names the sea or ocean.

volitaka.title: Selling changes who has the goods
volitaka.intro: Volitaka means to sell something. Makete is a market, the place where a sale may happen; a word for the place does not name the act.

cards.question: A seller volitaka produce at a makete. Which word names what the seller does?
cards.answer: Volitaka is the selling; makete is the market.

cards.question: Someone carries produce through a makete but makes no sale. Can you infer volitaka from their presence there alone?
cards.answer: The market is a setting; the verb requires an actual selling action.

qarava.title: Care as an action
qarava.intro: Qarava can mean to attend to someone or something, including in medical care. Vuniwai names a medical practitioner; the action and person are distinct.

cards.question: A vuniwai qarava a patient. Which word names the action of attending to them?
cards.answer: Qarava is the attending or caring action; vuniwai names the practitioner.

cards.question: Must every use of qarava be medical?
cards.answer: Qarava also has the wider sense of looking after or attending to someone or something.

veisau.title: Notice what changed
veisau.intro: Veisau can name a change or an exchange. The context tells you whether something became different or things were exchanged.

cards.question: A plan is revised but nothing changes hands. Which veisau reading fits?
cards.answer: Veisau can name change without an exchange of objects.

cards.question: Two people swap items. Does the exchange reading of veisau fit better than a mere change of weather?
cards.answer: An exchange involves what passes between participants; the same word can also refer to change in a different context.

masima.title: Salt is one taste
masima.intro: Masima is salt. Katakata may describe spicy heat in food, so the two clues tell a cook different things.

cards.question: A dish needs more masima. What ingredient is missing?
cards.answer: Masima is salt; katakata describes heat, including spicy heat in food.

cards.question: Can a dish contain masima and also taste katakata from chilli?
cards.answer: Salt and spicy heat are different parts of a dish's flavour. One does not rule out the other.

sagavulu.title: Building tens
sagavulu.intro: Sagavulu participates in compound numbers for tens. Ruasagavulu is a recorded form for twenty, while tini separately names ten.

cards.question: In the recorded number ruasagavulu, how many tens does rua contribute?
cards.answer: Rua is two, so ruasagavulu is twenty in this recorded pattern.

cards.question: Does the existence of sagavulu mean tini has disappeared as a word for ten?
cards.answer: Tini is another recorded word for ten. Sagavulu participates in longer compound number forms.

link.label: See recorded number forms in a Fijian language handbook

karobo.title: The light at dusk
karobo.intro: Karobo is dusk or twilight. Sigalevu names midday; yadra names waking or being awake rather than a time of day.

cards.question: The light fades near karobo. Which time is being named?
cards.answer: Karobo is dusk; sigalevu is midday.

cards.question: Someone is still yadra at karobo. Does that make karobo another word for waking?
cards.answer: Karobo is a time of day. Yadra describes wakefulness or waking.

tala.title: The person sent and the message carried
tala.intro: Tala can mean sending a person, often on an errand. Tukuna is telling or saying something; the acts can occur together but are not identical.

cards.question: A person is tala to deliver a message. Which word names the sending?
cards.answer: Tala names sending the person; tukuna names telling or saying the message.

cards.question: If you tukuna a message while staying in the same place, have you necessarily tala someone?
cards.answer: You can tell something without sending a person on an errand.

veitau.title: Friendship goes both ways
veitau.intro: Veitau describes people being friends with one another. The reciprocal vei- pattern helps point to a shared relationship, but a similar-looking form still needs its own checked meaning.

cards.question: Two people are veitau. Is the relationship mutual or one-sided in this meaning?
cards.answer: The reviewed meaning is being friends with one another; vei- can mark reciprocity in checked forms.

cards.question: If one person only admires another from afar, does that by itself establish veitau?
cards.answer: Veitau names a friendship between them, not one person's unreturned feeling.

ivola.title: From writing to a written thing
ivola.intro: Ivola can be a book, letter, mark or record. An attested i- nominal pattern relates a written item to the base vola, so the full context decides which kind of written thing is meant.

cards.question: In the attested pairing vola → ivola, what does the attached i- help form?
cards.answer: Ivola can name a book or other written record. The prefix i- is one recorded noun-forming pattern.

cards.question: A printed newspaper is niusiveva. Does ivola alone tell you that the item is specifically a newspaper?
cards.answer: Ivola is broader; niusiveva identifies a newspaper.

link.label: Read a linguistic analysis of i- and ivola

yalo.title: More than one English word
yalo.intro: Yalo can refer to spirit, soul, mind or inward disposition. Yaloqaqa names courage; the longer word points to a particular quality rather than every sense of yalo.

cards.question: A person is described as yaloqaqa. Which quality is named more particularly?
cards.answer: Yaloqaqa concerns courage; raba names width.

cards.question: Does translating yalo as 'mind' in one phrase prove it must mean 'mind' in every phrase?
cards.answer: Yalo has several related English readings. The complete Fijian phrase decides which is active.

lelevu.title: Large things, plural
lelevu.intro: Lelevu can describe more than one large person or thing. Levu is the related singular form in this contrast; lalai describes the opposite size for several things.

cards.question: Several objects are lelevu. Which related word could describe a single large object?
cards.answer: Lelevu is plural here; levu is the corresponding singular size word.

cards.question: A set of objects changes from lalai to lelevu. What has changed?
cards.answer: Both forms can describe several items. Lalai is small; lelevu is large.

lewe.title: People in a group
lewe.intro: Lewe can point to the people of a place or group. Tamata can name a person; lewe in this sense draws attention to membership.

cards.question: A notice names the lewe of a village. Is it focusing on people or on the buildings?
cards.answer: Lewe can name the people who belong to a place or group.

cards.question: If a story first introduces one tamata and then the lewe of a village, which word points to the group?
cards.answer: Tamata can name an individual person. Lewe here draws attention to the people belonging to a group.

raba.title: How wide?
raba.intro: Raba is width. Balavu describes length or longness; titobu concerns depth, so each asks about a different dimension.

cards.question: A table is measured from side to side. Which word is about that width?
cards.answer: Raba is width; titobu is depth.

cards.question: If a mat is long but narrow, does its balavu alone give its raba?
cards.answer: Length and width are separate measurements. Balavu does not by itself tell you the width.

waitui.title: Water from the sea
waitui.intro: Waitui is sea water and can also refer to the sea. Wasawasa gives the broader sea or ocean setting.

cards.question: A container holds waitui. Is the water from the sea or from a freshwater stream?
cards.answer: Waitui means sea water in this use; wasawasa names the wider sea.

cards.question: If a boat crosses the wasawasa, does waitui have to mean a cup of water?
cards.answer: Waitui can also refer to the sea. The wider setting and phrase choose the reading.

link.label: See waitui and wasawasa in Fiji weather writing

pae.title: The pastry and its filling
pae.intro: Pae is pie, a pastry dish with a filling. Madrai is bread and keke is cake; the three baked foods are not interchangeable names.

cards.question: A baker encloses a filling in pastry. Which word from these entries fits the finished dish?
cards.answer: Pae names pie; madrai is bread.

cards.question: If the baker also makes a keke, does that automatically make the cake a pae?
cards.answer: Keke names cake. Pae points to the pastry dish with a filling.

ti.title: What is in the cup?
ti.intro: Ti names tea. Yaqona names a different drink, and bilo names a vessel rather than either beverage.

cards.question: A guest asks for ti instead of yaqona. Which drink do they want?
cards.answer: Ti is tea; yaqona is kava.

cards.question: Someone holds a bilo containing ti. Which word names the vessel?
cards.answer: Bilo is a drinking vessel; ti is the tea inside it.

jisi.title: A food that can go into another food
jisi.intro: Jisi is cheese. Keke is cake; a food can contain an ingredient without taking that ingredient's name.

cards.question: A cook adds jisi to a dish. Which ingredient has been added?
cards.answer: Jisi means cheese; jokeliti means chocolate.

cards.question: Could a keke contain jisi while keke still names the finished cake?
cards.answer: An ingredient and the food containing it can have different names. Jisi is cheese; keke is cake.

jokeliti.title: Chocolate on its own or in baking
jokeliti.intro: Jokeliti is chocolate. It might be an ingredient in keke, but the word does not itself mean cake.

cards.question: A sweet is labelled jokeliti. Is the label naming chocolate or cheese?
cards.answer: Jokeliti is chocolate; jisi is cheese.

cards.question: A keke has jokeliti in it. Which word identifies the cake, not the chocolate ingredient?
cards.answer: Keke names the finished cake; jokeliti can name the chocolate used in it.

pusi.title: A cat among other animals
pusi.intro: Pusi is a cat. Lulu is an owl: both are animals, but one name does not identify the other.

cards.question: An animal curls up on a chair and is identified as pusi. What animal is it?
cards.answer: Pusi is a cat; lulu is an owl.

cards.question: A pusi hides from visitors. Does the animal name alone mean that it is kila?
cards.answer: Pusi identifies the cat. Kila can describe an animal as wild or shy; that needs its own observation.

lulu.title: Which animal is the owl?
lulu.intro: Lulu is an owl. The dictionary also has pusi for cat; knowing the broad English word animal is not enough to choose between them.

cards.question: A bird is identified as lulu. Which animal has been named?
cards.answer: Lulu is an owl; pusi is a cat.

cards.question: Does lulu alone tell you which species of owl was seen?
cards.answer: The checked meaning is owl. A particular species needs more evidence than the broad bird name gives.

tavako.title: The item and what rises from it
tavako.intro: Tavako can name tobacco or a cigarette. Kuvu can describe smoke rising or drifting; the item and the smoke are different things.

cards.question: Someone buys tavako. Have they named tobacco or the smoke after it burns?
cards.answer: Tavako names the item. Kuvu can describe rising smoke.

cards.question: A room is filled with kuvu after tavako is lit. Which word points to what is in the air?
cards.answer: Kuvu concerns the drifting smoke; tavako is the tobacco or cigarette.

drega.title: From a tree to two uses
drega.intro: Drega is sticky gum or tree resin. It can be chewed or used as glue; those uses do not turn it into two different plants.

cards.question: A tree produces a sticky material that can be used as glue. Is that drega or drifting kuvu?
cards.answer: Drega is sticky gum or resin; kuvu can describe smoke or dust drifting in air.

cards.question: One person chews drega and another uses it to stick things together. Must the word have changed to name two unrelated substances?
cards.answer: The same sticky material can be described by different practical uses in the checked meaning.

kaya.title: Thought, speech and a written record
kaya.intro: Kaya means to say or tell something. Nanuma concerns thinking or remembering; ivola can be a written record.

cards.question: You nanuma an answer but have not spoken. Which word names the act of saying it?
cards.answer: Nanuma stays with thought or memory; kaya is saying or telling.

cards.question: An ivola contains a story. Has the book itself performed kaya aloud?
cards.answer: Ivola names a written thing. Kaya names the act of saying or telling something.

vakaitavi.title: Taking part and leading
vakaitavi.intro: Vakaitavi means to take part or have a role. Veiliutaki is leadership; participation does not automatically make someone the leader.

cards.question: A volunteer helps at a soqo. Which word describes taking part?
cards.answer: Vakaitavi is participation; veiliutaki is leadership.

cards.question: If everyone at an event is vakaitavi, must everyone also hold veiliutaki?
cards.answer: People can contribute in different roles without all directing the work.

veiwekani.title: Family ties and friendship
veiwekani.intro: Veiwekani names kinship ties or relatives linked through family or traditional relationship. Veitau concerns friendship; vuvale focuses on a household.

cards.question: Two people are veitau but have no known family tie. Does friendship alone establish veiwekani in its kinship sense?
cards.answer: Veitau is friendship; veiwekani here points to kinship or a recognised family relationship.

cards.question: Can relatives live in different vuvale and still have veiwekani?
cards.answer: Vuvale is a household grouping. A kinship tie can connect people across households.

link.label: Read a USP account of kinship and care

yavusa.title: A kin group within a wider place
yavusa.intro: Yavusa is a traditional kin group that may include several mataqali. Yasana names a province; vuvale names a household, so these labels answer different questions.

cards.question: A person names their yavusa and their yasana. Which label identifies a kin group rather than a province?
cards.answer: Yavusa names a kin grouping; yasana names a province.

cards.question: Could a yavusa include more than one vuvale?
cards.answer: A yavusa is a wider kin grouping than a single household. Vuvale names the people of one household.

link.label: See Fiji's published account of yavusa and mataqali

vuvale.title: The people of a household
vuvale.intro: Vuvale points to the people of one household. Yavusa is a wider kin grouping; veiwekani can connect relatives beyond one home.

cards.question: Several relatives live together as one household. Which word names the household people?
cards.answer: Vuvale is the household group; yasana is a province.

cards.question: Do relatives living in separate vuvale lose all veiwekani just because their homes differ?
cards.answer: Separate households can still be connected by kinship ties.

loloma.title: A feeling that can become action
loloma.intro: Loloma names love, affection or caring. Qarava names attending to someone; the feeling and the care given may be connected without being the same word.

cards.question: Someone feels deep loloma for a child. Which word names the affection?
cards.answer: Loloma is the love or affection; qarava can name the action of looking after someone.

cards.question: If a person qarava a neighbour by bringing food, does that action alone specify every feeling they have?
cards.answer: An act of care can express loloma, but the action and the inner feeling are not identical.

link.label: Read a USP account of loloma and care

maliwa.title: Space between things
maliwa.intro: Maliwa is the space between things, or the middle. Raba tells how wide something is; it does not simply name the gap beside it.

cards.question: Two chairs have a gap between them. Which word points to that space?
cards.answer: Maliwa is the intervening space; raba is width.

cards.question: A person stands in the middle of two chairs. Is the middle reading of maliwa about one chair's width?
cards.answer: Maliwa can point to the position between them, not the dimensions of either chair.

veikau.title: Forest and coastal mangroves
veikau.intro: Veikau means forest or bushland. Veidogo names mangrove vegetation, a more particular coastal plant community.

cards.question: A path crosses dense bushland. Which word names the vegetated area generally?
cards.answer: Veikau is forest or bushland; wasawasa is the sea.

cards.question: At a muddy coast, a guide points specifically to mangroves. Which word is more particular than veikau?
cards.answer: Veidogo names mangroves; veikau is the broader forest or bushland word.

titobu.title: Depth in water and in thought
titobu.intro: Titobu means deep. It can describe physical depth and can also be used in a phrase about thought; raba measures width instead.

cards.question: A pool is titobu. Which dimension is being described?
cards.answer: Titobu is deep; raba is width.

cards.question: Someone speaks of titobu thought. Must the word now be measuring water?
cards.answer: The reviewed meaning also allows depth in a phrase about thought; the full phrase decides the reading.

salusalu.title: A garland, not just any adornment
salusalu.intro: Salusalu is a garland made with flowers or fragrant leaves. Qato names a bracelet or similar band worn on an arm or ankle.

cards.question: Flowers and scented leaves are woven into a garland. Which word names the finished adornment?
cards.answer: Salusalu is the floral garland; qato is a bracelet or band.

cards.question: If an ornament is worn around the wrist, may you call it salusalu merely because it is decorative?
cards.answer: The material and kind of adornment matter. Qato is the checked word for a bracelet or similar band.

sautu.title: More than a quiet moment
sautu.intro: Sautu brings together peace, well-being and prosperity. Maravu can describe calm sea conditions; these are different kinds of calm.

cards.question: A community speaks of sautu. Is it only the surface of a calm sea?
cards.answer: Sautu concerns peace and well-being in life; maravu can describe smooth or calm water.

cards.question: A household is peaceful but struggling to meet basic needs. Has the prosperity side of sautu necessarily been established?
cards.answer: The word can include both peace and a sense of enough or well-being; one aspect alone does not settle the whole picture.

rerevaki.title: Danger and what might happen
rerevaki.intro: Rerevaki can describe something feared or dangerous. Mavoa names an injury, which need not have happened yet for danger to be recognised.

cards.question: A path is rerevaki. Does the word describe the danger, or merely the feeling of rere in a person?
cards.answer: Rere is fear; rerevaki can describe something feared or dangerous.

cards.question: If a path is rerevaki but everyone passes safely, must someone be mavoa?
cards.answer: A danger can be present without a person being injured. Mavoa names injury.

magiti.title: Food in a feast setting
magiti.intro: Magiti is food prepared for a feast or ceremonial presentation. Kakana is a broader food word; soqo names a gathering of people.

cards.question: Food is prepared for a feast. Which word brings that occasion into the meaning?
cards.answer: Magiti has the feast or ceremonial-food sense; kakana is food more broadly.

cards.question: People meet for a soqo with no food mentioned. Has the word soqo alone told you there is magiti?
cards.answer: Soqo names a gathering; magiti names food in a feast or presentation setting.

vuso.title: Foam on the water
vuso.intro: Vuso is froth or foam, especially on water. Kuvu can be smoke, dust, steam or spray rising into the air.

cards.question: Bubbles gather as froth on the water. Which word fits that surface layer?
cards.answer: Vuso is foam or froth; kuvu points to material rising or drifting, such as smoke or spray.

cards.question: A sea is maravu with a smooth surface. Would a patch of visible vuso be describing that same smoothness?
cards.answer: Maravu describes calmness or smoothness; vuso identifies froth on the surface.

vakaisulu.title: Wearing the garment
vakaisulu.intro: Vakaisulu describes being dressed or wearing clothes. Isulu names clothing itself; sote is a shirt, one particular garment.

cards.question: A person is vakaisulu for a visit. Which word identifies their dressed state?
cards.answer: Vakaisulu describes the person as dressed; isulu names clothing or a garment.

cards.question: Someone chooses a sote. Has the word sote alone said whether the person is already vakaisulu?
cards.answer: Sote identifies a shirt. Having or choosing a garment is distinct from wearing it.

maravu.title: A calm sea still has a name
maravu.intro: Maravu describes calm or smooth conditions, especially at sea. Wasawasa is the sea itself; vuso is visible froth or foam.

cards.question: The wasawasa is maravu. Which word names the sea rather than its calm condition?
cards.answer: Wasawasa is the sea; maravu describes its calmness.

cards.question: Foam appears on a patch of water. Which word identifies the froth rather than the smooth state?
cards.answer: Vuso is froth or foam; maravu is calm or smooth.

kuvu.title: What rises into the air?
kuvu.intro: Kuvu can refer to smoke, dust, steam or fine spray drifting or rising. Vuso is froth on water rather than that drifting material.

cards.question: A lit tavako sends something drifting through the air. Which word can describe the rising smoke?
cards.answer: Kuvu includes smoke; vuso is froth or foam.

cards.question: A spray rises above the wasawasa. Does kuvu by itself prove it is smoke from a fire?
cards.answer: Kuvu can cover fine spray as well as smoke, dust or steam; the scene settles which one.

delana.title: At the top of the hill
delana.intro: Delana is a hilltop. Dela is separately recorded as 'top'; cabecabe can point to the slope or path leading upward.

cards.question: A walker reaches the delana after climbing a cabecabe. Where are they now?
cards.answer: Delana names the top; cabecabe can be the steep slope or path up it.

cards.question: Dela can mean 'top' more generally. What does delana pick out in this entry?
cards.answer: The checked delana meaning is the top of a hill; raba would concern width.

link.label: See dela in an independent Fijian word list

kila.title: An animal's manner, not its name
kila.intro: Kila can describe an animal as wild or shy. Pusi tells you the animal is a cat; it does not tell you whether that cat is kila.

cards.question: A pusi keeps away from people and is called kila. Which word identifies the cat itself?
cards.answer: Pusi names the cat; kila describes its wild or shy behaviour in this sense.

cards.question: If a tame animal becomes shy around strangers, has its species necessarily changed?
cards.answer: Kila can describe a way an animal behaves. It need not replace the name of the animal.

koula.title: A material and a kind of valuable
koula.intro: Koula is gold. Tabua is a whale tooth used in formal exchange; kamunaga is a wider category of ceremonial valuables.

cards.question: A valuable object is made of koula. What material is it made from?
cards.answer: Koula is gold; tabua is a whale tooth.

cards.question: A speaker mentions kamunaga. Can you conclude that every ceremonial valuable is koula?
cards.answer: Kamunaga includes different kinds of ceremonial valuables, including tabua and mats. The category does not mean gold alone.

teri.title: A wetland bird
teri.intro: Teri is a swamp hen. Lulu names an owl; the broader label 'bird' does not identify which of the two has been seen.

cards.question: A bird at the edge of a wetland is identified as teri. Which English bird name fits?
cards.answer: Teri is a swamp hen; lulu is an owl.

cards.question: If another bird visits the same wetland, does its location alone make it a teri?
cards.answer: The habitat helps you look, but the bird still needs its own identification. Teri is a particular bird name.

dawai.title: Unmarried now does not tell the whole story
dawai.intro: Dawai can refer to an adult without a spouse. It can include a bachelor or someone widowed, so English 'single' alone may hide different histories.

cards.question: An adult never married. Could dawai fit the current absence of a spouse?
cards.answer: The checked meaning includes an adult without a spouse, including a bachelor.

cards.question: An adult's spouse has died. Must dawai be excluded because that adult was once married?
cards.answer: The recorded sense also allows a widowed person. The word does not by itself tell the person's entire history.

gatu.title: A particular barkcloth in Lau
gatu.intro: In Lau, gatu can name a large barkcloth piece prepared for presentation. Masi is the broader Fijian barkcloth word; kamunaga names ceremonial valuables as a category.

cards.question: A large presentation cloth from Lau is described as gatu. What material family does it belong to?
cards.answer: Gatu is a kind of barkcloth; masi is the broader Fijian barkcloth term.

cards.question: When gatu is presented among kamunaga, does kamunaga mean the cloth's material?
cards.answer: Kamunaga groups ceremonial valuables; gatu identifies a particular barkcloth item in this context.

link.label: Explore Lau barkcloth in a museum collection

matabani.title: A group that makes music
matabani.intro: Matabani names a band or orchestra. Mataqiriqiri is another recorded musical-group label; laga names the action of beginning or leading a song.

cards.question: A performance has a matabani and one singer who laga the song. Which word names the group?
cards.answer: Matabani is the band or orchestra; laga is beginning or leading the song.

cards.question: Matabani and mataqiriqiri both have musical-group glosses. Does that alone prove they are interchangeable in every community?
cards.answer: Their recorded English glosses overlap. A complete local phrase is needed before claiming the same use everywhere.

qato.title: Which adornment is worn?
qato.intro: Qato is a bracelet or similar band worn around an arm or ankle. Salusalu is a garland made with flowers or scented leaves.

cards.question: An ornament circles a wrist. Which of these words is the checked bracelet word?
cards.answer: Qato is a bracelet or band; salusalu is a floral garland.

cards.question: Can a qato in this meaning be worn at an ankle rather than only at a wrist?
cards.answer: The recorded meaning includes a band worn on an arm or ankle.

yavato.title: The grub in wood
yavato.intro: Yavato names a large tree grub. A comparative study places the Fijian word beside related Pacific forms for grubs found in timber; the label alone does not give an exact insect species.

cards.question: Someone finds a yavato inside wood. Are they looking at a grub or a marine fish?
cards.answer: Yavato is a tree grub. Qio, by contrast, is a shark.

cards.question: Related Pacific words also name wood grubs. Does that prove each community is naming exactly the same insect species?
cards.answer: Related words can share a broad meaning while local identifications still need checking.

link.label: Read the comparative study of Pacific grub names

kalou.title: Context changes the reading
kalou.intro: Kalou can refer to a spirit or deity. In Christian Fijian it can mean God; a complete phrase and setting help show which reading is intended.

cards.question: A traditional account refers to several kalou. Which reading is being used here?
cards.answer: One checked sense of kalou covers spirits or deities.

cards.question: In a Christian Fijian prayer, can kalou be read as 'God'?
cards.answer: That is a separate checked use. The same spelling does not erase the older spirit or deity reading.

bala.title: A turtle, but which one?
bala.intro: Bala names a male turtle. The checked word does not, on its own, settle the turtle's species.

cards.question: A turtle is called bala. What does this word specify?
cards.answer: Bala specifies a male turtle; qio names a shark.

cards.question: Can bala alone confirm that a turtle belongs to one particular scientific species?
cards.answer: The recorded meaning identifies the sex, not a precise species. A species claim needs separate identification.

bakewa.title: A suckerfish beside a larger animal
bakewa.intro: Bakewa is a remora or suckerfish that attaches to larger sea animals. FishBase records the Fiji name for Echeneis naucrates; a host fish is not itself a bakewa.

cards.question: A bakewa rides attached to a qio. Which animal is the suckerfish?
cards.answer: Bakewa names the remora; qio names the shark it may attach to.

cards.question: FishBase matches one recorded bakewa name to Echeneis naucrates. Does that one match prove every local use has been identified to species?
cards.answer: A species identification is useful evidence, but local names and identifications still need to be checked in context.

link.label: See the Fiji bakewa record in FishBase

ceguoca.title: What happens to the breath?
ceguoca.intro: Ceguoca is to pant or breathe with difficulty. Oca names tiredness; the breathing sign and its possible cause are not identical.

cards.question: After hard exercise, someone is ceguoca. Which sign is directly named?
cards.answer: Ceguoca names difficult or rapid breathing in this context; oca names tiredness.

cards.question: If someone is ceguoca, does the word alone prove that oca is the cause?
cards.answer: Panting may have several causes. The word reports the breathing difficulty, not a diagnosis.

rube.title: Hanging up, not falling down
rube.intro: Rube means to hang up or suspend something. Ceba can describe a thin object fluttering downward; isulu names clothing that might be hung.

cards.question: A garment is hung up to dry. Which word names the garment itself?
cards.answer: Isulu is clothing; rube is the hanging or suspending action.

cards.question: A leaf flutters toward the ground. Is that the same motion as keeping it suspended overhead?
cards.answer: Ceba points to fluttering down; rube concerns suspending something.

rairai.title: An appearance can leave room for doubt
rairai.intro: Rairai can mean to seem or appear. Basika more specifically points to something coming out or emerging.

cards.question: An object physically comes out from hiding. Which word points more clearly to that emergence?
cards.answer: Basika names appearing or emerging; rairai can also be an impression that something seems a certain way.

cards.question: A proposal seems promising. Does that appearance alone prove it will work?
cards.answer: Rairai can report how a thing seems. Its eventual result still needs to be seen.

basika.title: From hidden to visible
basika.intro: Basika means to appear or emerge. Yali can mean missing or gone; rairai can be an appearance or impression without an emergence.

cards.question: A lost object appears again. Which earlier state does that reverse?
cards.answer: Yali can mean missing; basika means appearing or emerging.

cards.question: A plan merely seems promising. Has anything necessarily emerged from hiding?
cards.answer: Rairai can describe an impression. Basika can describe something coming into view.

cavacava.title: The end of an account or a place
cavacava.intro: Cavacava can name a conclusion, an ending, or a boundary. The thing being discussed tells the reader which sort of end is meant.

cards.question: A story reaches its cavacava. Which reading fits?
cards.answer: Cavacava can mean the ending or conclusion of an account.

cards.question: A surveyor marks the cavacava of a plot. Is that more likely a boundary or the final page of a story?
cards.answer: The checked meaning also allows an outer edge or boundary.

waqaca.title: Lighting and what follows
waqaca.intro: Waqaca means to light a fire or lamp. Buka can be fire or firewood; kuvu can be the smoke that rises afterward.

cards.question: Someone lights a lamp. Which word names the action of lighting it?
cards.answer: Waqaca is the lighting action; buka can name fire or firewood.

cards.question: Smoke begins to rise after the fire is lit. Which word can name that drifting smoke?
cards.answer: Kuvu can be smoke; waqaca is lighting the fire or lamp.

ceba.title: A thin thing comes down
ceba.intro: Ceba means to flutter down, as a leaf or another thin flat thing can. Cagi is wind; rube is to hang or suspend something.

cards.question: A leaf moves downward in the air. Which word captures that fluttering?
cards.answer: Ceba is fluttering down; rube is hanging or suspending.

cards.question: The cagi changes a leaf's path while it ceba. Does ceba itself name the wind?
cards.answer: Cagi names wind. Ceba names the leaf's fluttering descent.

daru.title: Just you and me
daru.intro: In this subject use, daru is the short form of kedaru: 'we two', including the listener. Keirau is also two people, but excludes the listener.

cards.question: A speaker addresses you and means only the two of you. Which form fits the inclusive pair?
cards.answer: Daru includes the listener. Keirau is a two-person 'we' that leaves the listener out.

cards.question: Which full pronoun does subject-form daru shorten here?
cards.answer: Kedaru is the corresponding full two-person inclusive pronoun; kedatou covers a small larger group.

datou.title: A small group including you
datou.intro: In this subject use, datou is short for kedatou: 'we few' including the listener. Daru keeps the group to exactly two people.

cards.question: A speaker includes you and a few others. Which short form fits this group rather than the pair daru?
cards.answer: Datou is the small inclusive group; daru is just two people including you.

cards.question: Which full pronoun corresponds to datou in this use?
cards.answer: Kedatou is the full inclusive few-person form; keirau excludes the listener and refers to two.

tou.title: A shorter form needs its setting
tou.intro: In one subject use, tou is a still shorter form associated with kedatou, meaning 'we few' including the listener. Tou also occurs elsewhere, so a full phrase is needed.

cards.question: In the inclusive few-person subject use, which full form helps explain tou?
cards.answer: Tou can shorten the kedatou group in this use; kedaru refers to two people.

cards.question: If you see tou by itself, may you always translate it 'we few including you' without context?
cards.answer: Tou has other uses. Check who is speaking, who is included and the complete phrase before choosing this reading.

da.title: A larger 'we' that includes you
da.intro: In this subject use, da is short for keda, 'we many' including the listener. Keimami is 'we many' with the listener excluded.

cards.question: A speaker addresses you as part of a large group. Which short form includes you?
cards.answer: Da includes the listener in this use; keimami excludes the listener.

cards.question: Which full pronoun corresponds to this subject-form da?
cards.answer: Keda is the full inclusive many-person form. Kedaru is the inclusive two-person form.

vakanomodi.title: The manner is silent
vakanomodi.intro: Vakanomodi means silently or in silence. It tells how an action happens; the action itself must be supplied by context.

cards.question: Someone reads a book without speaking aloud. Which word adds the quiet manner?
cards.answer: Ivola is the book or written record; vakanomodi says the activity happens silently.

cards.question: A singer leads a song aloud. Could we describe that same audible singing as vakanomodi without changing the scene?
cards.answer: Laga concerns beginning or leading a song; vakanomodi means silently. The description would need a different context.

cauna.title: What remains after the meal
cauna.intro: Cauna is a remainder or leftover portion, especially food. Kakana names food more generally; maca can describe a supply that has run out.

cards.question: After a meal, some kakana is left. Which word focuses on the leftover portion?
cards.answer: Cauna is what remains; magiti is food for a feast or presentation.

cards.question: A pot has nothing left because its supply has run out. Can the empty pot's contents be called cauna?
cards.answer: Cauna requires something to remain; maca can describe a supply that has been used up.

batikadi.title: Waiting with a different intention
batikadi.intro: Batikadi is a historical word for lying in wait to attack. Waraka is the broader act of waiting; the intended attack changes the scene.

cards.question: Someone is waiting for a friend to arrive. Does that alone make their action batikadi?
cards.answer: Waraka can be ordinary waiting. Batikadi carries the hostile ambush sense recorded in the older dictionary.

cards.question: The historical entry also uses batikadi for a person who ambushes. Is that a separate use from the action of lying in wait?
cards.answer: The same recorded form has both an action sense and a person sense; the phrase must tell you which one is meant.

beta.title: Bloom is one stage, not the harvest
beta.intro: Beta describes a tree in full bloom. Burebu names fruit that falls before ripening; botatoka names a ripe nut still on the tree.

cards.question: A tree is beta. Has that word alone told you that its fruit is ripe?
cards.answer: Full bloom concerns the flowers, not the later ripeness of a fruit or nut.

cards.question: Fruit drops before maturity. Which word names that event rather than the tree's full bloom?
cards.answer: Burebu is the premature fruit fall; beta describes a tree flowering fully.

bibivoro.title: A bruise is not every kind of break
bibivoro.intro: Bibivoro describes something crushed or bruised. Dabuiloa focuses on a dark bruise; cabola can describe something broken open.

cards.question: Fruit is crushed and bruised but has not cracked open. Which word still fits?
cards.answer: Bibivoro covers crushing or bruising; cabola concerns a break or crack.

cards.question: A bruise has left a dark mark on skin or fruit. Which related word names that visible mark more specifically?
cards.answer: Dabuiloa is the checked dark-bruise word; bibivoro can describe the crushing or bruising more broadly.

biri.title: Swelling is one visible sign
biri.intro: Biri is recorded for swelling, particularly a thigh. Mavoa describes injury; bubuta can describe sunburn or blistering.

cards.question: A person's thigh is swollen. Which checked word names the swelling itself?
cards.answer: Biri is the swelling description in this older use; mavoa is injury or damage.

cards.question: Skin blisters after sun exposure. Does biri alone tell you that sunburn was the cause?
cards.answer: Bubuta can describe sunburn or blistering. Biri names swelling without settling its cause.

bou.title: A post that holds the roof
bou.intro: Bou names the tall house post supporting the ridgepole. Boto names an interior space of a traditional house, not that structural post.

cards.question: Which word identifies the support beneath a ridgepole?
cards.answer: Bou is the tall supporting post; boto is a space inside the house.

cards.question: The ridgepole needs support. What work does the bou do in the house?
cards.answer: Bou names the tall post with that roof-supporting job; calovei are leaves used to line a food container.

bowai.title: Look at the object, then its name
bowai.intro: Bowai is a Fijian pole club. Museum examples show both a plain staff and decorated examples; the decoration alone does not define the word.

cards.question: A long hardwood pole is catalogued as a Fijian club. Is bowai the club or a snare for animals?
cards.answer: Bowai names the pole club. Dai is a snare or trap.

cards.question: One museum bowai has a wrapped grip while another is decorated. Must every bowai have the same ornament?
cards.answer: Bowai identifies a club form; museum examples differ in their surface treatment.

link.label: See a Fijian bowai in the Smithsonian collection

buawa.title: What is hard to see?
buawa.intro: Buawa describes short-sighted or indistinct vision. Wanonova is deliberately watching or staring at something; the two words do different work.

cards.question: Someone watches a distant object closely but the view is still blurred. Which word names the difficulty of seeing clearly?
cards.answer: Buawa concerns unclear vision; wanonova concerns close watching.

cards.question: A thing merely rairai different in poor light. Does that prove the observer is permanently buawa?
cards.answer: Rairai can report an appearance or impression. A blurred view in one scene is not enough to decide a person's lasting eyesight.

bui.title: A woman in a family relationship
bui.intro: Bui can refer to an older woman or grandmother. The recorded phrase bui ni gone relates the woman to a child; yalewa is a broader word for a woman.

cards.question: Which word can carry a grandmother or older-woman sense rather than only naming a woman generally?
cards.answer: Bui carries the older-woman or grandmother reading; yalewa names a woman more broadly.

cards.question: In the recorded phrase bui ni gone, does gone help identify whose family relationship is being discussed?
cards.answer: The phrase relates bui to a child. The relationship matters more than translating bui as a generic label for any woman.

buroro.title: A plant comes back after damage
buroro.intro: Buroro is recorded for grass shooting up again after it has been burned or destroyed. Beta, by contrast, describes a tree in full bloom.

cards.question: Grass shoots up again after fire. Which word brings that return of growth into view?
cards.answer: Buroro concerns growth returning after damage; beta is full bloom of a tree.

cards.question: If a tree is beta, must it first have been burned?
cards.answer: Full bloom and regrowth after destruction are different stages. The extra history belongs to buroro here.

cabola.title: The object breaks; the sound is another clue
cabola.intro: Cabola describes something broken or cracked. Cabolo can name a burst or loud report, while cadruti is especially recorded for a snapped rope.

cards.question: A vessel is found cracked open, but no one heard it happen. Which word names its condition?
cards.answer: Cabola concerns the broken condition; cabolo can describe an explosion or report.

cards.question: A rope snaps. Which older word singles out that kind of break more closely?
cards.answer: Cadruti is especially recorded for a broken rope; cabola is a broader broken condition.

cabolo.title: A burst can be heard
cabolo.intro: Cabolo has an event sense, to burst or make a loud report, and a separate sense for the explosion or report itself. Cabola names something broken.

cards.question: A sudden report is heard like a gunshot. Which recorded word names the loud event?
cards.answer: Cabolo can be the burst or loud report; cabola describes a break.

cards.question: If an object is cabola, must somebody have heard a cabolo?
cards.answer: A broken object need not have made an audible explosion. The two spellings keep condition and sound apart.

cadruti.title: A break in a rope
cadruti.intro: Cadruti is especially recorded for a rope that has broken or snapped. Cabola is the wider broken or cracked description.

cards.question: A rope parts in two. Which historical word points especially to that material?
cards.answer: Cadruti is chiefly recorded of a broken rope; cabola is less specific.

cards.question: The rope is still hanging intact. Does the act of rube, hanging something, say that it has become cadruti?
cards.answer: Rube concerns suspending an object; cadruti requires a break or snap in the rope.

draudrau.title: Leaves can serve as a surface
draudrau.intro: Draudrau names leaves used for serving food or as a covering. Calovei more specifically names leaves placed as a lining inside a pot or basket.

cards.question: Food is presented on a layer of leaves. Which word names the serving leaves?
cards.answer: Draudrau are the serving leaves; gatu is barkcloth, not the food-serving leaf layer.

cards.question: Leaves are placed inside a basket as a food lining. Which related word gives that more precise placement?
cards.answer: Calovei names lining leaves; draudrau can cover serving or wrapping leaves more broadly.

dreke.title: The hollow holds different things
dreke.intro: Dreke is a cavity or hollow. A cup has an inside, and a ship has a hold; this entry records both uses of the same word.

cards.question: A ship's cargo is placed in its dreke. Does dreke name the hold or the sail?
cards.answer: The recorded maritime use is the hold, the space where cargo is carried.

cards.question: Does dreke refer only to ships, or can it also name the hollow of a cup or oven?
cards.answer: The common feature is an inner cavity; a ship's hold is one application among others.

link.label: See a separately recorded ship phrase for dreke

kibo.title: Out of sight in a hole
kibo.intro: Kibo is recorded for an animal withdrawing into its hole and disappearing from view. Basika points in the other direction: appearing or emerging.

cards.question: An animal moves back into its hole. Which word records that disappearance?
cards.answer: Kibo is the retreat into a hole; basika means to appear or emerge.

cards.question: An animal is yali from sight. Does yali alone tell you it entered a hole?
cards.answer: Yali means missing or gone. Kibo gives a more specific way an animal disappears.

bona.title: A smell tells you something has spoiled
bona.intro: Bona can describe a foul smell from decay or name that stench. Savasava means clean, but a clean appearance alone does not settle how something smells.

cards.question: Food gives off a rotten smell. Which word names that unpleasant quality?
cards.answer: Bona is the rotten-smell word; savasava means clean.

cards.question: Could the same recorded form bona refer to the stench itself rather than only describing food?
cards.answer: The dictionary has a separate sense for the foul smell as a thing, beside the description of smelling rotten.

botatoka.title: Ripe, but still on the tree
botatoka.intro: Botatoka names a ripe nut that has not fallen. Burebu is the opposite timing for fruit: it drops before it is mature.

cards.question: A nut is mature and still attached to its tree. Which word fits this precise stage?
cards.answer: Botatoka is ripe but still attached; burebu is fruit falling before maturity.

cards.question: A green coconut is called bu at its drinking stage. Does bu alone tell you it is a botatoka ripe nut?
cards.answer: Bu names a coconut at the drinking stage; botatoka makes a different claim about a ripe nut still on the tree.

botonikete.title: Finding the part of the body
botonikete.intro: Botonikete names the abdomen. Kete can name the stomach or belly; bilobilo is the kneecap, a different body part.

cards.question: A person points to the abdomen rather than the knee. Which checked form fits?
cards.answer: Botonikete is the abdomen; bilobilo is the kneecap.

cards.question: Kete can mean the belly or stomach. Does that make botonikete a word for a kneecap?
cards.answer: The related belly meaning stays in the abdominal area; the knee has its own word.

bubuta.title: Sunburn and blisters are visible
bubuta.intro: Bubuta can describe skin sunburned or blistered through illness. Biri names swelling, which does not alone say how the skin was affected.

cards.question: Skin is blistered after exposure to the sun. Which recorded description fits?
cards.answer: Bubuta includes sunburn; biri is swelling.

cards.question: If someone is bubuta because of illness, must the cause have been sunshine?
cards.answer: The older entry also records blistering from disease. The scene tells you which cause is intended.

buisokoloa.title: Ink from a sea creature
buisokoloa.intro: Buisokoloa is the dark fluid released by a cuttlefish. Kuvu can name smoke, dust or spray drifting in air, which is a different material.

cards.question: Dark fluid comes from a cuttlefish. Is it buisokoloa or smoke called kuvu?
cards.answer: Buisokoloa is the cuttlefish's dark fluid; kuvu covers smoke and other drifting material.

cards.question: Does the dark colour alone let you identify every black mark in the sea as buisokoloa?
cards.answer: The word identifies a material by its source, a cuttlefish, not by colour alone.

bukebuke.title: A mound with a planting purpose
bukebuke.intro: Bukebuke is a soil mound, especially one prepared for yams. Bulubulu names placing yams into prepared mounds; uvi is the crop.

cards.question: A grower prepares an earth mound for uvi. Which word names the mound itself?
cards.answer: Bukebuke is the mound; bulubulu is the planting action.

cards.question: An anthill also rises from the ground. Would its shape alone make it a bukebuke prepared for planting?
cards.answer: Buri is an anthill. Bukebuke is a soil mound, especially a planting mound made for yams.

bulowa.title: One spelling, two recorded meanings
bulowa.intro: Bulowa has a pumice-stone sense and a separate historical sense for swelling of the mouth. Neither meaning can be selected from the spelling alone.

cards.question: A light porous volcanic stone is being handled. Which bulowa meaning fits?
cards.answer: The stone is the material sense of bulowa; the mouth condition is a separate recorded sense.

cards.question: A person has a swollen mouth. Should the stone meaning be inserted into that sentence?
cards.answer: The historical source records a different bulowa sense for the condition. A full phrase is needed to distinguish the readings.

butoleka.title: Daylight briefly turns dark
butoleka.intro: Butoleka names a solar eclipse. Bogi is ordinary night; buto names darkness more broadly, including when daylight is obscured.

cards.question: The sun is obscured during the day. Which word names the event rather than ordinary night?
cards.answer: Butoleka is the solar eclipse; bogi is night.

cards.question: Does buto on its own necessarily tell you that a solar eclipse is happening?
cards.answer: Buto is darkness more generally. Butoleka names the specific eclipse event.

buna.title: A reef beneath the surface
buna.intro: Buna can name a submerged reef or deep water with the bottom still visible. Daveta is a passage through a reef where a boat can pass.

cards.question: A boat seeks a passage through the reef. Which word names that opening rather than a submerged reef?
cards.answer: Daveta is the passage; buna can be the submerged reef.

cards.question: The water is deep but its bottom can still be seen. Is that also included in the recorded buna meaning?
cards.answer: The older entry records both a sunken reef and deep water whose bottom remains visible.

burebu.title: Fruit falls before its time
burebu.intro: Burebu is fruit that drops before it matures. Botatoka identifies a nut that is ripe and still attached to the tree.

cards.question: A fruit falls while still immature. Which word names this early fall?
cards.answer: Burebu is premature fruit fall; botatoka is a ripe nut not yet fallen.

cards.question: A tree is beta, in full bloom. Has its fruit necessarily become burebu?
cards.answer: Bloom does not mean fruit has already formed and fallen before ripening.

balala.title: A spear remains lodged
balala.intro: Balala describes being pierced by a spear that stays in place. Moto is the spear itself; mavoa is the wider idea of being injured.

cards.question: A moto has struck and remains lodged. Which word describes that particular result?
cards.answer: Moto names the spear. Balala describes the condition after it has pierced and remained in place.

cards.question: Someone is mavoa after a fall, with no spear involved. Does mavoa alone establish balala?
cards.answer: Mavoa covers injury more broadly; balala specifies the lodged spear in this historical sense.

bilobilo.title: Find the part, then the condition
bilobilo.intro: Bilobilo is the kneecap. Kete is the stomach or belly, while mavoa can describe an injury anywhere on the body.

cards.question: Someone points to the hard cap at the front of a knee. Which word identifies that part?
cards.answer: Bilobilo is the kneecap; kete points to the stomach or belly.

cards.question: A person says they are mavoa. Can you tell from that word alone whether their bilobilo is hurt?
cards.answer: Mavoa reports an injury. It does not locate that injury at the kneecap.

buku vere.title: A plan can be hidden
buku vere.intro: Buku vere is to plan or conspire together, particularly against someone. Batikadi is the separate act of lying in wait for an attack; bolebole was a public challenge.

cards.question: People secretly make a hostile plan together but have not yet lain in wait. Which term names the planning?
cards.answer: Buku vere concerns the conspiracy; batikadi is lying in wait to attack.

cards.question: A challenge is proclaimed openly before a chief. Is that the same hidden action as buku vere?
cards.answer: The recorded bolebole was public. Buku vere points to planning or conspiring together.

buli.title: A shell, not every ceremonial valuable
buli.intro: In this sense, buli is a white cowrie shell. The older dictionary also records white cowries used to ornament canoes; tabua is a whale tooth.

cards.question: A white cowrie is being named. Is it a buli or a tabua?
cards.answer: Buli is a cowrie shell in this sense. Tabua is a whale tooth used in formal exchange.

cards.question: An older account describes cowries adorning a canoe. Does the shell's use as ornament turn it into barkcloth called masi?
cards.answer: The object remains a shell; masi names Fijian barkcloth.

burotu.title: A spirit place and a figure of speech
burotu.intro: Burotu is a beautiful place of departed spirits in Fijian tradition. The older dictionary also uses it figuratively for a delightful place.

cards.question: In a traditional account of departed spirits, is Burotu an ordinary name for any town?
cards.answer: The recorded tradition gives Burotu a spirit-world meaning. A town name would need its own evidence.

cards.question: Someone calls a pleasant place Burotu figuratively. Must they be claiming they have literally entered the spirit world?
cards.answer: The historical entry records a figurative delightful-place use beside the traditional spirit-place sense.

link.label: See Borutu, a recorded spelling, in a Fiji museum collection

cadri.title: Hard to overcome
cadri.intro: Cadri was recorded especially for a difficult or resistant thing. Rerevaki names something feared or dangerous; difficulty and danger need not coincide.

cards.question: A problem is stubbornly hard to overcome. Which older word points to that resistance?
cards.answer: Cadri was used of things difficult to overcome; rerevaki concerns danger or fear.

cards.question: If a route is cadri to complete, must it also be rerevaki?
cards.answer: A demanding task need not be dangerous. The two descriptions ask different questions.

caqu.title: A gift at departure
caqu.intro: In the older usage, caqu is property presented to friends as they leave. Butu instead points to valuables presented at a solevu gathering.

cards.question: Friends are departing and receive an item of property. Which historical word identifies that parting gift?
cards.answer: Caqu is recorded for an item presented on departure; butu belongs to a solevu presentation.

cards.question: Does caqu by itself tell you exactly whether the item is cloth, food or another possession?
cards.answer: The word identifies the parting presentation, not a fixed material or object type.

bolebole.title: A challenge spoken openly
bolebole.intro: Bolebole was a public declaration of courage and loyalty before a chief ahead of war. Buku vere is planning together against someone, often hidden.

cards.question: A person proclaims courage publicly before a chief. Which word names that historical practice?
