cards.answer: Bolebole was the public challenge or declaration; buku vere is conspiracy or plotting.

cards.question: If a group quietly makes a plan but issues no public challenge, has it necessarily performed bolebole?
cards.answer: The public declaration is the important part of the recorded bolebole practice.

bolomo.title: A step in preparing dalo
bolomo.intro: Bolomo is the older word for soaking dalo when preparing pudding. Dalo names the taro crop; buta describes food cooked enough to eat.

cards.question: Dalo is being steeped for a pudding. Which word names the preparation action rather than the crop?
cards.answer: Bolomo is the steeping step; dalo is taro.

cards.question: If dalo has only been soaked, does bolomo alone tell you the pudding is already buta, cooked enough to eat?
cards.answer: Soaking and reaching a cooked state are different stages. Buta supplies the cooked-enough meaning.

boroa.title: Crowded reeds in a fence
boroa.intro: Boroa describes reeds packed close together in a fence. The older record warns against extending it freely to anything that happens to be crowded.

cards.question: Reeds are fitted tightly side by side in a fence. Which recorded description fits?
cards.answer: Boroa was recorded for the crowded reeds; maravu describes calm or smooth conditions.

cards.question: A street is full of people. May the fence-reed gloss alone prove boroa is the normal word for that crowd?
cards.answer: The older source marks a restricted use. A complete local phrase would be needed for a different setting.

boto.title: Locate the space inside the house
boto.intro: Boto names a particular interior space of a traditional house, between the lalaga and matadravu. Bou, by contrast, is a tall post supporting the ridgepole.

cards.question: A description points to an area inside the house rather than a load-bearing post. Which word fits?
cards.answer: Boto is the interior space in this sense; bou is the post carrying the ridgepole.

cards.question: Does the word boto by itself identify the material used for that house's roof?
cards.answer: It locates a space in the layout. The roof material requires a different description.

bubului.title: What is invoked in an oath?
bubului.intro: Bubului is recorded for an oath sworn in the name of a deceased person or a deity. Kalou names a spirit or deity, not the oath itself.

cards.question: An oath invokes a kalou. Which word names the oath rather than the being invoked?
cards.answer: Bubului is the oath in this older usage; kalou can name the deity or spirit.

cards.question: If the oath invokes a departed person, does the recorded bubului meaning require that person to be a deity?
cards.answer: The historical entry gives a deceased person and a deity as two possible referents.

bulivovo.title: The fence has parts and a pattern
bulivovo.intro: Bulivovo are horizontal reeds at the top or bottom of a traditional house fence. Boroa describes reeds packed close together; bai can name the enclosing fence as a whole.

cards.question: Which word points to the horizontal reeds, rather than the fence itself?
cards.answer: Bulivovo names the particular fence reeds; bai can name the enclosing fence.

cards.question: The reeds are tightly crowded. Does that density tell you whether they are the horizontal top or bottom pieces?
cards.answer: Boroa concerns closeness; bulivovo identifies the reeds' position in the fence.

bulubulu.title: Planting action and prepared mound
bulubulu.intro: Bulubulu names placing yams into prepared earth mounds. Bukebuke is the mound; uvi is the cultivated yam.

cards.question: A grower prepares a bukebuke but has not planted. Has the bulubulu action happened yet?
cards.answer: Bukebuke is the mound; bulubulu is putting the yam into it.

cards.question: In this recorded gardening use, which crop is placed in the mound: uvi or dalo?
cards.answer: The older description specifically speaks of yams. Uvi is yam; dalo is taro.

bunua.title: Many bats, one branch
bunua.intro: Bunua is a group of bats hanging together from a single branch. It names the cluster, not one bat singled out from it.

cards.question: Several bats hang together from one branch. Does bunua identify the cluster or a single bat?
cards.answer: The older entry describes a lot of bats hanging together on one branch.

cards.question: Bats hang separately on branches far apart. Has the one-branch detail in the recorded bunua scene been met?
cards.answer: The recorded picture is a group sharing one branch. Other arrangements need their own contextual check.

buri.title: A mound made by insects
buri.intro: Buri is an anthill. Bukebuke is an earth mound especially prepared for planting yams; the similar shape does not give them the same use.

cards.question: A mound belongs to ants rather than to a yam garden. Which word names it?
cards.answer: Buri is an anthill; bukebuke is a planting mound.

cards.question: If a grower places uvi into a prepared mound, have the ants necessarily made that mound?
cards.answer: Uvi is yam. A prepared yam mound is bukebuke; buri is an anthill.

butabutako.title: The person and the act
butabutako.intro: Butabutako is an older form for a thief. The historical source relates it to butako, to steal; buku vere is plotting, which by itself does not establish a theft.

cards.question: An account identifies someone as a thief. Does butabutako name the person or a place?
cards.answer: The recorded sense is a thief, not a location.

cards.question: People secretly plan something against another person. Does buku vere alone establish that anyone has stolen property?
cards.answer: Buku vere concerns a conspiracy; butabutako identifies a thief. The action still needs evidence.

butayari.title: A nut before it fills out
butayari.intro: Butayari is a nut with only a little flesh developed inside. Botatoka is a ripe nut still attached to a tree; those are different observations.

cards.question: A nut is opened and has very little flesh inside. Which word describes that condition?
cards.answer: Butayari concerns how little flesh has developed; botatoka concerns a ripe nut still on the tree.

cards.question: A nut has not fallen. Does that fact by itself tell you whether its flesh is well developed?
cards.answer: Remaining attached and developing flesh are separate details. The first matters for botatoka; the second for butayari.

butu.title: What is presented at a solevu?
butu.intro: Butu is property or valuables presented at a solevu gathering. The particular item varies; tabua is one kind of ceremonial valuable and magiti names feast food.

cards.question: At a solevu, valuables are presented. Which word names the presented property in this older use?
cards.answer: Butu identifies the presented property; magiti names food for a feast or formal presentation.

cards.question: Does the word butu alone tell you that every presented object is a tabua?
cards.answer: Tabua is a whale tooth. A museum account records different kinds of valuables at solevu, so the broader presentation does not fix one material.

link.label: See objects presented at solevu

cabecabe.title: Up the slope, then the summit
cabecabe.intro: Cabecabe can mean a steep hillside or path upward. Delana is the hilltop reached after a climb.

cards.question: A walker is still climbing the steep cabecabe. Have they necessarily reached the delana?
cards.answer: Cabecabe can be the slope or uphill path; delana is the top.

cards.question: One recorded cabecabe sense describes the terrain as hilly. Must that description identify one exact path?
cards.answer: The checked entry also has a hilly-terrain sense; a particular path needs more context.

calovei.title: Leaves line the food container
calovei.intro: Calovei are leaves placed inside a pot or basket as a food lining. Draudrau can name leaves used under food for serving or as a cover.

cards.question: Leaves are fitted inside a basket before food is placed there. Which word highlights that lining?
cards.answer: Calovei specifically names leaves lining a food container; draudrau has a wider serving or covering use.

cards.question: Food is set directly on serving leaves, without a pot or basket. Does that scene establish the container-lining use of calovei?
cards.answer: The broader draudrau sense covers serving leaves. Calovei in this entry is tied to lining a container.

wanonova.title: Watching closely is an action
wanonova.intro: Wanonova is to stare or watch closely. Buawa concerns indistinct vision; rairai can mean to seem or appear, without deliberate watching.

cards.question: A person deliberately keeps their eyes on something. Which word names that act?
cards.answer: Wanonova is close watching; buawa is difficulty seeing distinctly.

cards.question: A plan rairai promising. Does that impression prove someone was physically staring at it?
cards.answer: Rairai can express how something seems. Wanonova is a deliberate act of watching.

dabuiloa.title: A bruise you can see
dabuiloa.intro: Dabuiloa is a dark bruise on skin or fruit. Bibivoro can describe crushing or bruising more broadly; mavoa is a broader injury word.

cards.question: A piece of fruit has a dark bruise. Which word identifies the visible mark?
cards.answer: Dabuiloa is recorded for a dark bruise on skin or fruit; mavoa is injury or damage more generally.

cards.question: Something is bibivoro after pressure. Must it always show a dark dabuiloa mark?
cards.answer: Bibivoro can be crushed or bruised. Dabuiloa supplies the dark-mark detail.

qio.title: Which sea animal is it?
qio.intro: Qio is a shark. Fiji fish-name records include more specific shark names, so qio alone does not settle the species; bakewa is a remora that may attach to a shark.

cards.question: A bakewa rides attached to a qio. Which of the two is the shark?
cards.answer: Qio is the shark; bakewa is the smaller remora.

cards.question: FishBase records a name such as qio saga for a particular shark. Does qio by itself identify that one species?
cards.answer: Qio is the broader shark name. The added name and a checked identification narrow it further.

link.label: See recorded Fiji shark names

dai.title: A trap is not a net
dai.intro: Dai is a snare or trap for catching an animal. Lawa can be a fishing net; bowai is a pole club, a different kind of implement.

cards.question: An animal is caught in a snare. Which word names the catching device?
cards.answer: Dai is the snare or trap; lawa can be a net, especially for fishing.

cards.question: A museum labels a hardwood object bowai. Does that make it a dai snare?
cards.answer: Bowai is a club. Dai is a device set to catch an animal.

link.label: Read a linguistic study of the Fijian snare word

vakavuqa.title: How often, not how strongly
vakavuqa.intro: Vakavuqa means frequently. Vakalevu can concern degree or intensity; a single strong event is not thereby frequent.

cards.question: An action happens again and again. Which word answers 'how often'?
cards.answer: Vakavuqa concerns frequency; vakalevu concerns an increase or intensification in the relevant construction.

cards.question: An event happens once but very strongly. Does its strength alone make it vakavuqa?
cards.answer: Frequency needs repeated occurrence. Intensity is a different question.

cakulea.title: Searching by moving things aside
cakulea.intro: Cakulea is a search that involves moving things aside. Wanonova is close watching; merely looking is not yet the same action.

cards.question: Someone shifts items out of the way while searching. Which word fits that action?
cards.answer: Cakulea is the searching action with things moved aside; wanonova is watching closely.

cards.question: A lost object basika, appears, while no one is searching. Has that appearance alone established cakulea?
cards.answer: Basika concerns appearing; cakulea describes a particular way of searching.

caca.title: The amount beyond full tens
caca.intro: In this counting sense, caca is the remainder beyond a multiple of ten. Cauna can mean a portion left over, especially food; its setting is different.

cards.question: Twenty-three items are grouped into tens. How many are left beyond the two full tens?
cards.answer: The three extra items are the remainder that caca identifies in this counting use.

cards.question: A meal leaves a portion of kakana in the pot. Does the counting sense of caca automatically name that leftover food?
cards.answer: Cauna focuses on a remaining food portion; caca here concerns the amount beyond full tens.

dawa.title: A fruit with a season and a tree
dawa.intro: Dawa names the edible fruit of the dawa tree, identified in a botanical reference as Pometia pinnata. Fiji's seasonal account lists dawa among fruits available during Vula i Nuqalevu.

cards.question: A seasonal list mentions dawa alongside other fruits. Is it naming an edible fruit or a reef fish?
cards.answer: Dawa is the fruit of a tree, not a fish.

cards.question: Fruit falls before it is ripe. Does the fruit's name dawa itself describe that early fall?
cards.answer: Dawa names the fruit; burebu is the separate word for fruit falling before maturity.

link.label: See a Fiji seasonal account mentioning dawa

ikuri.title: A piece attached to a word
ikuri.intro: Ikuri is an addition attached to a yavu. Vei- can go before a base; a dewa ending follows certain predicate bases. The whole word and phrase decide the meaning.

cards.question: Which checked piece can be attached before a base: vei- or a dewa ending?
cards.answer: Vei- is a prefix, an ikuriliu. A dewa follows a base in the constructions recorded for it.

cards.question: If you see a familiar attached piece, can you translate the whole new form without checking its use?
cards.answer: An ikuri is a clue to structure; the meaning and Tuvavosa role still need a complete attested phrase.

dravukasi.title: A colour with a dirty cast
dravukasi.intro: Dravukasi describes a dirty grey colour. Savasava describes cleanliness; a colour word and a cleanliness judgement answer different questions.

cards.question: A surface is described as dirty grey. Which word gives that colour?
cards.answer: Dravukasi is the dirty-grey description; savasava means clean.

cards.question: An object is washed until savasava. Must its original grey colour have disappeared?
cards.answer: Cleaning changes the dirt, but the material may still be grey. Dravukasi carries a dirty cast rather than naming every clean grey object.

momona.title: Flesh, size and the wrong body part
momona.intro: In this sense momona can describe shellfish rich in flesh. For large round eyes, the owner instead uses ka levu and mokimokiti; the same English word 'big' does not settle the Fijian choice.

cards.question: A shellfish has plenty of flesh inside. Which word fits this recorded sense?
cards.answer: Momona can describe that fleshy fullness; maca can mean empty or used up.

cards.question: Someone wants to describe eyes as large and round. Should momona be chosen merely because English says 'big'?
cards.answer: The owner's phrasing uses ka levu and mokimokiti for the eyes. Momona here is about fullness of flesh, not simply size.

donu.title: A grouper in a reef setting
donu.intro: Donu can name coral trout or related groupers. Fiji's census fish list places it with groupers, while saqa is a trevally name.

cards.question: A fish is listed with coral trout and groupers. Which name fits that group: donu or saqa?
cards.answer: Donu belongs with coral trout and groupers; saqa belongs with trevallies.

cards.question: Kavu is recorded as a giant grouper. Does the word donu alone prove the fish is that exact giant grouper?
cards.answer: These names can share a broader grouper setting without identifying the same particular fish.

link.label: See Fiji's official fish-name list

saqa.title: Which kind of reef fish?
saqa.intro: Saqa is used for trevallies, including the giant trevally in Fiji fish lists. Donu names a coral trout or grouper, another fish group.

cards.question: A fish is identified as a trevally. Which of these names matches that group?
cards.answer: Saqa belongs to the trevally group; donu to coral trout or groupers.

cards.question: The official list also records saqaleka for giant trevally. Does saqa alone force every fish so called to be that one species?
cards.answer: The wider name and a more specific listed form should not be flattened into one exact species without a local identification.

nuqa.title: A fish name in a seasonal calendar
nuqa.intro: Nuqa is a rabbitfish. An iTaukei seasonal account says rabbitfish are abundant during Vula i Nuqalevu; the season helps remember the fish without turning the name into a month name.

cards.question: The seasonal account mentions many nuqa. Which fish group does it mean?
cards.answer: Nuqa is the rabbitfish name; saqa belongs with trevallies.

cards.question: Does the name Vula i Nuqalevu make nuqa itself a word for the whole month?
cards.answer: Nuqa names the fish. The month name is a longer seasonal expression that includes it.

link.label: Read the Fiji seasonal account of nuqa

ceruma.title: A small drink, not just any drink
ceruma.intro: Ceruma is used for sipping liquid. Gunu names drinking more generally, without telling you whether the drink is taken in little sips.

cards.question: A person takes a little liquid at a time from a bowl. Which word tells you the manner of drinking?
cards.answer: Ceruma adds the sipping manner; gunu only says that someone drinks.

cards.question: If someone gulps down the whole drink, does the English word 'drink' alone justify ceruma?
cards.answer: Ceruma is the more particular sipping action. The broader translation 'drink' loses that difference.

caucau.title: A breeze with a direction
caucau.intro: Caucau is a land breeze. It is a kind of cagi, but its direction matters: the air moves from land toward the water, commonly at night.

cards.question: At the coast at night, a breeze moves out from land toward the sea. Which name is more specific?
cards.answer: Caucau names the land breeze; cagi can name wind without specifying this coastal movement.

cards.question: A daytime sea breeze moves from water toward land. Is that also a land breeze merely because both are winds?
cards.answer: The direction reverses. A land breeze blows seaward; a sea breeze blows shoreward.

link.label: See the land-breeze explanation

cavika.title: The empty-handed return
cavika.intro: Cavika is about a fishing trip that ends with no catch. It names the outcome, not just the trip out to fish.

cards.question: Someone goes fishing and returns without fish. What does cavika pick out?
cards.answer: Cavika applies when the fishing trip ends without a catch.

cards.question: If a person is still heading out with a line, has cavika already been established?
cards.answer: You need the result: a return with nothing caught. The journey alone does not tell you that.

link.label: Read cavika in a Fijian account

leva.title: When a question hits a nerve
leva.intro: Leva can mean taking offence when a matter one does not want addressed is raised. It is a response to the issue, not simply any disagreement.

cards.question: A person takes offence because a sensitive matter was raised. Which word fits the response?
cards.answer: Leva is the offended or resentful response; daumaka gives a favourable judgement.

cards.question: In the recorded sentence 'Au sega ni cudru se leva e na vuku ni lomatarotaro', does the speaker say they are offended by the questioning?
cards.answer: Sega ni negates the response: the speaker denies being angry or offended by the questioning.

baba siga.title: A place and its nickname
baba siga.intro: Baba Siga is a nickname associated with Macuata in northern Fiji. It evokes sunny, dry slopes; it is not the name of a separate province.

cards.question: Someone calls Macuata Baba Siga. Are they naming a second province or using a regional nickname?
cards.answer: The nickname points back to Macuata and its landscape.

cards.question: If a visitor hears Baba Siga, what landscape clue does the name carry?
cards.answer: Baba Siga evokes the sunnier, drier side of Macuata; siga contributes the sun or daylight idea.

link.label: Read a local account of Baba Siga

balagi.title: Surgeonfish is a group, not one name
balagi.intro: A Fiji fish list records balagi with surgeonfish, while ta is used for a bluespine unicornfish. Both are reef fish, but the names are not interchangeable.

cards.question: The fish is listed as a yellowfin surgeonfish. Which Fijian name is attached to it?
cards.answer: The Fiji list gives balagi with yellowfin surgeonfish; ta is listed for a bluespine unicornfish.

cards.question: Does hearing 'reef fish' tell you whether the fish is balagi or corocoro?
cards.answer: Balagi belongs with surgeonfishes; corocoro is a soldierfish. The reef setting alone cannot settle the identification.

link.label: See Fiji's fish-name list

corocoro.title: A soldierfish with another local name
corocoro.intro: Fiji's fish list pairs corocoro with matalevu for blotcheye soldierfish. A similar reef setting does not make it a surgeonfish such as balagi.

cards.question: A Fiji fish list prints 'Corocoro, Matalevu' beside one English fish name. Which fish is it?
cards.answer: These two Fijian names are recorded together for blotcheye soldierfish; balagi is the surgeonfish name in that list.

cards.question: Would a catch from the reef alone prove it is corocoro rather than balagi?
cards.answer: Both may be reef fish. The type of fish, not simply where it was caught, distinguishes the names.

link.label: Compare the named reef fishes

delabulewa.title: A grouper with a particular identity
delabulewa.intro: Delabulewa names the brown-marbled grouper in Fiji Fisheries material. Donu is used for coral groupers, so the broader reef-fish setting does not merge their identities.

cards.question: A fish guide labels the brown-marbled grouper. Which name should you look for?
cards.answer: Delabulewa names this grouper; kawago is an emperor fish.

cards.question: The guide also groups donu with coral trout. Are delabulewa and donu automatically the same species?
cards.answer: Their names point to different fish within a wider grouper setting. The brown-marbled identification is particular to delabulewa.

link.label: See the Fiji Fisheries fish guide

doko ni vudi.title: Look at the snout
doko ni vudi.intro: Doko ni vudi is recorded for a long-faced or long-nosed emperor. The pointed, elongated snout helps separate this fish from other emperors such as kawago.

cards.question: Which fish name accompanies a long, pointed snout in the Fiji fish guide?
cards.answer: Doko ni vudi is the long-nosed emperor; kawago is the spangled emperor.

cards.question: Both names belong with emperors. Does that make the two names one fish?
cards.answer: They share a fish family, but the guide identifies different emperors. The longer snout is a useful clue here.

link.label: See Fiji emperor names and habitats

kabatia.title: One emperor name, several identifications
kabatia.intro: Kabatia is an emperor-fish name. Fiji guides associate it with small sea bream and identify particular kabatia in more than one way, so the name needs a place and a fish to pin it down.

cards.question: In a fish-size table, kabatia is paired with kake under small sea bream. Does that turn kake into the same fish in every list?
cards.answer: One table groups them for a purpose; other fish lists distinguish kake among snappers. Check the local identification.

cards.question: A guide names a thumbprint emperor as kabatia, while another local survey records more than one emperor under that name. What should a learner avoid?
options: Assuming one name always proves one species
cards.correct: Assuming one name always proves one species
cards.answer: Local fish names may cover different identified fish. A photograph, place and knowledgeable speaker help resolve the reference.

link.label: Compare Fiji emperor identifications

kacika.title: The yellow-lipped emperor
kacika.intro: Kacika is used for a yellowlip emperor in a Fiji fish profile. Kawago is another emperor, the spangled emperor; shared family does not erase the different names.

cards.question: A fish description calls out yellowish lips. Which Fiji name is linked to that emperor?
cards.answer: Kacika is the yellowlip emperor identification in that account; kawago names the spangled emperor.

cards.question: The same description mentions a red spot near the pectoral fin. Would the word 'emperor' alone give that detail?
cards.answer: The family word is broad. The combination of features helps identify the fish called kacika in this account.

link.label: See the Fiji kacika description

kaikai.title: A little fish at the estuary
kaikai.intro: Kaikai names a ponyfish. A Fiji fisheries survey records it in estuaries and lagoons; kawago is an emperor associated with reefs.

cards.question: A Fiji fish appendix lists Cebe/Kaikai among ponyfish in estuaries and lagoons. Is kaikai naming a ponyfish or a grouper?
cards.answer: The list identifies kaikai as a ponyfish, a different group from kavu the grouper.

cards.question: Does the spelling kaikai prove it means the same thing as kai, the freshwater mussel?
cards.answer: The repeated-looking fish name identifies a ponyfish here. A similar spelling does not license a guessed word-building analysis.

link.label: See Fiji fish names and habitats

kava.title: Kava in this entry swims
kava.intro: Here kava is a mullet recorded in Fiji's estuaries and lagoons. The English word 'kava' for a drink can mislead a learner; Fijian yaqona names the drink.

cards.question: A Fiji fish list places kava in estuaries and lagoons. What is it naming there?
cards.answer: The Fiji fish record identifies kava as a mullet in this setting.

cards.question: Would translating this fish name as yaqona keep the same meaning?
cards.answer: Yaqona is the drink or plant name; the kava in this entry is a fish. Context is essential when a word resembles a familiar English name.

link.label: See kava in Fiji's fish-name appendix

kavu.title: The giant among groupers
kavu.intro: Kavu is identified as the giant grouper in a Fiji fisheries survey. Delabulewa is a brown-marbled grouper, and donu is used for coral groupers.

cards.question: Which of these names is recorded for the giant grouper?
cards.answer: Kavu is the giant grouper; delabulewa identifies the brown-marbled grouper.

cards.question: A Fiji Fisheries profile names both kavu and donu among groupers. Does that make them the same species?
cards.answer: Kavu is listed as giant grouper; donu names coral groupers in the same profile.

link.label: See kavu in the Fiji Fisheries profile

kawago.title: One emperor among several
kawago.intro: Kawago is the spangled emperor in Fiji fish lists. Doko ni vudi is a long-nosed emperor. Their shared family name does not make them the same fish.

cards.question: A Fiji fish list places spangled emperor and long-nosed emperor beside different local names. Which one is kawago?
cards.answer: Kawago is the spangled emperor; doko ni vudi is the long-nosed emperor.

cards.question: If both kawago and kabatia are emperors, can the word emperor alone select one?
cards.answer: The shared fish family is only the start. Their local names and physical identifications differ.

link.label: See Fiji emperor names and habitats

qitawa.title: A perch near the shore
qitawa.intro: A Fiji fish appendix records qitawa, a crescent perch, in estuaries and lagoons. Sakelo is a different fish associated with rivers.

cards.question: The appendix reports a crescent perch in estuaries and lagoons. Which name is attached to it?
cards.answer: Qitawa is the name recorded there. Sakelo is a flagtail linked to river water.

cards.question: Does that same estuary setting make qitawa the ponyfish called kaikai?
cards.answer: Habitat helps narrow a search, but the appendix lists qitawa and kaikai as different fish.

link.label: See Fiji fish names and habitats

reve.title: Fresh water with a coastal connection
reve.intro: Reve is recorded as a native fish of fresh and brackish water. A fisheries list places it with the grunters, not with the river flagtail sakelo.

cards.question: A fish is observed where river water mixes with seawater. Does that setting rule out reve?
cards.answer: Reve is recorded in freshwater and brackish water, so a mixed-water setting can fit.

cards.question: Reve and sakelo may both be discussed beside rivers. Are they the same kind of fish?
cards.answer: Reve is listed with grunters; sakelo is a flagtail. Place alone cannot substitute for an identification.

link.label: See Fiji fish families and habitats

sabutu.title: An emperor with a yellow tail
sabutu.intro: A Fiji Fisheries list identifies sabutu with the Pacific yellowtail emperor. Kawago is a spangled emperor; they share a family but not the same specific fish name.

cards.question: Which name is paired with Pacific yellowtail emperor in the Fiji list?
cards.answer: Sabutu is the name in that identification; kawago is paired with spangled emperor.

cards.question: A market sign says 'emperor fish'. Has it told you whether the fish is sabutu or kabatia?
cards.answer: Both can be placed among emperors. The general English group leaves the Fijian identification open.

link.label: Compare Fiji emperor names

sakelo.title: A flagtail in the river
sakelo.intro: Sakelo is a flagtail fish recorded in rivers in a Fiji fish appendix. The same appendix also gives drava as a local name.

cards.question: The appendix lists sakelo beside drava. Are these two names attached to a flagtail or a snapper?
cards.answer: Sakelo/drava is the flagtail identification in the appendix.

cards.question: Could you identify a fish as sakelo merely because another fish, qitawa, occurs in a nearby estuary?
cards.answer: Qitawa is listed for estuaries and lagoons; sakelo is tied to rivers. Identify the fish itself, not only the place.

link.label: See Fiji river-fish names

sokisoki.title: Spines change the identification
sokisoki.intro: Sokisoki is a porcupinefish; a Fiji fish list specifies spotfin porcupinefish. Sumusumu names a pufferfish, another fish often confused with it.

cards.question: The fish list pairs sokisoki with spotfin porcupinefish. Which English group fits?
cards.answer: Sokisoki is the porcupinefish name in this list; tanabe names a snapper.

cards.question: If a fish is called sumusumu in the same list, should you silently relabel it sokisoki?
cards.answer: The list distinguishes a pufferfish from a porcupinefish. Confirm the actual fish before switching names.

link.label: Compare the Fiji fish names

sumusumu.title: The puffer and its named variety
sumusumu.intro: Sumusumu is a pufferfish name. Fiji Fisheries also records the longer name sumusumu sevula for a white-spotted pufferfish.

cards.question: A fish guide labels sumusumu sevula. What does the longer name identify?
cards.answer: The longer recorded name is a particular pufferfish identification; ulavi is a parrotfish name.

cards.question: Does the shorter name sumusumu alone tell you the fish must be that one white-spotted kind?
cards.answer: The base name is broader. The extra word in sumusumu sevula narrows the identification in the fish guide.

link.label: See the Fiji Fisheries fish guide

tanabe.title: Which snapper has the black tail?
tanabe.intro: A Fiji list records tanabe for blacktail snapper. Regua is used for rivulated snapper in another identification; both are snappers, but the second word matters.

cards.question: Which local name is paired with blacktail snapper?
cards.answer: Tanabe is recorded for blacktail snapper; regua has a different snapper identification.

cards.question: If a catch is labelled only 'snapper', can you know from that label whether it is tanabe or kake?
cards.answer: The English family name covers several listed Fijian names. A closer identification is needed.

link.label: See the Fiji snapper list

ulavi.title: One name across many parrotfish
ulavi.intro: Ulavi is a general Fijian parrotfish name. Fiji reef research also describes local colour distinctions; ulurua names one particular parrotfish in a fish list.

cards.question: A reef survey says 'ulavi' without a species. Should you assume it must be the steephead parrotfish?
cards.answer: Ulavi can be broad; ulurua is the name attached to that particular parrotfish in the Fiji list.

cards.question: Why might parrotfish matter beyond the fishing catch?
cards.answer: Fiji reef research describes parrotfish grazing as one way reefs stay clear of excessive algae.

link.label: Read about parrotfish in Fiji reefs

ulurua.title: A particular parrotfish
ulurua.intro: Ulurua is listed as the steephead parrotfish. Ulavi can cover parrotfish more generally, so a specific fish name is useful when the species matters.

cards.question: Which is the more specific name in the Fiji fish list: ulurua or ulavi?
cards.answer: Ulurua is paired with steephead parrotfish; ulavi is a broader parrotfish name.

cards.question: Does every fish called ulavi have to be an ulurua?
cards.answer: A group name does not force every member to be the one particular fish named ulurua.

link.label: See the Fiji parrotfish list

vuvula.title: Two Fiji names for one tarpon
vuvula.intro: A Fiji fish appendix pairs vuvula and yavula with the same Indo-Pacific tarpon; it lists yavula in its river-fish section. Ulavi is a separate parrotfish name.

cards.question: A Fiji appendix pairs Vuvula/Yavula with one fish. Is that a tarpon or a parrotfish?
cards.answer: Both names are listed for Indo-Pacific tarpon; ulavi is a parrotfish name.

cards.question: The appendix places yavula among river fishes. Does that make the paired name vuvula a kind of reef emperor like kawago?
cards.answer: The appendix identifies one as tarpon and the other as spangled emperor. Their names and fish groups differ.

link.label: See tarpon in Fiji's fish-name appendix

bokola.title: A word from a difficult history
bokola.intro: Bokola has a specific historical sense connected with an enemy killed in war and intended for consumption. A Fiji account of Naililili discusses this past practice; mate is a wider word for death.

cards.question: Does bokola simply mean anyone who has died, as mate can in a wider context?
cards.answer: The historical meaning is much narrower and tied to violence and consumption. Do not replace a general death word with it.

cards.question: In the Naililili account, are bokola the war victims discussed, or the people telling the story?
cards.answer: The account uses the word while describing victims brought to Naililili. It is a historical account, not a model for casual address.

link.label: Read the Naililili historical account

ba ni ika.title: A fence made for fish
ba ni ika.intro: Ba ni ika is recorded in Wayan Fijian for a fish weir. Its barrier guides or traps fish as water moves; vuvu is a different, basket-like fish trap.

cards.question: If a fisher sets a barrier across a channel, is the recorded implement ba ni ika or vuvu?
cards.answer: The Wayan form names a fish weir; vuvu refers to a narrow basket trap.

cards.question: What does the ika in ba ni ika tell you the barrier is for?
cards.answer: Ika names fish. The full expression identifies a fishing barrier, rather than every fence called ba.

link.label: Explore the fish-weir comparison

ajibisovi.title: An office in a Fiji church letter
ajibisovi.intro: A bilingual letter from the Archdiocese of Suva uses Ajibisovi for Archbishop. It also uses Bisovi for the related bishop role and Ajidaiosisi for the wider church district.

cards.question: When the writer says noqu cakacaka vaka-Ajibisovi, is Ajibisovi the writer's personal name or an office?
cards.answer: The bilingual letter speaks of the writer's work as Archbishop. The term names a church role.

cards.question: The same letter uses both Ajibisovi and Bisovi. Would you erase the difference by translating both only as 'bishop'?
cards.answer: Ajibisovi is Archbishop in the letter; Bisovi is Bishop. The added title matters to the office being described.

link.label: Read the bilingual Archdiocese letter

vosa veiganiti.title: Choose words for the occasion
vosa veiganiti.intro: Vosa veiganiti concerns language fitted to a purpose or audience. A Fiji Year 13 exercise asks learners to consider the purpose and method of legal language, conversation, a public presentation and sports commentary.

cards.question: A learner is drafting a public legal explanation. Should the same register automatically fit a casual chat?
cards.answer: The worksheet treats legal language and conversation as different settings. Consider who is listening and why before choosing wording.

cards.question: In the worksheet, sports commentary is listed alongside conversation. What makes both relevant to vosa veiganiti?
options: Each has its own purpose and audience
cards.correct: Each has its own purpose and audience
cards.answer: The task is to match wording and delivery to the setting, not to memorise one style for every occasion.

link.label: Try the Fiji Year 13 register worksheet

mataqiriqiri.title: A group that makes music
mataqiriqiri.intro: Mataqiriqiri names a band or orchestra. Fiji writing uses it for named groups such as Spinning Wheels, while the surrounding text can distinguish the group from a singer.

cards.question: In an account of Lagani singing with Spinning Wheels, which one is called the mataqiriqiri?
cards.answer: The account names the accompanying band as mataqiriqiri and refers separately to Lagani's singing.

cards.question: If another report calls Makare Band a mataqiriqiri, does the word require only traditional instruments?
cards.answer: The attested use includes a named contemporary band. The word identifies the music group, not one fixed instrument or style.

link.label: Read mataqiriqiri in a Fiji music account

tabua.title: An object with a ceremonial role
tabua.intro: A tabua is a sperm whale tooth presented on significant occasions in Fiji. Its material and the reason for presenting it are both worth noticing.

cards.question: At a formal welcome, officials present a tabua. What is the object itself?
cards.answer: The Fiji Prime Minister's Office identifies the presented tabua as a whale tooth. The occasion explains its use; it does not change what the object is.

cards.question: A government account mentions tabua in a welcome, while another discusses their movement as cultural artefacts. Does 'tabua' by itself tell you the purpose of every presentation?
cards.answer: The same valued object can enter different occasions. Read the surrounding account to learn why it was presented.

link.label: See a Fiji state welcome involving tabua

kamunaga.title: The value of a presentation
kamunaga.intro: Kamunaga can refer to ceremonial valuables; a tabua is a prominent example. Fiji accounts place the presentation in particular relationships and occasions.

cards.question: In a Fiji speech, a tabua is presented as kamunaga. Is kamunaga the same as the English material label 'whale tooth'?
cards.answer: Tabua names the tooth. Kamunaga draws attention to a valuable presented within a ceremony; the terms are related but do different work.

cards.question: The same speech says a kamunaga was presented during a boka after a long absence. What helped explain that presentation?
cards.answer: The speaker connects the offering to return, thanks, and family ties. The occasion matters to what the presentation communicates.

link.label: Read a Fiji account of kamunaga and tabua

vakasisila.title: A word whose target matters
vakasisila.intro: Vakasisila can express disgust or disgrace. Fiji usage applies it to foul surroundings and also to conduct judged shameful.

cards.question: A resident describes sewage below a bridge as vakasisila. What is being judged there?
cards.answer: The report describes a polluted river setting. Vakasisila conveys the resident's strong revulsion.

cards.question: A separate Fiji report uses i tovo vakasisila about behaviour. Is the word limited to visibly dirty places?
cards.answer: It can also condemn conduct. The word beside it, such as tovo, tells you what is being judged.

link.label: Read vakasisila in a Fiji river report

daumaka.title: Good for what?
daumaka.intro: Daumaka takes its shade of 'good' from what follows. Fiji writing uses it for learning something worthwhile and for the quality of a service.

cards.question: In daumaka sara mo vulica, what is being encouraged?
cards.answer: The invitation is to learn something worth knowing. The following mo vulica makes the good action clear.

cards.question: A government health report discusses na daumaka ni noda veiqaravi. Is it praising one person's appearance or the quality of service?
cards.answer: The surrounding words ni noda veiqaravi make the service the thing being evaluated.

link.label: Read daumaka in a Fiji heritage learning context

bogi ni gone.title: A child’s head, not a time of day
bogi ni gone.intro: The recorded bogi ni gone is the soft area on a young child's head where the skull bones have yet to close. Bogi on its own can also mean 'night'; the whole phrase is essential here.

cards.question: Would translating bogi ni gone word by word as 'the child's night' identify the recorded body part?
cards.answer: The whole expression is used for a part of a young child's head. A separate sense of bogi alone means night.

cards.question: Why does the older description mention a young child rather than an adult?
options: The skull bones have not yet closed there
cards.correct: The skull bones have not yet closed there
cards.answer: The age matters to this anatomical meaning. Present-day local usage still needs a fluent-speaker check.

vakalevu.title: An effect of a form, not the form itself
vakalevu.intro: In the Tuvavosa description of repetition, vakalevu names an increased or intensified effect. Drua names the repetition pattern; the two labels answer different questions.

cards.question: If a repeated form conveys a stronger effect, which label names that effect: vakalevu or drua?
cards.answer: Vakalevu labels the increased force in this analysis. Drua is the word-shape process being examined.

cards.question: Can a repeated-looking word be called vakalevu without checking its base and use?
cards.answer: A repeated shape alone does not prove a live intensified meaning. Compare the word in a complete phrase before assigning the effect.

link.label: Read a Fijian grammar treatment of repetition

badamu.title: An eel in quieter water
badamu.intro: Fiji fisheries research identifies badamu with the Pacific short-finned eel. It tends toward still or marshy water, while the recorded diria and tautaubale favour faster streams.

cards.question: A Fiji freshwater eel is found in still, marshy water. Which recorded name is a better starting clue?
cards.answer: Badamu has the still-water association in the fishery profile; tautaubale is more associated with faster, upper river water.

cards.question: When mature badamu move down rivers toward the sea, have they become a different named reef fish?
cards.answer: The fishery profile describes a freshwater eel's life cycle: adults migrate seaward to spawn. Duna remains the broad local eel category.

link.label: Read the Fiji freshwater-eel profile

diria.title: A different river eel
diria.intro: Diria is recorded as the giant mottled eel. Fiji fisheries research distinguishes it from the short-finned badamu and records it in faster water.

cards.question: Which recorded eel name goes with the giant mottled eel rather than the Pacific short-finned eel?
cards.answer: The fisheries profile pairs diria with the giant mottled eel and badamu with the short-finned eel.

cards.question: A mature diria leaves a river and heads toward the sea. Does that movement make it a saltwater-only eel throughout its life?
cards.answer: These eels grow in rivers and later migrate seaward for spawning. The movement is part of a life cycle, not a different species name.

link.label: Compare Fiji's three freshwater eels

tautaubale.title: The eel of upper rivers
tautaubale.intro: Tautaubale is the Polynesian long-finned eel in Fiji's fisheries profile. It is associated with faster water and river headwaters.

cards.question: A report places an eel in upper, faster-flowing river water. Which of these recorded names fits that setting better?
cards.answer: Tautaubale is associated with headwaters; badamu tends toward still or marshy water. Habitat guides identification but does not replace looking at the fish.

cards.question: Do the names tautaubale and diria mean the same species merely because both prefer faster water?
cards.answer: The profile identifies tautaubale as a long-finned eel and diria as the giant mottled eel. Shared habitat does not erase that distinction.

link.label: See the Fiji eel names and habitats

keteleka.title: A mullet name that can change with size
keteleka.intro: In fisherwomen's recorded naming practice, keteleka can name a small mullet in a sequence that later uses other names as the fish grows.

cards.question: In the recorded size sequence keteleka, tumō, kanace, yawa, which name is used for the small fish?
cards.answer: Keteleka is the small stage in that reported sequence; kanace is used later for a larger fish.

cards.question: If a fish called keteleka grows, does the study suggest its local name must stay unchanged at every size?
cards.answer: The fisherwomen reported size-related names. This is a documented community naming pattern, not a rule to impose on every village.

link.label: Read the fisherwomen's naming study

moka.title: A trap built into the shore
moka.intro: A moka is a stone fish trap. At Vatulele on Koro, a community account describes a stone enclosure that fills at high tide and holds fish when the water falls.

cards.question: When the tide retreats from a stone enclosure, what can remain inside a moka?
cards.answer: The account describes fish entering at high tide and being enclosed as the tide falls. A vuvu is a different, narrow trap.

cards.question: The Vatulele account says four mataqali helped build the moka. Does that make it just a portable tool one person carries away after each catch?
cards.answer: This moka is a shore structure built through communal work. Keep that local account tied to Vatulele rather than assigning its history to every moka.

link.label: Read the Vatulele account of moka

vuvu.title: One spelling, several meanings
vuvu.intro: Vuvu can name a narrow bamboo fish trap in the recorded fishing sense. Other dictionary senses involve jealousy or muddy water, so a whole sentence is needed.

cards.question: A fisher sets a long narrow bamboo trap rather than a stone shore enclosure. Which recorded fishing word fits?
cards.answer: The historical fishing record uses vuvu for the narrow trap; moka is a stone enclosure working with the tide.

cards.question: If someone says vuvu in a conversation about envy, should you automatically picture the bamboo trap?
cards.answer: The same spelling has a separate jealousy sense. Let the surrounding sentence select the sense instead of joining the meanings together.

link.label: Explore the Oceanic history of the fish-trap word

dairo.title: A sea cucumber, not a finfish
dairo.intro: Dairo identifies the sandfish sea cucumber in a Fiji fisheries survey. The longer dairo kula is listed separately for golden sandfish.

cards.question: The Fiji survey identifies dairo as sandfish. Is that a sea cucumber or a finfish with scales?
cards.answer: The survey classifies dairo among sea cucumbers. The English trade name 'sandfish' can mislead if read as a finfish label.

cards.question: A field team records dairo kula separately. Should the word dairo alone force every specimen to be golden sandfish?
cards.answer: The survey distinguishes sandfish from golden sandfish. The extra word matters to that identification.

link.label: See dairo in the Fiji sea-cucumber survey

kake.title: A snapper name at two levels
kake.intro: A Fiji census fish list pairs kake with Russell's snapper; fisherwomen's research also records kake as a wider snapper name covering several species. The context decides how specific an identification is.

cards.question: In the Fiji census list, which fish is paired with kake: Russell's snapper or blacktail snapper?
cards.answer: The list pairs kake with Russell's snapper and tanabe with blacktail snapper.

cards.question: A fisherwoman's report groups three snapper species under kake. Can every use of kake then be assigned one exact scientific species without inspecting the fish?
cards.answer: The research records a broader local category. The census's narrower pairing is useful, but it does not settle every community use.

link.label: See fisherwomen's snapper naming research

novu.title: A stonefish on the reef
novu.intro: Fijian fisherwomen's research records novu as a reef stonefish. The same study reports it alongside a coral-banded shrimp, showing that a fish name also leads to a habitat story.

cards.question: Which fish does the study identify by the name novu?
cards.answer: Novu is recorded for the reef stonefish; keteleka is a mullet name in the same research setting.

cards.question: The report notes a shrimp near novu. Does that make novu a word for the shrimp?
cards.answer: The fish and shrimp are separate animals observed together. Association in a habitat is not identity.

link.label: Read the Fiji fisherwomen's reef observations

daniva.title: A named fish in two catches
daniva.intro: Fiji fisheries records list daniva among baitfish catches and also name it in a Rewa River survey. The catch tables distinguish daniva from sardines and anchovies.

cards.question: The baitfish table gives daniva and sardines separate rows. Should you combine them into one count?
cards.answer: The report records them separately, even though both are small fish used in baitfish fisheries.

cards.question: The Rewa River list includes daniva. Does that make the name a reef-only fish label?
cards.answer: The recorded Rewa catch is a reminder to check the local water and fish, rather than assume one habitat from a short English gloss.

link.label: See daniva in Fiji fisheries records

tovisi.title: The ribbonfish in a river survey
tovisi.intro: A Fiji fisheries survey names tovisi as ribbonfish among catches from the Rewa River. The same list records yavula as tarpon; these are different fish, despite appearing in one survey.

cards.question: In the Rewa River list, which recorded name is paired with ribbonfish?
cards.answer: Tovisi is the ribbonfish entry; yavula is the tarpon entry.

cards.question: Does appearing beside yavula in the survey make tovisi another name for tarpon?
cards.answer: A survey lists different catches together. It does not make their Fijian names interchangeable.

link.label: Compare the Rewa River fish list

yavula.title: A tarpon with two recorded names
yavula.intro: The Rewa River survey pairs yavula with tarpon. Another Fiji fish-name appendix gives vuvula and yavula together for the Indo-Pacific tarpon.

cards.question: Which other recorded Fijian name is paired with yavula for the Indo-Pacific tarpon?
cards.answer: The appendix pairs vuvula and yavula. Tovisi is listed separately as ribbonfish.

cards.question: If you find yavula in the Rewa River list, which English fish name does that list give?
cards.answer: The survey gives yavula as tarpon; the neighbouring tovisi entry is ribbonfish.

link.label: See the Rewa River survey

ogo.title: A barracuda name with narrower relatives
ogo.intro: The Fiji Agriculture Census lists ogo among barracuda names and gives ogobuidromo specifically for pickhandle barracuda. The wider name and the more precise name serve different purposes.

cards.question: A Fiji catch is labelled ogo. Which fish group does the census place it with?
cards.answer: The census groups ogo with barracuda. Its snapper list uses other names, such as kake.

cards.question: A record says ogobuidromo. Can you discard the extra part and still claim the exact pickhandle identification from ogo alone?
cards.answer: Ogobuidromo is listed specifically for pickhandle barracuda; ogo is also used as a broader barracuda label.

link.label: See barracuda names in Fiji's census list

bati-ni-siwa.title: The hook in a fishing line
bati-ni-siwa.intro: Bati ni siwa names a fish hook in a Fiji museum collection. A fishing account places the hook with wa ni siwa, the line; the two are connected but are not the same piece of gear.

cards.question: A museum object is labelled Bati ni Siwa. Is it the hook or the fishing line?
cards.answer: The museum label identifies it as a fish hook; wa ni siwa names the line.

cards.question: If a fisher replaces only the wa ni siwa, have they necessarily replaced the bati ni siwa too?
cards.answer: Line and hook work together but remain distinct parts of the fishing gear.

link.label: See a Fiji fish hook in the museum collection

wa ni siwa.title: The line, not the hook
wa ni siwa.intro: Wa ni siwa is a fishing line. A Fiji fishing account names it with bati ni siwa, the hook that can be attached to it.

cards.question: In the pair wa ni siwa and bati ni siwa, which one is the line?
cards.answer: Wa ni siwa is the line; bati ni siwa names the hook.

cards.question: If a museum display has only a bati ni siwa, does its label alone tell you what the whole fishing line was made from?
cards.answer: The hook is one piece of gear. The material and length of a particular wa ni siwa need their own evidence.

link.label: Read about hook and line in Fiji fishing

iqoliqoli.title: Fishing waters and community ties
iqoliqoli.intro: Iqoliqoli names a customary fishing area, with its boundaries and customary interests recorded in Fiji. It refers to waters associated with a community, not a single fish or one trip to catch it.

cards.question: A record maps an iqoliqoli boundary. Is it mapping a fishing area or naming one species of fish?
cards.answer: Fiji's records describe iqoliqoli boundaries and customary interests; ika is a fish.

cards.question: Someone says they will qoliva nearby waters. Is that action the same thing as the iqoliqoli area itself?
cards.answer: Qoliva describes fishing an area; iqoliqoli names an area with a customary relationship. One is an activity, the other a place and its community context.

link.label: Read about Fiji's recorded iqoliqoli boundaries

qoliva.title: Fishing a particular stretch
qoliva.intro: In a Fiji fisheries account, people 'qoliva na wai e tokaravita na nodra itikotiko': they fish the waters around their homes. Qoliva is the activity, while iqoliqoli names a customary fishing area.

cards.question: In 'qoliva na wai e tokaravita na nodra itikotiko', what is being fished?
cards.answer: Na wai is the waters being fished; the rest of the phrase locates them near people's homes.

cards.question: If a village identifies its iqoliqoli, have they merely used another word for the act of qoliva?
cards.answer: Iqoliqoli identifies customary fishing waters; qoliva describes fishing them. The community relationship matters to the first term.

link.label: Read qoliva in a Fiji fisheries account

qolua.title: A bamboo refuge used as a trap
qolua.intro: A Fiji freshwater fisheries profile describes qolua as hollow bamboo stalks set as a trap, mainly for eels. It differs from a moka, which is a stone enclosure on a tidal shore.

cards.question: A fisher places hollow bamboo stalks for eels. Which recorded trap is this?
cards.answer: The freshwater fisheries profile describes qolua with hollow bamboo; the documented moka is a stone shore trap.

cards.question: If a trap depends on fish entering a stone enclosure with the tide, should you call that the same gear as a bamboo qolua?
cards.answer: The materials and settings differ. The stone tidal enclosure is a moka, while the bamboo qolua mainly targets eels in freshwater fishing.

link.label: Read about Fiji river-fishing methods

tugadra.title: A fish that brought a village together
tugadra.intro: Tugadra is recorded as bigeye scad. A Cicia study describes villagers fishing together when tugadra appeared near Tarukua and then sharing the catch between households.

cards.question: In the Cicia account, what was spotted near Tarukua: tugadra or an eel called diria?
cards.answer: The account names tugadra; fish records identify it as bigeye scad, a schooling fish.

cards.question: After the Tarukua villagers caught tugadra, how was that particular catch used?
cards.answer: The account describes a collective fishing party and an equal share for households. It describes that event, not a rule for every tugadra catch.

link.label: Read the Cicia fishing account

guru.title: A group name with a local relationship
guru.intro: In Vanua Navakavu, guru is a broad name for damselfishes. Research also records a particular fish within that group as a clan fish totem there, so the group name alone does not identify that one species.

cards.question: If several damselfish species are called guru locally, does guru alone identify one exact scientific species?
cards.answer: The Vanua Navakavu study records guru as a broad group name. A closer identification needs the fish and local knowledge.

cards.question: A particular guru is important as a fish totem in Vanua Navakavu. Does that make every fish called guru the same totem species?
cards.answer: The research distinguishes the broader damselfish category from a particular species with a clan relationship. Ask locally before attaching that relationship to another fish.

link.label: Read the Vanua Navakavu fish-name study

tivitivi.title: One name across many reef fish
tivitivi.intro: Fijian fisher knowledge records tivitivi as a broad butterflyfish name. A fish list may apply it to several distinct species, whereas ulavi refers to parrotfish.

cards.question: A survey lists two different butterflyfish as tivitivi. Must they be the same scientific species?
cards.answer: A broad local name can cover more than one species; the survey lists several butterflyfish under tivitivi.

cards.question: If a fish is a parrotfish rather than a butterflyfish, which of these recorded names is the better clue?
cards.answer: The fisher-knowledge table puts ulavi with parrotfish and tivitivi with butterflyfish. Local identification still needs the fish and the speaker's usage.

link.label: See Fiji fisher knowledge of reef-fish groups

tabace.title: A surgeonfish name in Fiji surveys
tabace.intro: Fiji fisheries surveys record tabace among surgeonfish; one species list pairs it with the convict surgeonfish. Balagi is another surgeonfish name, so the family alone does not settle the local name.

cards.question: One Fiji species list pairs tabace with which fish: convict surgeonfish or a parrotfish?
cards.answer: The survey labels a convict surgeonfish tabace; ulavi is a parrotfish name.

cards.question: If two fish are both surgeonfish, may you automatically replace tabace with balagi?
cards.answer: The fisheries report lists tabace and balagi separately within the surgeonfish family. A shared family is not a licence to swap local fish names.

link.label: See Fiji's surgeonfish survey

ta.title: How specific is a unicornfish name?
ta.intro: A Fiji census list pairs ta with bluespine unicornfish, while FishBase records ta for several Naso species. The fish and the source matter when someone asks for an exact scientific identification.

cards.question: Which fish does the Fiji census list pair with ta?
cards.answer: That is the census pairing; tabace is used for convict surgeonfish in a separate fisheries survey.

cards.question: FishBase lists ta with several unicornfish species. Can the short name alone always settle which Naso species you saw?
cards.answer: The name has multiple recorded species pairings. Describe the actual fish or seek a knowledgeable local identification.

link.label: Compare recorded ta fish names

tunatuna.title: A conger, rather than a river eel
tunatuna.intro: FishBase records tunatuna for a conger eel. Fiji fisheries research lists diria among freshwater eels, so the two names should not be treated as interchangeable just because both fish are long and eel-shaped.

cards.question: A fish record identifies Conger cinereus. Which Fijian name is listed for it?
cards.answer: FishBase pairs tunatuna with the conger; Fiji's river-eel profile identifies diria differently.

cards.question: Does an eel-shaped body alone tell you whether to use tunatuna or diria?
cards.answer: One record concerns a conger and the other a freshwater eel. Check the fish and its setting instead of guessing from its shape.

link.label: See the recorded conger identification

dabea.title: A moray name with more than one match
dabea.intro: FishBase records dabea for two moray species in Fiji. Tunatuna is recorded for a conger eel; saying only 'eel' hides the distinction between those groups.

cards.question: FishBase pairs dabea with two Gymnothorax species. Are those morays or congers?
cards.answer: The two listed species are morays. Tunatuna is paired with a conger eel.

cards.question: Can dabea by itself guarantee one precise scientific species in the two Fiji FishBase records?
cards.answer: Two moray species are recorded with that name. A species label needs more evidence than the local name alone.

link.label: Compare Fiji's dabea records

davilai.title: A flatfish seen in Fiji records
davilai.intro: Fiji fish records use davilai for flatfish. FishBase pairs it with a flounder, while an older Fijian account describes the fish's flatness through a story; the story and biological identification answer different questions.

cards.question: When a Fiji fish list gives davilai as a flounder, which body plan should you expect?
cards.answer: Davilai is a flatfish name; a moray such as dabea belongs to another fish group.

cards.question: An older account tells why davilai became flat. Does that tale by itself establish the fish's scientific species?
cards.answer: The account preserves a story about the fish. Biological identification requires a specimen and a fish record; both kinds of knowledge can be read without confusing them.

link.label: Read the older davilai account

regua.title: When a fish name has different identifications
regua.intro: FishBase records regua for rivulated snapper in Fiji and also connects the same local name to sea chubs. A single English gloss cannot settle every use without a fish specimen and local context.

cards.question: One Fiji record pairs regua with Lutjanus rivulatus. What English fish group is that?
cards.answer: Lutjanus rivulatus is a snapper; kaboa is a catfish name.

cards.question: Another record places regua with sea chubs. Should the snapper pairing automatically override that other local use?
cards.answer: Both pairings appear in FishBase. Keep the identification tied to the fish, place and source rather than force one species on every regua.

link.label: Compare Fiji's regua records

bonu.title: Which eel did you see?
bonu.intro: Bonu appears with several eel species in Fiji fish records, from a freshwater eel to marine morays. A location or a more specific name helps narrow the identification.

cards.question: A Fiji fish list calls both a freshwater eel and several morays bonu. Does bonu alone tell you whether the fish came from a river or reef?
cards.answer: The recorded name spans both settings. Ask where the fish was found and what it looked like before settling on a species.

cards.question: The longer name bonu dadarikai is recorded for a particular freshwater moray. Does the added word provide more identification than bonu alone?
cards.answer: Bonu dadarikai names a recorded freshwater moray, while plain bonu is paired with several eels. The added name narrows the search but a specimen still matters.

link.label: See Fiji's recorded bonu names

kaboa.title: An eel-shaped fish that is a catfish
kaboa.intro: FishBase pairs kaboa with the striped eel catfish. Its eel-like outline is misleading: it is a catfish with barbels, and its fin spines can sting.

cards.question: A long fish has stripes and whisker-like barbels. Does the Fiji name kaboa lead to a catfish or a moray?
cards.answer: Kaboa is recorded for the striped eel catfish. Dabea is a moray name, although both fish can look eel-like at a glance.

cards.question: FishBase warns that this catfish has venomous fin spines. Is its eel-like body a safe reason to handle it like a harmless eel?
cards.answer: The striped eel catfish has venomous spines. Identification matters before anyone handles a fish.

link.label: See the striped eel catfish record

uluqa.title: A snapper with more than one English name
uluqa.intro: A Fiji fish list pairs uluqa with Paracaesio kusakarii. FishBase gives that species the English name saddleback snapper and also records Bedford.

cards.question: A fish list gives uluqa and ulavi. Which name is paired with the saddleback snapper?
cards.answer: Uluqa is paired with saddleback snapper; ulavi names a parrotfish. Similar openings do not make the fish the same.

cards.question: A seller calls an uluqa 'Bedford'. Must that be a different species from the saddleback snapper?
cards.answer: FishBase records Bedford and saddleback snapper for the same species paired with uluqa. English fish names can vary too.

link.label: Compare names for uluqa

vocivoci.title: Spot the pufferfish
vocivoci.intro: FishBase pairs vocivoci with the white-spotted puffer, Arothron hispidus. The recorded fish is poisonous to eat, so recognising the name has a practical safety point.

cards.question: A Fiji fish guide pairs vocivoci with a puffer marked by white spots. Which English name fits?
cards.answer: Vocivoci is recorded for a pufferfish; uluqa is paired with a saddleback snapper.

cards.question: If someone recognises vocivoci as a fish, does that mean it is safe to eat?
cards.answer: FishBase marks this puffer poisonous to eat. A fish name and an edible-fish label are different things.

link.label: See the vocivoci fish record

variivoce.title: One reef fish, several local names
variivoce.intro: NatureFiji identifies variivoce as the humphead wrasse and also records Draudrau and Dagava, the latter in Lau. Adult and young fish can look different.

cards.question: A speaker from Lau says Dagava. Could they be naming the fish also recorded as variivoce?
cards.answer: NatureFiji lists Dagava (Lau) among local names for the humphead wrasse. A regional name need not mean a different species.

cards.question: Would a young variivoce always show the prominent head hump of a large adult?
cards.answer: The hump develops with growth. Age and appearance matter when trying to match a local name to a fish.

link.label: Meet the humphead wrasse in Fiji

moci.title: Small prawns, important waters
moci.intro: A Fiji fisheries profile identifies moci as a mangrove prawn. Another community plan records moci among the resources people collect near mangroves and estuaries.

cards.question: If a community lists moci with mangrove resources, is it talking about small prawns or reef parrotfish?
cards.answer: Moci are prawns or shrimps; ulavi is a parrotfish name. The habitat gives another clue.

cards.question: The fisheries profile gives a female moci a maximum length of about 7 cm. Is this the same scale as the much larger banana prawn listed there?
cards.answer: The profile distinguishes the small mangrove prawn from larger commercial prawns. English 'prawn' alone hides that size difference.

link.label: Explore Fiji's prawn profiles

vavaba.title: Which kind of lobster?
vavaba.intro: Fiji fisheries material identifies vavaba as a slipper lobster, Parribacus caledonicus. Its broad, flattened shape differs from that of a spiny lobster.

cards.question: Would you expect a vavaba to have the broad flattened body of a slipper lobster or the long feelers of a spiny lobster?
cards.answer: Vavaba is a slipper lobster. 'Lobster' is a broad English label, so its body shape helps identify the group.

cards.question: A Fiji species list also calls Parribacus caledonicus ivinibola. Does this second recorded Fijian name necessarily mean a second species?
cards.answer: The Fiji Government lists vavaba and ivinibola for the same slipper-lobster species. Local naming and scientific identification answer different questions.

link.label: See Fiji's recorded slipper-lobster names

vevewai.title: A more particular ray name
vevewai.intro: FishBase records vevewai in Fiji for Mobula birostris, the giant oceanic manta ray. Vai is a broader ray or stingray name, so the two are not interchangeable labels for every ray.

cards.question: A fish record says vevewai and Mobula birostris. Which English identification fits?
cards.answer: Vevewai is paired with the giant oceanic manta; kaboa names a striped eel catfish.

cards.question: If someone says vai for a ray, can you conclude from that broad word alone that it was a vevewai?
cards.answer: Vai can refer to rays or stingrays generally. Vevewai has a particular recorded manta-ray pairing.

link.label: See the vevewai species record

rosi ni bogi.title: Follow the fish, not the English nickname
rosi ni bogi.intro: FishBase pairs Rosinibogi with Lutjanus malabaricus, the Malabar blood snapper. The species also has several English market names and changes habitat as it grows.

cards.question: A record calls a rosi ni bogi 'saddletail snapper'. Does that necessarily make it a different species from the Malabar blood snapper?
cards.answer: FishBase records both English names for Lutjanus malabaricus. Compare the species, rather than assuming every English market name denotes a different fish.

cards.question: Where would FishBase lead you to look for a larger adult: the shallow inshore water used by juveniles, or deeper water?
cards.answer: Its species profile says juveniles tend to occupy shallow inshore water while larger fish live deeper. Age changes where the fish may be found.

link.label: See the Malabar blood snapper profile

tidaloko.title: A fish on the mangrove mud
tidaloko.intro: A Fiji mangrove study records tidaloko, also written tiloko, for mudskippers seen on wet mud and mangrove roots. The setting helps distinguish them from fish seen only underwater.

cards.question: If you see a small fish moving over wet mud by mangrove roots, which recorded name fits: tidaloko or uluqa?
cards.answer: Tidaloko is a mudskipper name in the Fiji mangrove study. Uluqa is paired with a snapper.

cards.question: The same mangrove list gives tidaloko and tiloko. Should a reader automatically treat them as two different animal species?
cards.answer: The study records both forms for mudskipper. A spelling or local-name variation is not by itself a species difference.

link.label: Explore the Fiji mangrove species list

sarau.title: Look for the blue lines
sarau.intro: A University of the South Pacific fish guide identifies sarau, also listed as kake, with the blue-lined snapper. Its yellow body carries narrow blue lines.

cards.question: A yellow snapper has several thin blue lines along its side. Which recorded name fits: sarau or kaboa?
cards.answer: The Fiji guide pairs sarau with the blue-lined snapper. Kaboa is a striped eel catfish.

cards.question: If another list uses kake for that blue-lined snapper, does this alone prove a different species?
cards.answer: The USP guide lists sarau and kake together for the same blue-lined snapper. Check the actual fish and local usage before treating names as separate species.

link.label: See the USP Fiji fish guide

visako.title: Two herons near Fiji shores
visako.intro: A survey of Nasoata Island records visako as a mangrove heron and belo as a reef heron. Both can be near the coast, but the survey names different birds.

cards.question: In the Nasoata bird list, which Fijian name belongs to the mangrove heron?
cards.answer: The survey pairs visako with the mangrove heron, Butorides striatus; belo is paired with the reef heron, Egretta sacra.

cards.question: Would a bird seen on a coastal mudflat be identified as visako just because mangroves are nearby?
cards.answer: The Nasoata survey records several shore birds. Habitat narrows the search, but the bird's features are needed for identification.

link.label: Read the Nasoata Island bird survey

vai.title: A ray name that needs context
vai.intro: A Wainunu resource plan lists vai as a ray. FishBase also records longer Fiji names such as vai da for particular rays; the extra words can narrow an identification.

cards.question: A community lists vai among coastal resources. Is it referring to a ray or a reef snapper?
cards.answer: The Wainunu plan pairs vai with ray. A snapper such as uluqa belongs to a different fish group.

cards.question: FishBase records the longer name vai da for a round ribbontail ray. Does plain vai alone identify that one species?
cards.answer: The shorter name is broad. Vai da is a more particular recorded name; a confirmed species still needs a good look at the fish.

link.label: Read the Wainunu coastal-resource plan

itaraki.title: The net in two Fiji stories
itaraki.intro: A Fijian school passage places itaraki among the gear carried to a reef fishing trip. Another Fijian account lists it among ways people gathered balolo. It names a handheld net, not the catch itself.

cards.question: In a school passage, the group carries itaraki and siwa, while two men carry moto. Which item is the hand net?
cards.answer: Itaraki is the hand net. Moto is a spear in that passage; the three words describe different fishing gear.

cards.question: An account of collecting balolo lists a bucket, itaraki and even bare hands. Is itaraki the creature being collected or a tool used to collect it?
cards.answer: Balolo is the creature in that account. Itaraki is one of the gathering tools.

link.label: Read the reef-fishing school passage

carawabobota.title: A stage before soft ripeness
carawabobota.intro: A Fiji school text uses carawabobota for fruit that has gone beyond its earlier ripening stage but has not yet become soft and fully ripe. Its story applies the word to vudi.

cards.question: In the school story, carawabobota describes the vudi. Is the word naming the fruit's stage or a kind of fishing net?
cards.answer: The story describes vudi at a stage before soft ripeness. Itaraki, by contrast, is a hand net.

cards.question: The text contrasts carawabobota with dreucavu, fruit fully ripe. Would you use both terms for exactly the same stage?
cards.answer: Carawabobota is nearly ripe but not yet soft; dreucavu marks fruit that has ripened fully. A fruit can pass from one stage to the next.

link.label: Read the Fiji school word note

uga vule.title: The crab that comes back to shore
uga vule.intro: A University of the South Pacific report writes this name as ugavule and identifies the coconut crab. Adults live on land, while females release larvae into the sea.

cards.question: If you find an adult uga vule in coastal forest, is its presence on land surprising for this species?
cards.answer: The report describes adult coconut crabs sheltering and foraging on land. They still depend on the sea at the larval stage.

cards.question: Does the English name 'coconut crab' mean an uga vule eats only coconuts?
cards.answer: The Fiji report describes an omnivore that also eats other fruit, leaves and animals. A familiar name does not describe its whole diet.

link.label: Read Fiji's coconut-crab research

vosa vakavarada.title: When the setting changes the words
vosa vakavarada.intro: Vosa vakavarada is informal or slang language. A Fijian interpreter guide recommends plain, widely understood wording when accuracy across speakers matters.

cards.question: In a medical conversation through an interpreter, would the guide favour vosa vakavarada or clear everyday wording?
cards.answer: The guide warns against slang in that setting because it may obscure the intended message. That does not mean friends never use informal language.

cards.question: The guide lists uncommon terms, vosa vakavarada and idioms separately. Does calling something slang automatically make it an idiom?
cards.answer: They can all make interpretation harder, but slang and idioms are different kinds of expression. The context decides which description fits.

link.label: Read the Fijian interpreter guide

vosanisucu.title: A language a child grows into
vosanisucu.intro: Vosanisucu is a mother-tongue term. A Fijian school text places it beside vosanisusu while urging families and schools to help children keep speaking their own language.

cards.question: The school text says 'nona vosanisucu se vosanisusu'. Is it naming two ways to refer to a child's mother tongue, or two kinds of fishing gear?
cards.answer: The text uses se between the two names in a discussion of the child's language. Vosanisusu is another recorded form.

cards.question: If a child learns another language later at school, does vosanisucu automatically become the name of every language the child knows?
cards.answer: The term points to the language nurtured from early life. Someone may also learn and use other languages.

link.label: Read the school discussion of mother tongue

vosanisusu.title: Another way to name mother tongue
vosanisusu.intro: Vosanisusu is recorded alongside vosanisucu in a Fijian school discussion of a child's own language. The pair offers two names in the same context, rather than a rule that every child speaks just one language.

cards.question: When the school text joins vosanisucu se vosanisusu, what does se help the reader recognise?
cards.answer: The passage offers the two forms in the same mother-tongue discussion. It does not count languages or people.

cards.question: The passage asks adults to keep using a child's vosanisusu. Is its concern the child's language in daily life or only a word on a school list?
cards.answer: The text argues for continuing to speak and teach the language. The word carries a lived relationship, not just a vocabulary label.

link.label: Read the Fijian school passage

vosararaba.title: The shared language and a family's variety
vosararaba.intro: Vosararaba names general Fijian used across communities. Fijian educators also distinguish this shared variety from the forms children learn at home and in their own communities.

cards.question: If people from different districts use a shared Fijian variety, does vosararaba name that common form or one family's mother tongue?
cards.answer: General Fijian helps communication across communities. A family's vosanisucu or vosanisusu may preserve local words and forms alongside it.

cards.question: A speaker uses general Fijian at school and a local variety at home. Must one erase the other?
cards.answer: Fijian language educators call for children's home varieties to be taught even while a common variety is used. Knowing both can serve different conversations.

link.label: Read the Fiji discussion of common and home varieties

vosa vakaviti raraba.title: What VVR is meant to name
vosa vakaviti raraba.intro: Vosa VakaViti Raraba, or VVR, is the fuller name for a shared Fijian variety used across communities. The name leaves room to talk separately about local varieties and mother tongues.

cards.question: A worksheet asks for wording in Vosa VakaViti Raraba. Is it asking for a shared form or insisting on one family's local dialect?
cards.answer: The phrase names a common variety. Local varieties remain real and may use different words or patterns.
