cards.question: If a child knows VVR and also a home variety, are VVR and that child's vosanisucu automatically identical?
cards.answer: A shared form may overlap with the home language without replacing its local vocabulary. Ask which form is used in the family's own speech.

link.label: See Vosa VakaViti Raraba in a school worksheet

ka-.title: When a result is damaged
ka-.intro: Ka- appears in recorded forms such as kabasu, which describes something broken. The pattern is limited: a familiar prefix does not let us invent a new word from any base.

cards.question: An object has broken: which recorded form belongs to the ka- family, kabasu or tasere?
cards.answer: Kabasu names a broken result. Tasere is a different recorded form, used when something comes untied.

cards.question: Does ka- in kabasu by itself tell you who broke the object?
cards.answer: The form draws attention to the broken result. A whole sentence and its context are needed to identify any person who caused it.

link.label: Read a linguistic account of Fijian result forms

ta-.title: When an event happens without naming an actor
ta-.intro: Tasere describes something coming untied. This recorded ta- form can report what happened without saying who, if anyone, brought it about.

cards.question: In tasere, does the ta- form itself name the person who untied the thing?
cards.answer: The form reports the event or resulting state. Look at the whole phrase before deciding whether an actor is known.

cards.question: Kabasu and tasere both describe results. Which one is the recorded ta- form?
cards.answer: Tasere belongs with ta-. Kabasu belongs with ka-, a different limited pattern associated here with a damaged result.

link.label: Read about Fijian spontaneous forms

ca-.title: A sound in the word
ca-.intro: Cabolo and calidi are recorded ca- forms associated with sounds. One can describe a loud report; the other can describe a sharp click or detonation. The complete word and context tell you which sound is meant.

cards.question: A sudden loud report is described as cabolo. Does the ca- pattern point here to sound or to a place name?
cards.answer: The recorded example cabolo belongs to the sound-associated ca- family.

cards.question: Can ca- alone tell you whether the sound is the loud report of cabolo or the sharper click that calidi can describe?
cards.answer: The prefix alone does not identify an exact sound. The rest of the word and its context matter; ca- is not a free recipe for coining new sound words.

link.label: Read about the Fijian ca- family

tago-.title: Hear the word in beats
tago-.intro: In Fijian language teaching, a tago is a spoken syllable. A word can have a different number of letters and tago; the beat you hear is what matters here.

cards.question: Say vosa slowly as vo-sa. Does it have two tago or four?
cards.answer: Vo-sa has two spoken syllables, though vosa has four written letters.

cards.question: Say vinaka as vi-na-ka. With a short final vowel, which syllable normally carries the main stress?
cards.answer: The middle syllable is next to last. Fijian stress often falls there when the final syllable is short; long final vowels and other patterns need their own check.

link.label: Read the Fijian teaching handbook on syllables

cabarakuraku.title: When haste costs you the message
cabarakuraku.intro: Cabarakuraku is more than moving fast: the explanation recorded in Fijian includes failing to hear properly what was said to you. A Fiji writer brought this older word back to readers in a 2025 column.

cards.question: Someone walks quickly but listens carefully to an instruction. Is speed alone enough to show cabarakuraku?
cards.answer: The recorded explanation includes both quick movement and not hearing what was said properly. Speed by itself leaves out the important detail.

cards.question: The word appears in an older list discussed in a 2025 column. Does that prove every community uses it in everyday speech now?
cards.answer: A historical record establishes that the word was recorded, not how widely it is used today. A complete local example from a speaker would tell us more.

link.label: Read the Fiji Times discussion of older Fijian words

matailalai.title: Small details, close attention
matailalai.intro: Matailalai can point to fine detail. In a Fiji education notice, it qualifies itukutuku: the fuller information that readers can use to plan. A Fiji conservation plant list also uses it with leaves.

cards.question: A public notice promises itukutuku matailalai. Should you expect detailed information or just a list of tiny objects?
cards.answer: In that setting, matailalai is about the level of detail in the information, not the physical size of a thing.

cards.question: A plant list names drau ni danidani matailalai. Is the word qualifying written instructions or the leaves being described?
cards.answer: The same form appears in a different setting: a plant's leaves. Read the whole phrase before deciding whether fine detail is about text, workmanship or a visible feature.

link.label: See matailalai in a Fiji education notice

adi senitoa.title: A flower in the name of a festival
adi senitoa.intro: Adi Senitoa is used as a Fijian name for Fiji's Hibiscus Festival. A Fiji TV bilingual event list pairs the names; the senitoa flower also appears in Fiji's festival history.

cards.question: In Fiji TV's list of events it broadcast, Adi Senitoa is paired with which English event: the Hibiscus Festival or a rugby sevens tournament?
cards.answer: The bilingual list names the same public festival in Fijian and English. Rugby sevens appears as a separate event in that list.

cards.question: Does the senitoa in Adi Senitoa mean the festival has no connection to a real flower?
cards.answer: Senitoa also names hibiscus. A Pacific plant guide describes Fiji's hibiscus flower and a commemorative stamp celebrating the festival. The event name reaches beyond the plant itself.

link.label: See the Fiji TV bilingual event list

imasuti.title: Who hears the call?
imasuti.intro: An imasuti is the person named or addressed after an expressive call. In 'Isa na luvequ', the call is Isa and na luvequ identifies the child being addressed.

cards.question: In 'Isa na luvequ', which part identifies the person being addressed?
cards.answer: Isa is the expressive call; na luvequ points to the child. Together they show how the call can be directed to someone.

cards.question: Must an imasuti always be a personal name? Compare 'Sobo Setoki' with 'Isa na luvequ'.
cards.answer: The first example names Setoki; the second uses a relationship phrase, na luvequ. Both can identify whom the expressive call concerns.

link.label: Read a Fijian speaker's use of Isa na luvequ

vuveisoli.title: An action between participants
vuveisoli.intro: A vuveisoli is a vei- form that expresses an action between participants. Veiraici can describe people looking at one another; veibolebolei can involve challenging one another. The rest of the word matters as much as vei-.

cards.question: When a passage says 'e ratou sa veiraici', is it describing people looking at one another or a single person looking at a wall?
cards.answer: The context describes several people facing and looking at one another. The action is shared among participants.

cards.question: A historical account uses veibolebolei around warlike challenges. Does a vuveisoli have to be a friendly exchange?
cards.answer: Vei- can help express a two-way action, but the base and context tell us whether the participants are looking, challenging or doing something else.

link.label: See veibolebolei in a Fijian historical account

salanicagi.title: Follow the air
salanicagi.intro: Salanicagi names the passage that carries air on its way from the lungs toward the voice. A Fijian diagram of speech places it between yatevuso and the parts of the throat that shape sound.

cards.question: In the diagram of the voice, does air reach the salanicagi from the yatevuso or from the bati?
cards.answer: The yatevuso are the lungs. The air then travels along the salanicagi; bati are teeth, farther along in shaping some sounds.

cards.question: Does salanicagi name the air passage or the uanidomo that vibrate when someone speaks?
cards.answer: The diagram labels salanicagi as the route for air and uanidomo as the folds that can vibrate. Breathing supplies the air; vibration helps make the voiced sound.

link.label: See the Fijian diagram of the voice

rūrū.title: Listen to the r sound
rūrū.intro: Rūrū is recorded as a name for the trilled r sound. A linguistic account describes Fijian r as ranging from a brief tongue tap to a longer trill; it treats dr separately.

cards.question: Does every Fijian r have to be held for a long roll?
cards.answer: The pronunciation account describes a range from a short tap to a trill. Listen to the speaker and the whole word, rather than fixing one length for every r.

cards.question: When you see dr in a Fijian word, is it simply another way of writing the plain r sound?
cards.answer: The consonant account lists r and dr separately. The sound written dr has a nasal beginning, so the extra letter signals a real pronunciation difference.

link.label: Read the Fijian consonant account

burogo.title: Which beetle is meant?
burogo.intro: An older Fijian word list calls burogo a small beetle with an unpleasant smell. A later Fijian translation uses the word in an article about a dung beetle. Those descriptions do not establish one scientific species for every use.

cards.question: An older word list notes the smell of a burogo. Does that detail alone identify its scientific species?
cards.answer: Many beetles can have a noticeable smell. The older description does not give a species name, so a particular identification still needs local evidence.

cards.question: A Fijian article uses burogo for a dung beetle. Does that prove the older strong-smelling beetle and the article's dung beetle are one exact species?
cards.answer: The article is a translation about a dung beetle; the older list gives a different description. A shared Fijian label in these sources does not settle the insect's species.

link.label: See burogo in a Fijian article

māmada.title: A light sound, not a light load
māmada.intro: In a pronunciation guide, māmada describes a vowel said lightly. The unmarked mamada can describe something light in weight; read the setting before choosing a sense.

cards.question: If a teacher calls a vowel māmada, are they describing its sound or the weight of an object?
cards.answer: This is the pronunciation-guide use. Mamada in an everyday weight comparison is a different entry.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does the line over ā mean “say this lightly”?
cards.answer: The macron marks a long vowel. That spelling mark is a different matter from the guide’s description of how strongly a vowel is spoken.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read a study of Fijian vowel length

sovuniyame.title: Where is the tip?
sovuniyame.intro: A Fijian guide to speech sounds calls the tip of the tongue sovuniyame. It distinguishes this small part from batiniyame, the sides.

cards.question: A mouth diagram points to the very front of the tongue. Which label fits?
cards.answer: Sovuniyame labels the tip; batiniyame labels the sides.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A phonetic account calls the Fijian r a tongue-tip trill or tap. Which named part would you pay attention to while trying that sound?
cards.answer: The r account concerns a movement of the tongue tip. Listen to a speaker too: a short tap and a longer trill are both reported.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the Fijian consonant account

batiniyame.title: Find the tongue edge
batiniyame.intro: Batiniyame names the sides of the tongue in a Fijian guide to speech sounds. Sovuniyame names its tip.

cards.question: A speech diagram points to the sides of the tongue. Which label fits?
cards.answer: Batiniyame is the side of the tongue; sovuniyame points to the tip.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does batiniyame label the whole tongue, or a particular part of it?
cards.answer: It singles out the sides. Knowing that location helps when following a diagram of how a sound is formed.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read a Fijian body-parts list

cecelevu.title: What kind of ground?
cecelevu.intro: An older definition uses cecelevu for open ground without trees or bushes. Older Fijian Bible passages also use it for upland terrain, so the full range needs local checking.

cards.question: In the older open-ground sense, would a densely wooded patch be cecelevu?
cards.answer: The older description singles out land without trees or bushes.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A Bible passage uses vanua cecelevu near a mountain. Does that prove every cecelevu is both high and treeless?
cards.answer: It shows another historical setting for the word. A fuller local account is needed before treating height and lack of trees as one fixed definition.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See an older Fijian passage

ba via.title: A particular dalo
ba via.intro: Ba via names a taro variety, not every dalo.

cards.question: A grower calls one dalo ba via. Are they naming a variety or the whole taro crop?
cards.answer: Ba via identifies a named variety of dalo.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A report also calls Ba via Tusi Tusi in an Australian planting. Does that make the two names separate crops?
options: No, names for the same reported variety
cards.correct: No, names for the same reported variety
cards.answer: The report pairs the names for this variety. Local naming still needs context.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the taro variety report

babakau.title: Breakfast, or a house wall?
babakau.intro: The same spelling has been used for a fried food and for a wooden wall. The context decides.

cards.question: Someone buys babakau to eat with breakfast. Which sense is intended?
cards.answer: Here babakau is fried bread made from dough, sold as food.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Would the food sense alone tell you what babakau means in a description of a house?
cards.answer: No. The wall sense is separate and still needs its own checking. Read the whole phrase before choosing a meaning.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read a Fiji market account

babale.title: What is a babale?
babale.intro: Babale names a dolphin. Longer names can distinguish kinds of dolphin.

cards.question: Dolphins swim like fish. Is a babale a fish or a marine mammal?
cards.answer: A dolphin is a marine mammal; its life in the sea does not make it a fish.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Can the single word babale reliably identify one scientific dolphin species?
cards.answer: No. Fiji records use additional words with babale to distinguish particular dolphins. A species needs more than this broad name.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See Fiji’s species list

baca.title: A worm or bait?
baca.intro: Baca has two recorded senses. One names worms; another names bait placed on a hook or in a trap.

cards.question: You see baca ni qele in a word list. Is it an earthworm or a fishhook?
cards.answer: Baca ni qele names an earthworm. The added ni qele narrows the kind of baca.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A fisher puts baca on a hook. Which sense fits this scene?
cards.answer: Here baca is the bait. The worm and bait senses may meet in fishing, but they remain separate dictionary meanings.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See baca in a Fijian learning course

balabala sa.title: One fern, several names
balabala sa.intro: Balabala can cover tree ferns more widely. Balabala sa points to a traditionally named kind.

cards.question: Does balabala sa mean every fern in Fiji?
cards.answer: It is a named tree fern; balabala is a wider name in the accounts checked.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Can a historical plant name alone settle its modern scientific species?
cards.answer: No. The older identification and today’s botanical assignment still need comparison with a specimen. The name is useful even while the species is being checked.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Explore Fiji tree ferns

balaka.title: A palm with several species
balaka.intro: Balaka is a Fijian palm name that also gave its name to a botanical genus.

cards.question: If someone points to a balaka, are they pointing to a palm or a bamboo cane?
cards.answer: Balaka names a palm; bitu is bamboo.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does the name balaka alone identify one and only one scientific species?
cards.answer: No. Several Balaka species are recorded. A photographed example cannot identify every palm bearing the name.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See a Fiji conservation account of Balaka

bale, baleca.title: Falling, and falling onto
bale, baleca.intro: The two recorded forms direct attention differently: the fall itself and what the fall reaches.

cards.question: A tree falls. Which form can describe the fall without naming what it lands on?
cards.answer: Bale can describe falling from an upright position.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A phrase names the thing a falling tree strikes. Which form makes that target relevant?
cards.answer: Baleca is recorded when the thing fallen on or towards is named. A complete Fijian sentence is still needed for its role.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read a local use of bale about a tree

bali, balia.title: Kneading and the mixture
bali, balia.intro: These forms are recorded for working a soft food mixture by hand.

cards.question: A cook works soft dough by hand. Is that bali or a word for cutting it?
cards.answer: Bali can describe kneading a soft mixture.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: The recipe names the dough being kneaded. Which recorded form points to that named mixture?
cards.answer: Balia is used when the thing being kneaded is named. Keep the full recipe phrase in view.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See balia in a Fijian bread recipe

balu-na.title: A cheek and its ending
balu-na.intro: The old written form balu-na displays an attached ending associated with a possessor.

cards.question: On a face, what does balu name?
cards.answer: Balu is the fleshy side of the face. The longer written form shows an attached ending.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: In the recorded form balu-na, is -na a separate word placed before balu?
cards.answer: The form shows -na after balu. Its use in a full phrase still needs checking before we assign a grammatical role.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the historical Fijian word list

banuve.title: A growing insect
banuve.intro: Banuve is a caterpillar, the feeding stage before a moth or butterfly becomes an adult.

cards.question: A banuve eats a bean pod. Is the insect an adult moth or a caterpillar?
cards.answer: The Fiji pest guide describes a bean-pod borer caterpillar as one example of banuve.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does that bean-pod example prove every banuve is the same insect species?
cards.answer: No. Banuve is a wider word for caterpillars. A pest name may narrow it to one kind.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the Fiji pest guide

bari, baria.title: Nibbling at what?
bari, baria.intro: These recorded forms concern gnawing or nibbling.

cards.question: An animal takes little bites along an edge. Does bari suggest nibbling or carrying?
cards.answer: Bari is recorded for gnawing or nibbling, rather than carrying.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: When the phrase names what is being gnawed, which recorded form can include that target?
cards.answer: Baria can name the object of the nibbling. The particular sentence decides what was bitten.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the historical Fijian word list

basu, basuka.title: Break a thing, break a rule
basu, basuka.intro: The physical and figurative uses share a break-apart idea, but the object changes the scene.

cards.question: If a person basuka na lawa, is the thing broken a branch or a law?
cards.answer: A Fiji government statement uses basuka na lawa for breaking a law.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does that legal example mean basu has no physical breaking sense?
cards.answer: Historical sources also record breaking or forcing a physical thing apart. The phrase tells you which sense is intended.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

bati leka.title: A traditional guarding role
bati leka.intro: Bati leka is used for a traditional warrior or guard group, with duties that depend on the community.

cards.question: Is bati leka here a tooth or a traditional warrior role?
cards.answer: The full expression names people with a close guarding role, not the body part bati alone.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does one account of bati leka tell us the exact duties in every village?
cards.answer: No. Local relationships and responsibilities vary. Compare the related bati balavu term before treating the two as identical.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read a local account of bati leka

bati madramadra.title: A plant with bati in its name
bati madramadra.intro: Bati madramadra identifies a herb, Bidens pilosa, in a Fiji plant-medicine record.

cards.question: Would you look for this bati madramadra among plants or among teeth?
cards.answer: The whole name identifies a herb. A word inside a plant name does not turn it into a body part.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does the historical plant name itself tell you how to prepare a medicine safely?
cards.answer: No. A university thesis records the plant identification, but the older preparation claim has not been independently checked. The name and a treatment instruction are different kinds of information.

bati-ni-sucu.title: First teeth, later teeth
bati-ni-sucu.intro: A school passage uses bati ni sucu for a child’s first teeth. Spacing in the passage differs from this older lookup spelling.

cards.question: Are bati ni sucu a child’s first teeth or the teeth acquired in adulthood?
cards.answer: They are baby or milk teeth. The school passage gives the number as 20.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: The school text writes bati ni sucu with spaces. Should we assume the older hyphens prove a different body part?
cards.answer: No. The spacing varies in the sources; the first-teeth meaning is shared. Standard spelling still needs review.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the Fijian school passage

batibasaga.title: Which small creature?
batibasaga.intro: Batibasaga is recorded for a scorpion. Older sources also list other creatures under the same form.

cards.question: In the checked local report about a sting, what kind of creature is batibasaga?
cards.answer: The reported animal is a scorpion.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Can every old occurrence be assigned to the same scorpion species from the spelling alone?
cards.answer: No. A historical list also gives other animal uses. The animal and the setting need to be identified in each passage.

link.label: Read a Fiji report about scorpions

batikaciwa.title: A seasonal shorebird
batikaciwa.intro: Batikaciwa names the bar-tailed godwit, a migratory bird recorded in Fiji.

cards.question: Is the bird described as returning seasonally or staying at one Fiji site all year?
cards.answer: A Pacific seasonal calendar records its return to Fiji in September.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Does a matching spelling in an older list of landforms prove every batikaciwa is this bird?
cards.answer: No. The bird and cliff-edge senses are separate. Read the context before choosing one.

batiri.title: Which kind of coast?
batiri.intro: Batiri points to a mangrove shore; baravi can point to a more open coast or beach.

cards.question: A place is lined with mangroves. Is batiri or baravi the more specific name?
cards.answer: Batiri identifies a mangrove shore in the accounts checked.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: If you move from mangrove roots to an open beach, would batiri still describe the same shore type?
cards.answer: No. The contrast with baravi helps locate the kind of coastline; local place names may have their own uses.

bau vudi.title: A tree name, more than one species
bau vudi.intro: Botanical surveys apply bau vudi to more than one Palaquium tree.

cards.question: Is bau vudi the name of a tree or a particular taro variety?
cards.answer: The botanical surveys list Palaquium trees under bau vudi.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Can the name alone give every bau vudi tree one scientific species?
cards.answer: No. Several Palaquium species are listed with this Fijian name. A specimen needs closer identification.

bavelo.title: Which canoe?
bavelo.intro: A bavelo is recorded as a small single-log canoe without an outrigger.

cards.question: Would an outrigger be part of the traditional bavelo described in the older dictionary?
cards.answer: No. The recorded form is dug from one log without an outrigger.

cards.question: A local account mentions paddling a bavelo. Does that prove every modern bavelo must be made from one exact timber?

beli.title: A fish on the banknote
beli.intro: Beli names a freshwater goby. Fiji’s $10 note depicts one identified as Lever’s goby.

cards.question: Where does the banknote’s beli live: a fast freshwater stream or a coral reef?
cards.answer: The Reserve Bank places the fish in fast-running freshwater.

cards.question: Is the $10-note identification enough to prove every fish called beli has the same life cycle?
cards.answer: No. Sources disagree about life history. The banknote identifies one beli as Lever’s goby; local fish identification still matters.

belo.title: From reef to inland stream
belo.intro: Belo is the reef heron Egretta sacra in a Fiji bird list.

cards.question: Would you expect a belo only at the ocean reef?
cards.answer: NatureFiji also records this heron by inland streams.

cards.question: Does the English name “reef heron” mean the bird can never forage in a forest stream?

bici.title: Meet a banded rail
bici.intro: Bici is the banded rail in a Malolo Island bird list.

cards.question: Is the bici on the Malolo list a rail or a reef heron?

cards.question: Does an old claim of extinction on the main islands prove you cannot see a bici anywhere in Fiji today?

liliwa.title: Cold in the weather
liliwa.intro: Draki liliwa is an attested phrase for cold weather.

cards.question: In draki liliwa, is liliwa describing cold or wind?
cards.answer: It describes the temperature of the weather.

cards.question: If the same word appears outside a weather report, should we assume draki is always present?

tubu.title: Growth in two settings
tubu.intro: Tubu can describe a plant growing or a number increasing.

cards.question: Mangroves have grown quickly. Does tubu describe growth or cutting?
cards.answer: In the founder-approved mangrove sentence, tubu describes the trees growing.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: A report uses tubu for a rising count. Must the thing increasing be a plant?
cards.answer: No. The growth idea also applies to numbers; the phrase tells you what is increasing.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: See tubu in a Fiji government report

vuca.title: What has decayed?
vuca.intro: Vuca can describe something rotten or decaying, including a crop affected by prolonged wet weather.

cards.question: After long heavy rain, a crop becomes vuca. Is it thriving or decaying?
cards.answer: The Fijian weather advisory uses the word for plants at risk of rot.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

cards.question: Would a bare vuca tell you which plant has rotted?
cards.answer: No. The surrounding phrase names the plant or material. A second historical Vuca record remains under review.
cards.incorrectHint: Read the word and the scene again.

link.label: Read the Fiji weather advisory

boutoka.title: What holds up the ridge?
boutoka.intro: A boutoka is a main upright above a cross beam. It carries the ridge at the top of the roof; the field study writes the name bou toka.

cards.question: Which timber does the boutoka help support?
cards.answer: The main upright carries the ridgepole, called doka.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: If the icoka is the cross beam, where does the boutoka stand in relation to it?
cards.answer: The main upright is placed on top of the cross beam in the recorded build.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

icoka.title: Follow a beam across the house
icoka.intro: Icoka is a cross beam. The same term is written i coka in the Cautata building study.

cards.question: Does an icoka run across the frame or along the very top ridge?
cards.answer: The top ridge is the doka; icoka names a cross or tie beam.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: In the recorded build, what is set on the cross beams after they are fixed?
cards.answer: The main roof uprights are placed above the cross beams.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

icavai.title: Read the layers of the roof
icavai.intro: Icavai is an upper purlin: a lengthwise timber fixed across the roof rafters. The field study writes i cavai.

cards.question: What is fitted first in the recorded building sequence?
cards.answer: The rafters are placed before the purlins are fixed over them.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: The study distinguishes icavai from bolo. Which sits higher in its list of roof purlins?
cards.answer: Icavai is the upper purlin; bolo is the middle purlin.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

latu.title: Look at the wall frame
latu.intro: Latu names an additional upright along the wall. It is not the main post carrying the roof ridge.

cards.question: Where does the Viti diagram point when it labels latu?
cards.answer: The label points to an upright in the wall frame.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: Which named part carries the ridge above a cross beam in the recorded build?
cards.answer: Boutoka is a main upright; latu is an additional wall upright.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

bolo.title: A word in the roof frame
bolo.intro: In this house-building sense, bolo is a middle purlin. The same spelling has other meanings, so the setting matters.

cards.question: In the house diagram, is bolo a roof timber or a wall post?
cards.answer: Here it names a purlin running through the middle part of the roof.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: Compared with icavai, where is bolo listed in the study?
cards.answer: The study calls icavai the upper purlin and bolo the middle purlin.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

kautabu.title: Find the top of the wall
kautabu.intro: Kautabu is a timber along the top of a house wall. The field study writes kau tabu and calls it a wall plate.

cards.question: Does the kautabu sit along the top of the wall or at the roof ridge?
options: Along the top of the wall
cards.correct: Along the top of the wall
cards.answer: The ridgepole is doka. Kautabu runs along the wall top.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

cards.question: In the recorded construction sequence, what goes in first?
cards.answer: The builders set the posts first, then fitted wall plates to their tops.
cards.incorrectHint: Compare where each timber sits in the house frame.

link.label: Explore this part in the Vale Vakaviti lesson

cawaki.title: The sea urchin on the menu
cawaki.intro: Cawaki is an edible sea urchin found in Fiji. A USP study identifies it as Tripneustes gratilla and discusses the edible roe.

cards.question: Which part of the cawaki is harvested for food in the USP study?
cards.answer: The roe is the edible part discussed in the study.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Both cawaki and nama come from the sea. Which one is an animal?
cards.answer: Cawaki is a sea urchin; nama is an edible seaweed.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the Fiji sea-urchin study

kai koso.title: An ark shell, not a sea snail
kai koso.intro: A Fiji marine inventory pairs kai koso with the ark shell Anadara cornea.

cards.question: A field list records kai koso. Would you look among bivalve shells or sea urchins?
cards.answer: The recorded identification is an ark shell, a bivalve.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Madrali is also collected for food. Which name points to the ark shell rather than a marine snail?
cards.answer: The inventory identifies kai koso as an ark shell and madrali as a nerite snail.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the Fiji marine inventory

madrali.title: A polished little shell
madrali.intro: Madrali is recorded as Nerita polita, a small marine snail with a smooth shell.

cards.question: A shell is smooth and polished. Which recorded name fits the nerite snail?
cards.answer: Madrali is paired with Nerita polita; kai koso is an ark shell.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Are madrali and sigawale the same kind of shellfish?
cards.answer: Madrali is a nerite snail. Sigawale is recorded as a surf clam.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the Fiji marine inventory

mana.title: Mana in the mangroves
mana.intro: In this food sense, mana is the mud lobster Thalassina anomala. Keep it apart from other uses of the same spelling.

cards.question: Where would you look for the mud lobster called mana?
cards.answer: This recorded mana is a mangrove mud lobster.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Which of these seafood names belongs to a crustacean rather than a seaweed?
cards.answer: Mana names a mud lobster in this sense; nama is sea grapes.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the Fiji fisheries report

nama.title: Sea grapes without a vine
nama.intro: Nama is an edible Caulerpa seaweed. One common Fiji species is Caulerpa racemosa.

cards.question: Are the “grapes” in sea grapes fruit from a vine?
options: Yes, they grow on a vine
cards.answer: The grape-like beads belong to an edible seaweed.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Does finding the name nama alone prove every sample is the single species C. racemosa?
cards.answer: C. racemosa is a common recorded species; the wider food name needs a specimen to settle exact species.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the USP sea-grapes study

sigawale.title: A clam from the sand
sigawale.intro: Sigawale is an edible surf clam from sandy shallows. Atactodea striata is one recorded species.

cards.question: Which setting fits the surf clam called sigawale?
cards.answer: The recorded surf clam lives in sand; mana is the mangrove mud lobster.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

cards.question: Can one recorded scientific species identify every sigawale someone collects?
cards.answer: The inventory records Atactodea striata, but the common name alone does not settle every specimen.
cards.incorrectHint: Look at where it lives and what kind of organism it is.

link.label: Read the Fiji marine inventory
